chapters.title: Chapter 1001
paragraphs: We ended up traveling with the Zhongnan Sect almost before I knew it.
Their Sect Leader, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, proposed it, and while I was still thinking it over, Jeok Cheongang cut in and accepted.
“Traveling together? That wouldn’t be a bad idea.”
“Old—no, Master.”
“What are you standing around for? Get your subordinates ready. And you too, Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord—start by kicking those lazy disciples of yours in the ass.”
Just like that, the preparations were over.
Our party, now a little over a thousand if I rounded generously, set off toward Gansu. The Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword came along too, neither looking pleased about it.
“Those two have looked downright miserable for a while now. If we’d met them exactly six months earlier, I’d have punched them in the jaw first thing.”
Jeok Cheongang smacked his lips. I clicked my tongue.
“If you didn’t want to look at them, you shouldn’t have accepted.”
“Is that why your lips are sticking out three inches?”
“Who says my lips are sticking out?”
“Correction. They’re sticking out four inches now.”
I shook my head at his teasing.
We’d taken the rear, a good thirty jang behind the Zhongnan Sect. Being far enough away to talk openly was about the only advantage I could see.
“Yes, I’m annoyed. Happy?”
“I can never quite figure you out. Why make up with them if it was only for show?”
Only for show.
I couldn’t have put it better myself.
I’d already guessed Jeok Cheongang had heard everything we’d said through Sound Transmission, so I answered without surprise.
“Well, obviously...”
“Because you need to?”
“Yes.”
“You make peace because you need to, and smile as if the old grudges are behind you... You’ve grown up.”
There was something odd about his tone.
I couldn’t tell whether that was praise or a rebuke. When I stared at him without answering, he gave a quiet laugh.
“Don’t overthink it. I’m glad to see you’ve grown, whichever direction it may be in.”
“Do you think it might be the wrong direction?”
“Who knows? What matters is the outcome.”
“Don’t people usually say the process matters just as much? Sometimes more?”
“The first is what narrow-minded fools say. The second is bullshit from people who’ve thoroughly botched the outcome.”
Jeok Cheongang answered with cutting certainty, then went on.

“If I thought you’d done wrong, I’d have given you a proper scolding. So far, though, you haven’t done too badly. Besides, driving those lazy bastards all the way to Gansu like cattle has its appeal.”
He wasn’t wrong. Even now, the Zhongnan Sect Disciples were running their asses off, thanks to the declaration Jeok Cheongang had made before we set out and he’d claimed the rear for himself.
“From now until we reach Gansu, anyone who falls even a little behind or tries to slack off gets a private meeting with this old man.”

A private lesson with an elder who’d reached a distant realm would be a fortuitous encounter anyone would pray for—unless the teacher was the Fire King. In that case, there was a good chance you’d become a dead man.
Whoosh, whoosh, whoosh!
Have you ever seen hyenas racing for their lives along a mountainside? Or rather, Zhongnan Sect Disciples?
I have.
Jeok Cheongang watched them sprint with every last bit of strength they had, looking thoroughly satisfied. Then he suddenly kicked off the ground.
Boom! Whoooosh!
A sharp boom rang out. His figure shot forward, leaving an afterimage behind.
Jeok Cheongang’s afterimage seemed to remain behind as he rapidly closed in. The Zhongnan Sect Disciples sucked in their breath, and panicked shouts rang out among them.
“Run!”
“If he catches us, we’re finished!”
“S-Senior Brother, I can’t go on. Don’t worry about this useless Junior Brother. Just go...”
“No! Don’t give up! You can make it!”
My thoughts on the scene were brief.
You’re all making a damn spectacle of yourselves.
“Anyone would think Dark Heaven had shown up or someth—huh?”
I was clicking my tongue at the Zhongnan Sect Disciples fleeing like locusts from a wildfire when I spotted something and narrowed my eyes.
Then I understood why Jeok Cheongang had suddenly sped ahead.
What’s that?

We had come out of the narrow mountain path, and a hill opened up the view ahead. In the distance stood a small village, its hundred or so thatched cottages huddled together. A crowd had gathered around it.
There had to be several hundred people.
Hyuk Mujin spotted the crowd at the village entrance a moment after I did. His eyes widened.
“Captain. Could that be...”
I could hear the urgency in his voice. Before he could finish, I said, “Don’t panic. They don’t look like enemies.”
“Huh? Then...”
“They’re all civilians.”
I thought for a moment and added, “At least, from what I can see.”

I wasn’t completely sure. Judging by our route, we were somewhere on the border between Shaanxi and Gansu. Dark Heaven had the dark art known as the Moving Formation, so running into its people disguised as civilians here wouldn’t be all that surprising.
They’d already disguised themselves as government troops in Sichuan once.
If something had happened in Gansu, word would’ve reached us by now. So what are that many people doing in a tiny mountain village? Is Dark Heaven preparing an ambush with a Moving Formation?
One question led to another.
Then, all of a sudden, I heard a chilling sound.
Shing.
At the sudden sound of a blade being drawn, I turned. Sama Pyo had drawn the Black Dragon Saber, the weapon that shared its name with his sobriquet.
“Whoever they are, it won’t hurt to be prepared. Wouldn’t you agree, Pavilion Master?”
His voice was calm, but his eyes were dark and intent. The closer we’d come to Gansu, the more somber Sama Pyo had grown.
I nodded and urged my horse on.
Thud, thud, thud, thud!
My grassland horse’s hooves pounded the ground.
I didn’t know who the people ahead of us were, but I was sure of one thing.
Even if Dark Heaven prepared an ambush, all we have to do is trample them and keep going.
We might be riding into a fierce battle. My heartbeat didn’t change.
I’d grown far too strong to be stopped in a mountain valley like this.
In the end, the disaster I’d feared never happened.
No. Let me correct that.
It never happened to our side.
“They’re here! Those bastards are here!”
“Aaaah!”
“E-Everyone, get out of the way!”

The shouts and screams were only natural. Close to a thousand suspicious people had come pouring over the steep hill like water through a broken embankment, and some already had blades in their hands.
To the hundreds gathered at the little village entrance, it must have looked like a catastrophe.
Their terror was impossible to fake. The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, racing at the front alongside Jeok Cheongang, shouted like thunder.
“Enough! Everyone, stop!”
Whoosh!
It was an order from the Sect Leader himself. His voice carried internal energy, and the Zhongnan Sect Disciples quickly slowed to a halt.
But there are always exceptions.
Whoosh.
A faint sound of air being cut, distinct from the rest.

Two figures kept shooting forward like the wind, ignoring the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s command. I’d been slowing with the Zhongnan Sect Disciples, but at the sight of their backs, I clicked my tongue to myself.
Yeah. I had a feeling they’d do that.
Old habits die hard.
The Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword.
Sect Leader or not, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord was their Junior Brother. Those two old dogs ignored his order and kept going.
I kicked off the ground after them.
Whoosh!
A gale wrapped around me as I crossed dozens of jang in an instant. The two old Daoists drew closer. So did the civilians’ screams.
Then a voice reached every ear, including mine.
“Stop.”
It was quiet—not a forceful shout, and it carried no particular internal energy.
One word was enough to stop the Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword in their tracks. More important than the word itself was the man who’d said it.
“Are you deaf? Those ears don’t seem much use. Want me to rip one off?”
The Roaring Fury Swordsman had stopped only a few steps away from a civilian who stood frozen with his eyes squeezed shut. His face stiff, he began to speak.
“Senior, I was only trying to make sure...”
“Answer the question. Should I rip it off or not?”
“I thought you were just deaf, but now it seems your mouth’s sealed shut too. Fine. You answer for your ailing Senior Brother.”
Fire flickered in Jeok Cheongang’s eyes. The Taeeul Merciless Sword met his gaze and bowed his head slightly.
“I only wanted to confirm who they were. I had no other intention. If my rash action upset you, Great Hero Jeok...”
“You didn’t upset me. You just made an even bigger mess.”
“I apologize.”
“At least one of you has a working mouth.”
Jeok Cheongang frowned at him and let out a small sigh.
“Save your apologies for the people you scared half to death.”
He was right. Unlike the few who’d been quick enough to flee, the civilians still standing there were trembling. One man who looked somewhat less shaken than the others hurriedly waved his hands.
“Oh, it’s all right, sir. It happened so suddenly that we were startled, but...”
He glanced at the Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword, letting the sentence trail off, then looked at Jeok Cheongang and me.
“Y-You’re from the Murim Alliance, aren’t you? The heroes?”
Calling ourselves heroes after the commotion we’d caused was embarrassing, but I nodded. The man relaxed, and so did the civilians around him.
“Good grief. That took ten years off my life.”
“The Murim Alliance... Isn’t that the group fighting those wicked foreign invaders?”
“That’s right. There’s been a little misunderstanding.”
“Damn it. I thought we were going to die.”
Sighs of relief rose all around us. The first man’s face brightened, and he spoke again.

“To think you’re the Murim Alliance heroes we’ve heard so much about! What a relief. When we saw a bunch of strange fellows coming, we thought you were them... Oh, listen to me. Calling you strange fellows!”
He hurriedly clapped a hand over his mouth, but neither Jeok Cheongang nor I cared about the slip. We had looked strange enough, and he’d said something far more important.
“Who did you think they were?”
The man answered without hesitation.
“Who else? That vicious gang of mounted bandits.”
What?

chapters.title: Chapter 1002
paragraphs: “Who else would it be? Those vicious mounted bandits.”
The moment I heard the man’s answer, Jeok Cheongang and I looked at each other.
And for good reason. Mounted bandits were the last people I’d expected to hear about now.
Mounted bandits.
Just what the name said: bandits on horseback.

Just as the Yangtze River Channel League had strongholds along every branch of the Yangtze, and the Green Forest Alliance had mountain strongholds on every mountainside with a road, mounted bandits could be found wherever broad plateaus and plains stretched out.
Pung Yang’s Red Wind Band had been one of them.
The vast northern Great Steppe wasn’t home to nomads alone.
It was a refuge for all kinds of people who’d crossed the Great Wall—and their only sanctuary.
For those who could never return to the lives they’d left behind, there were two choices.
Eat or be eaten.
Naturally, most chose the former.
It was a hundred, a thousand times better to survive as a predator than become prey.
Pung Yang had probably followed the same path.
I had no idea how he’d obtained a Temporary Strength Pill or learned demonic martial arts worthy of being called a secret technique, but he’d made quite a name for himself as a predator.
He’d even had the nerve to lead hundreds of subordinates across the Great Wall.
In the end, though, Pung Yang and the Red Wind Band had met their end at the Mount Heng Sword Sect.
However large they grew, they were still bandits.
Even in Shanxi Province, dismissed as a backwater compared with the Central Plains, there were clear limits to what a band of mounted bandits could do.
And now mounted bandits are hanging around here? Right on the border between Gansu and Shaanxi?
Even the craziest bastards knew to check whether they had somewhere to lie down before stretching out their legs.
With the Kongtong Sect and the Black Dragon Demon Gate standing firm in Gansu, and Huashan and the Zhongnan Sect in Shaanxi, it made no sense for mounted bandits to swagger around here.
Something’s going on. It has to be.
Jeok Cheongang must have been thinking the same thing.
He was frowning in thought, so I spoke to the man.
“Could you tell us more about them?”
“You mean the mounted bandits?”
“Yes. Their exact location and numbers, if you know them. If not, even a rumor would help.”
The man had been blinking at us in silence, apparently picking up on the serious mood. Then he spoke.
“How much will you pay?”
“What?”
“Four silver nyang. That should be enough.”
What was this guy’s deal all of a sudden?
Before I could answer, the man scratched his cheek awkwardly.
Or rather, he pretended to scratch it while tracing letters on his cheek.
The name of someone who wasn’t here—but whom I could never forget.
Wol...hwa. Wait. Wolhwa?
I finally understood. My mouth fell open as the man—or rather, the Lower District Sect member—winked at me.
“You seem to be in a hurry. Why don’t we talk on the way?”
I’d almost forgotten.
The Lower District Sect’s eyes and ears were everywhere.
I let out a quiet laugh at his shameless act, as though nothing had happened, then called out.
“Mujin.”
Hyuk Mujin came hurrying over and answered at once.
“Yes, Captain. What do you need?”
“Give this gentleman four silver nyang—no, ten. And provide him with a horse.”
I was turning away after delivering the order when Hyuk Mujin’s muttering reached my ears.
“You could at least toss me a money pouch before saying that. And if you give him a horse, what am I supposed to ride?”
“...Ahem.”
“See? You heard me, but you’re pretending you didn’t. I’m so fed up, I ought to just quit—”
“Ahem!”
“Uh, what is it? Did you have another order for me?”
Hyuk Mujin’s eyes went wide and innocent, as if he’d never said a thing. I gave him a cold look and tossed him the money pouch I’d just taken out of my Inventory.
“Oh my, you really shouldn’t have. You could just deduct whatever you spend from my monthly pay, and if it’s not enough, I could ask my family for more. Or beg.”
“I’m... sorry.”
“What do you have to apologize for, Captain? Even if the pillars of the Hyuk Family Textile Shop start shaking, that’s my problem. Right?”
“I get it. Just stop already. That should cover it, right?”
“What about the horse?”
“If you give away the horse too, what am I supposed to ride? Are my dead ancestors going to carry me?”
Out of answers, I quietly turned my head toward a nearby Zhongnan Sect Disciple.
More specifically, toward the fine horse he was riding.
After that whirlwind of shakedowns, we got an outcome everyone could be satisfied with and set off toward Gansu Province again.
Of course, one Zhongnan Sect Disciple had to climb down from his comfortable saddle and travel on his own two sturdy legs. But that wasn’t my problem.
What mattered to me was the information the Lower District Sect member had.
“You should all stay around here for the time being. No—better not stay anywhere near here. Head toward Shaanxi. Those vicious mounted bandits could attack at any moment.”

The Lower District Sect member repeated his warnings to the civilians who remained, then mounted his horse. The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord left a dozen or so Disciples behind to lead them safely to Shaanxi if danger arose.
As soon as we set off, the Lower District Sect member’s first words were enough to leave everyone feeling as if they’d been smacked in the back of the head.
“To be honest, there are no mounted bandits.”
After a brief silence, Hyuk Mujin fingered the hilt of the sword at his waist.
“Ten silver nyang. Spit it back out while I’m still asking nicely.”
“Enough! Hold your tongue! Threatening an ally—how are you any different from those demonic, heterodox villains?”
Jeok Cheongang sternly rebuked Hyuk Mujin, then turned to the frightened Lower District Sect member and spoke with unusual kindness.
“Don’t mind that fool. Go on. Ten silver nyang is a small price to pay for your fare to the afterlife.”
God, he’s terrifying.
Just from listening to them, you’d think we were the Demonic Path Alliance, not the Murim Alliance.
The Lower District Sect member, who didn’t seem to have a shred of internal energy, had gone pale under the pressure. He stammered out an explanation.
“To be precise, there were mounted bandits, but they’ve disappeared.”
“Oh? They were there, and now they’re gone.”
Jeok Cheongang let out an appreciative sound and smiled kindly.
“That makes perfect sense, given the situation. You’ll soon disappear from this world, too.”
“Eek!”
“I’ll take back nine silver nyang. You can keep one for the trip.”
“Gah!”
“Enough, all of you!”
Only after I stepped in did tempers, boiling like a cauldron over a charcoal fire, finally settle down. The poor Lower District Sect member hurriedly explained the details.
“So the mounted bandits in Ningxia Province really have started acting strangely?”
“Y-Yes.”
“Then all those people gathered in the village...”
“I deliberately spread an exaggerated rumor. Trouble is about to break out in the western region, so we wanted to keep the civilians from getting caught up in it as much as possible.”
“Dark Heaven is far away, but the mounted bandits are close?”

“Exactly. Ningxia Province is pretty close, so the mounted bandits there are a greater threat than Dark Heaven beyond the desert. All the more so for someone like me, who hasn’t learned martial arts.”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, riding alongside us, frowned and cut in.
“Wait. Ningxia was once a lawless land ruled by mounted bandits, but weren’t they put down long ago?”
What was this now?
Everyone turned toward him. The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord cleared his throat and continued.

“To start from the beginning, Ningxia used to be a longstanding headache for us. Hundreds of mounted-bandit groups, large and small, were scattered across the region. Even the government troops couldn’t control them.”
“If even the government troops wouldn’t step in, what happened to the civilians living in Ningxia Province?”
“Would any fish remain in a rotten stream? Most of the civilians either left or joined them.”
“So it was no different from the steppe.”

“You could call it another steppe. Ningxia lies between Gansu and Shaanxi, but it was also the final destination for nomads who’d come down from the north and minority peoples driven out of the Central Plains. And the final touch was...”
“Fugitives. People who’d fled after committing unforgivable crimes.”
Namho cut in, picking up where the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had left off.

“That’s why Ningxia had always been a prize the Murim sects of the Central Plains couldn’t quite bring themselves to claim. The land was small and barren, and the people left there were all sorts of vicious bastards. Even if a sect took losses securing the territory, dealing with it afterward would be another problem. Am I right?”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord smacked his lips softly and nodded.
“I don’t like admitting it, but I can’t deny it. Before the Great Faction War, we could only watch one another. Afterward, we suffered such heavy losses that we had to focus entirely on recovering.”

The Five Great Families.

No one.

sentences.text: “Who else would it be?
Those vicious mounted bandits.”
The moment I heard the man’s answer, Jeok Cheongang and I looked at each other.
And for good reason.
Mounted bandits were the last people I’d expected to hear about now.
Mounted bandits.
Just what the name said: bandits on horseback.

Just as the Yangtze River Channel League had strongholds along every branch of the Yangtze, and the Green Forest Alliance had mountain strongholds on every mountainside with a road, mounted bandits could be found wherever broad plateaus and plains stretched out.
Pung Yang’s Red Wind Band had been one of them.
The vast northern Great Steppe wasn’t home to nomads alone.
It was a refuge for all kinds of people who’d crossed the Great Wall—and their only sanctuary.
For those who could never return to the lives they’d left behind, there were two choices.
Eat or be eaten.
Naturally, most chose the former.
It was a hundred, a thousand times better to survive as a predator than become prey.
Pung Yang had probably followed the same path.
I had no idea how he’d obtained a Temporary Strength Pill or learned demonic martial arts worthy of being called a secret technique, but he’d made quite a name for himself as a predator.
He’d even had the nerve to lead hundreds of subordinates across the Great Wall.
In the end, though, Pung Yang and the Red Wind Band had met their end at the Mount Heng Sword Sect.
However large they grew, they were still bandits.
Even in Shanxi Province, dismissed as a backwater compared with the Central Plains, there were clear limits to what a band of mounted bandits could do.
And now mounted bandits are hanging around here?
Right on the border between Gansu and Shaanxi?
Even the craziest bastards knew to check whether they had somewhere to lie down before stretching out their legs.
With the Kongtong Sect and the Black Dragon Demon Gate standing firm in Gansu, and Huashan and the Zhongnan Sect in Shaanxi, it made no sense for mounted bandits to swagger around here.
Something’s going on.
It has to be.
Jeok Cheongang must have been thinking the same thing.
He was frowning in thought, so I spoke to the man.
“Could you tell us more about them?”
“You mean the mounted bandits?”
“Yes.
Their exact location and numbers, if you know them.
If not, even a rumor would help.”
The man had been blinking at us in silence, apparently picking up on the serious mood.
Then he spoke.
“How much will you pay?”
“What?”
“Four silver nyang.
That should be enough.”
What was this guy’s deal all of a sudden?
Before I could answer, the man scratched his cheek awkwardly.
Or rather, he pretended to scratch it while tracing letters on his cheek.
The name of someone who wasn’t here—but whom I could never forget.
Wol...hwa.
Wait.
Wolhwa?
I finally understood.
My mouth fell open as the man—or rather, the Lower District Sect member—winked at me.
“You seem to be in a hurry.
Why don’t we talk on the way?”
I’d almost forgotten.
The Lower District Sect’s eyes and ears were everywhere.
I let out a quiet laugh at his shameless act, as though nothing had happened, then called out.
“Mujin.”
Hyuk Mujin came hurrying over and answered at once.
“Yes, Captain.
What do you need?”
“Give this gentleman four silver nyang—no, ten.
And provide him with a horse.”
I was turning away after delivering the order when Hyuk Mujin’s muttering reached my ears.
“You could at least toss me a money pouch before saying that.
And if you give him a horse, what am I supposed to ride?”
“...Ahem.”
“See?
You heard me, but you’re pretending you didn’t.
I’m so fed up, I ought to just quit—”
“Ahem!”
“Uh, what is it?
Did you have another order for me?”
Hyuk Mujin’s eyes went wide and innocent, as if he’d never said a thing.
I gave him a cold look and tossed him the money pouch I’d just taken out of my Inventory.
“Oh my, you really shouldn’t have.
You could just deduct whatever you spend from my monthly pay, and if it’s not enough, I could ask my family for more.
Or beg.”
“I’m... sorry.”
“What do you have to apologize for, Captain?
Even if the pillars of the Hyuk Family Textile Shop start shaking, that’s my problem.
Right?”
“I get it.
Just stop already.
That should cover it, right?”
“What about the horse?”
“If you give away the horse too, what am I supposed to ride?
Are my dead ancestors going to carry me?”
Out of answers, I quietly turned my head toward a nearby Zhongnan Sect Disciple.
More specifically, toward the fine horse he was riding.
After that whirlwind of shakedowns, we got an outcome everyone could be satisfied with and set off toward Gansu Province again.
Of course, one Zhongnan Sect Disciple had to climb down from his comfortable saddle and travel on his own two sturdy legs.
But that wasn’t my problem.
What mattered to me was the information the Lower District Sect member had.
“You should all stay around here for the time being.
No—better not stay anywhere near here.
Head toward Shaanxi.
Those vicious mounted bandits could attack at any moment.”
The Lower District Sect member repeated his warnings to the civilians who remained, then mounted his horse.
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord left a dozen or so Disciples behind to lead them safely to Shaanxi if danger arose.
As soon as we set off, the Lower District Sect member’s first words were enough to leave everyone feeling as if they’d been smacked in the back of the head.
“To be honest, there are no mounted bandits.”
After a brief silence, Hyuk Mujin fingered the hilt of the sword at his waist.
“Ten silver nyang.
Spit it back out while I’m still asking nicely.”
“Enough!
Hold your tongue!
Threatening an ally—how are you any different from those demonic, heterodox villains?”
Jeok Cheongang sternly rebuked Hyuk Mujin, then turned to the frightened Lower District Sect member and spoke with unusual kindness.
“Don’t mind that fool.
Go on.
Ten silver nyang is a small price to pay for your fare to the afterlife.”
God, he’s terrifying.
Just from listening to them, you’d think we were the Demonic Path Alliance, not the Murim Alliance.
The Lower District Sect member, who didn’t seem to have a shred of internal energy, had gone pale under the pressure.
He stammered out an explanation.
“To be precise, there were mounted bandits, but they’ve disappeared.”
“Oh?
They were there, and now they’re gone.”
Jeok Cheongang let out an appreciative sound and smiled kindly.
“That makes perfect sense, given the situation.
You’ll soon disappear from this world, too.”
“Eek!”
“I’ll take back nine silver nyang.
You can keep one for the trip.”
“Gah!”
“Enough, all of you!”
Only after I stepped in did tempers, boiling like a cauldron over a charcoal fire, finally settle down.
The poor Lower District Sect member hurriedly explained the details.
“So the mounted bandits in Ningxia Province really have started acting strangely?”
“Y-Yes.”
“Then all those people gathered in the village...”
“I deliberately spread an exaggerated rumor.
Trouble is about to break out in the western region, so we wanted to keep the civilians from getting caught up in it as much as possible.”
“Dark Heaven is far away, but the mounted bandits are close?”
“Exactly.
Ningxia Province is pretty close, so the mounted bandits there are a greater threat than Dark Heaven beyond the desert.
All the more so for someone like me, who hasn’t learned martial arts.”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, riding alongside us, frowned and cut in.
“Wait.

What was this now?
Everyone turned toward him.

“Would any fish remain in a rotten stream?

chapters.title: Chapter 1003
paragraphs: The realization that we’d finally entered Gansu Province brought a strange tension over the group.
It reminded us why we’d come here.
And of the danger lurking somewhere in this land.
How many of us will make it out alive?
I swallowed the thought as soon as it came.
The great battle looming ahead was unavoidable. The only questions were when and where. Countless people would die, and blood would spill across the land.
If not Gansu, then Qinghai. If not Qinghai, then Tibet and Sichuan.
Or it could break out on several fronts at once.

If the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s information was right, Dark Heaven’s forces were approaching from beyond the desert. Their numbers rivaled those of the Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples—if they didn’t surpass them.
An army that size wouldn’t have to concentrate on a single target.
As many as the Hundred Thousand Demonic Disciples, even more dangerous, and they have Moving Formations on top of it all... This isn’t going well.
With the Great Nation joining us, our own forces were formidable. But there was no denying that the enemy had more options than we did.
And if even part of my vague suspicion was right, Dark Heaven wasn’t just a group held together by dark arts and fanaticism.
It can’t be helped. The Murim Alliance leadership knows what Dark Heaven is capable of. I’ll have to trust them.
I’d never once held back. I’d survived one brush with death after another, defeated opponents stronger than myself, and fought to prevent even greater disasters.
But I couldn’t solve everything alone.
This time was no different.
Just as they’d trusted me, I had to trust them.
One person could light a fuse. Dealing with the aftermath of the explosion took many.
My thoughts came to an end along with the mountain road.
Once we crossed the rugged range between Shaanxi and Gansu, a completely different landscape appeared, as if a layer of camouflage had been pulled away.
High ground, and the cold air that came with it.
Beyond lay a vast, open plain, with ocher-colored city walls rising at its center.
No one could mistake the city that appeared through the blowing sand. This was Tianshui, on the eastern edge of Gansu Province, bordering Shaanxi.
“...Well, that’s one hell of an atmosphere.”
Hyuk Mujin’s uneasy remark probably spoke for all of us.
Bleak. Desolate.
That was my first impression of Gansu, and I suspected most of the others felt the same.
“Ugh, what’s with this weather?”
Hyuk Mujin shivered in the chilly, dust-laden wind and pulled his collar shut. Plenty of people were breathing out white clouds.

There were exceptions, of course: those whose Supreme Peak martial arts had brought them to the realm of being Unaffected by Cold and Heat, and Peak masters who could at least use their internal energy to ward off the cold.
Or...
“Taishan likes it! Nice and cool!”
Right. One of them was from here in the first place.
Actually, make that two.
“It’s been a while, hasn’t it?”
At my question, Sama Pyo stopped looking around and answered.
“Hard to say. It feels strange. I’ve only been gone a little over a year, but... it feels like ten years.”
A little over a year could be short or long, depending on who you asked. I understood how Sama Pyo felt.
From the rebirth of the Murim Alliance to today, we’d faced too many crises together as members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion to fit into so little time.
Yeah. Has it really been that long already...?
Watching Sama Pyo and Taishan return to the place where they’d been born and raised stirred something in me, too.
So much had happened. We could have talked for days without getting through it all.
And at every desperate turn, those two had been beside us.
No. They were us.
Comrades bound by the name of the Fire Dragon Pavilion. Men we could trust to watch our backs.
Maybe that was why my gaze lingered on them. Sama Pyo looked back at me, his eyes trembling as though he felt it too.
“Pavilion Master. May I say something?”
“Sure. Anything.”
“I have no interest whatsoever in men.”
“...What?”
“I trust you don’t either, Pavilion Master, but I thought it best to say so, just in case. I hope there’s no misunderstanding. I’ll be going now.”
A moving moment, my ass.
Sama Pyo hurriedly rode ahead. I stared after him, then felt a pointed gaze from beside me and let out a long sigh.
“What? Got something to say?”
The Lower District Sect member who’d been keeping pace with me quickly shook his head.
“No, sir—well, actually, I do, but I’ll say it later.”
“Please say it now. Putting it off makes you look even more suspicious.”
“W-Would that be all right?”
“Oh, for the love of—”
He flinched as I scratched the back of my head, then studied my face and spoke.
“The mission I was assigned ends here.”
“Ends here...?”

“I was to evacuate the nearby residents and travelers, then tell Great Hero Jin what’s happened recently. Fortunately, we’ve entered Gansu without incident, so I believe it’s time for me to turn back.”
“Where to?”
“Our sect and the Beggars’ Sect have members watching the western region in case anything happens. I intend to report this to the Branch Leader as quickly as possible.”
The man belonged to the Lower District Sect’s Shaanxi branch, and I knew its Branch Leader well.
Wolhwa, proprietor of Honghwaru in Shanxi Province—and the first martial artist I’d met in this world.
“Give Wolhwa my regards. The Branch Leader, I mean. Tell her I appreciate her looking out for us.”
“The Branch Leader is looking forward to seeing you again, too. She originally planned to come in person while you were passing through Shaanxi, but circumstances...”
He trailed off, reached into his robe, and held something out.
“What’s this?”
“The Branch Leader ordered me to give it directly to you. She told me again and again—make sure, absolutely, don’t you dare forget!”
He offered me a tightly sealed bamboo tube, then gave me a suggestive smile and a thumbs-up.
“Personally, I have a great deal of respect for you.”
“...All of a sudden?”
“Doesn’t seem all that sudden to me.”
I followed his darting eyes and saw Ju Hwaran staring our way. More precisely, she was staring at the bamboo tube he’d extended toward me, her expression subdued.
But only for a moment. As soon as our eyes met, she turned away and began talking to the people beside her as naturally as could be.
It happened so quickly that I wondered if I’d imagined it.
What was that about?
I blinked, then took the tube. With his final task complete, the Lower District Sect member began to slow his horse.
“I’ll be going, then. I wish you good fortune in battle.”
He clasped his hands in farewell and turned his horse. Just then, something I’d left unresolved flashed through my mind.
“Oh, wait. May I ask one last favor?”
“What would that be?”
“I want to know everything that happens in Qinghai and Gansu. Even the smallest sign. Please get word to us as quickly as you can.”
“You needn’t worry about that. The Murim Alliance’s intelligence network has been operating for some time. Information should already be reaching every nearby sect under emergency orders.”

I’d asked out of caution, but I wasn’t too worried about it. The Hidden Shadow Pavilion had learned what was happening beyond the desert—a place called the Land of Ruin. That alone showed how broad and thorough our intelligence network was.
There was still one thing on my mind.
“Does that network include Ningxia Province?”
“You’re worried about those mounted bandits?”
“From what I’ve heard, I have reason to be.”
Of course I was.
A little over ten years ago, peace had suddenly come to a lawless land that could give the American Wild West a run for its money. At the center of it all was an unidentified Supreme Peak master.
If there was even a chance he was another hidden blade Dark Heaven had planted somewhere in the world, I had to consider turning my horse around right now.
Stopping the enemy coming at us head-on will be hard enough. If we end up fighting on two fronts, it’ll be a disaster.
But the Lower District Sect member smiled.
“It seems I didn’t explain it well enough. I’ve worried you for nothing, Great Hero Jin.”
“What do you mean?”

“Though it’s a frontier region, it’s still part of the world. Our sect and several other intelligence groups have been keeping an eye on Ningxia Province for a long time. We watched even more closely after the trouble there ended at the hands of that unidentified master.”
“Ah.”
I’d overlooked something. Information was money, and that wasn’t true only in the modern world. If anything, useful information was even more valuable here.
And despite being spoken of in the same breath as the Beggars’ Sect, the Lower District Sect was far less of a martial sect. They were information merchants through and through.
There was no way they’d ignored the major incident in Ningxia Province.
Sure enough, his next words were matter-of-fact enough to make my worries seem misplaced.

“The mounted-bandit gangs in Ningxia Province disbanded long ago. Their most notorious leaders were all killed, and the rest didn’t dare resist. We carefully reexamined everything that happened at the time and found nothing particularly suspicious.”
“Then what about the mounted bandits said to have appeared nearby?”
“Horse caravans. Or rather, horse caravans made up of people who used to be mounted bandits.”
Horse caravans.
They roamed the land with their horses and the stars for company. Merchants and guides alike, they were fixtures of the regions they traveled.
“So the disbanded mounted bandits became horse caravans.”
He nodded.
“They couldn’t remain mounted bandits. Some became horse caravans; others formed merchant companies or Escort Bureaus. They changed with the times.”
“Then what about the Supreme Peak master who pacified the mounted bandits?”

“That’s the one question we haven’t answered. We’re told he’s remained in Ningxia Province ever since, but no one knows who he is. All we know is that he isn’t a fiend. Even our best informants have thrown up their hands.”
If he wasn’t a fiend, perhaps he was an eccentric recluse from some remote mountain valley.
It wasn’t certain, but his answer eased my mind for now.
The Lower District Sect member set off, and when we reached Tianshui, we came face-to-face with someone we’d never expected to see.

“Personally, I have a great deal of respect for you.”
“...All of a sudden?”
“Doesn’t seem all that sudden to me.”
I followed his darting eyes and saw Ju Hwaran staring our way.
More precisely, she was staring at the bamboo tube he’d extended toward me, her expression subdued.
But only for a moment.
As soon as our eyes met, she turned away and began talking to the people beside her as naturally as could be.
It happened so quickly that I wondered if I’d imagined it.
What was that about?
I blinked, then took the tube.
With his final task complete, the Lower District Sect member began to slow his horse.
“I’ll be going, then.
I wish you good fortune in battle.”
He clasped his hands in farewell and turned his horse.
Just then, something I’d left unresolved flashed through my mind.
“Oh, wait.
May I ask one last favor?”
“What would that be?”
“I want to know everything that happens in Qinghai and Gansu.
Even the smallest sign.
Please get word to us as quickly as you can.”
“You needn’t worry about that.
The Murim Alliance’s intelligence network has been operating for some time.
Information should already be reaching every nearby sect under emergency orders.”
I’d asked out of caution, but I wasn’t too worried about it.
The Hidden Shadow Pavilion had learned what was happening beyond the desert—a place called the Land of Ruin.
That alone showed how broad and thorough our intelligence network was.
There was still one thing on my mind.
“Does that network include Ningxia Province?”
“You’re worried about those mounted bandits?”
“From what I’ve heard, I have reason to be.”
Of course I was.
A little over ten years ago, peace had suddenly come to a lawless land that could give the American Wild West a run for its money.
At the center of it all was an unidentified Supreme Peak master.
If there was even a chance he was another hidden blade Dark Heaven had planted somewhere in the world, I had to consider turning my horse around right now.
Stopping the enemy coming at us head-on will be hard enough.
If we end up fighting on two fronts, it’ll be a disaster.
But the Lower District Sect member smiled.
“It seems I didn’t explain it well enough.
I’ve worried you for nothing, Great Hero Jin.”
“What do you mean?”
“Though it’s a frontier region, it’s still part of the world.
Our sect and several other intelligence groups have been keeping an eye on Ningxia Province for a long time.
We watched even more closely after the trouble there ended at the hands of that unidentified master.”
“Ah.”
I’d overlooked something.
Information was money, and that wasn’t true only in the modern world.
If anything, useful information was even more valuable here.
And despite being spoken of in the same breath as the Beggars’ Sect, the Lower District Sect was far less of a martial sect.
They were information merchants through and through.
There was no way they’d ignored the major incident in Ningxia Province.
Sure enough, his next words were matter-of-fact enough to make my worries seem misplaced.
“The mounted-bandit gangs in Ningxia Province disbanded long ago.
Their most notorious leaders were all killed, and the rest didn’t dare resist.
We carefully reexamined everything that happened at the time and found nothing particularly suspicious.”
“Then what about the mounted bandits said to have appeared nearby?”
“Horse caravans.
Or rather, horse caravans made up of people who used to be mounted bandits.”
Horse caravans.
They roamed the land with their horses and the stars for company.
Merchants and guides alike, they were fixtures of the regions they traveled.
“So the disbanded mounted bandits became horse caravans.”
He nodded.
“They couldn’t remain mounted bandits.
Some became horse caravans; others formed merchant companies or Escort Bureaus.
They changed with the times.”
“Then what about the Supreme Peak master who pacified the mounted bandits?”
“That’s the one question we haven’t answered.
We’re told he’s remained in Ningxia Province ever since, but no one knows who he is.
All we know is that he isn’t a fiend.
Even our best informants have thrown up their hands.”
If he wasn’t a fiend, perhaps he was an eccentric recluse from some remote mountain valley.
It wasn’t certain, but his answer eased my mind for now.
The Lower District Sect member set off, and when we reached Tianshui, we came face-to-face with someone we’d never expected to see.

chapters.title: Chapter 1004
paragraphs: Everything in the world has its own atmosphere.
A feeling that belongs not only to a person, but to a place or an object, too.
Ordinary civilians have a hard time reading it clearly. Martial artists are different. Life-or-death battles and grueling training have honed their five senses to their limits.
Jeok Cheongang, for instance, was watching me with a grave, searching gaze.
Why?
Before I could ask, the question vanished.
As we drew closer to the ocher-colored walls rising from the middle of the vast plain, I began to feel it too.
“Hmm.”
A low murmur came from nearby.
I turned and met the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s gaze. He had been staring at me.
“You feel it too?”
“Yes.”
I nodded, then watched the walls draw closer with every pounding hoofbeat.
“It’s quiet. Too quiet.”
Anything in excess had poison hidden in it.
That was the feeling coming from the small city, now barely a hundred jang away.
The Great Nation’s flag flew above the walls, as it did everywhere, and below it stood a firmly shut iron gate.
But even setting aside the unusual desolation, something essential was missing.
People.
Civilians didn’t spend their whole lives inside city walls. Some worked the fields outside; others traveled the roads.
Yet the sun hadn’t set, and there were few signs of anyone.
No—not a single person was in sight.
No people meant no noise, making the place feel all the more eerie.
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had noticed it too. His voice grew heavier.
“Do you think it could be a trap?”
I fell silent for a moment.
According to the Lower District Sect member Wolhwa had sent, the Murim Alliance already had a tight surveillance network throughout the western region.
Could an entire city—not some small village—have been occupied without them knowing?
Besides...
It’s eerie, but that’s all.
I could see no signs of battle, and the wind carried not a trace of blood.
How much flesh and bone had I cut through by now? I knew the thick, cloying stench of blood wouldn’t vanish in a day or two. Not when taking a city would have spilled so much of it.
It’s not a trap.
Just as I reached that conclusion, Sama Pyo urged his horse up beside us. One calm remark turned my guess into certainty.
“There’s no harm in continuing on as we are. Nothing’s going to happen anyway.”
His voice was steady, his gaze just as calm.
A thought struck me.
“Could it be?”
“That’s right. It looks like they’ve prepared quite an extravagant welcome.”
At that moment—
Rumble.
Several dozen jang ahead, the firmly shut iron gate began to slowly open.
As the enormous mass of iron, weighing over a thousand geun, parted, a cold-faced middle-aged man appeared in the gap.
He was slender but powerfully built. Though he was entering old age, his neatly combed, jet-black hair held not a single gray strand.
He reminded me of a black panther, and an epithet and name I’d only heard spoken flashed through my mind.
The Black Night King, Sima Gong.

Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, which stood alongside the Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance as a great power of the unorthodox faction. Together with the Kongtong Sect, it divided Gansu Province between them.
But as I recognized the father, I noticed something else.
For some reason, the closer he came, the more his son’s eyes darkened.
“This junior martial artist, Sima Gong, pays his respects to you, Senior.”
Sima Gong’s greeting to Jeok Cheongang was more than polite. It was almost excessive, especially given his standing in Murim and his own considerable age.
Jeok Cheongang, of course, didn’t care in the slightest.
“Spare me the ‘junior martial artist’ nonsense.”
He snorted so hard I worried a booger might fly out, then looked at Sima Gong.
“Are you that desperate to pretend you’re young, or do you wish you were young again?”
Sima Gong lowered his clasped hands and straightened.
“That wasn’t my intention, but embarrassing as it is to admit, I suppose both.”
“Your silver tongue hasn’t changed.”
“Nor have you, Senior. Though your appearance has changed quite a bit.”
“The shell may change, but what’s inside stays the same. Speaking of shells, yours has grown rather grand.”
Jeok Cheongang paused to survey the area.
The streets were empty of civilians—not even a rat was in sight—and around a thousand armed men filled the space by the city gate.
Their black martial uniforms left no doubt that they belonged to the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
“You brought plenty with you. Swarming around like a pack of dogs. Quite a sight.”
Displeasure filled Jeok Cheongang’s eyes and voice.

For the three hundred years since its founding, the Fire Gate Clan had walked the line between the orthodox and unorthodox factions. If pressed, though, it leaned a little closer to the orthodox side.
The Black Night King Sima Gong and the Black Dragon Demon Gate he led, on the other hand, were heirs to the tradition of demonic, heterodox arts.
And judging from the things I’d heard about Sima Gong in the time we’d spent together, Jeok Cheongang’s opinion of him had been poor ever since the Great Faction War.
“Things have been looking rather strange lately, so it came to this.”
“So you emptied your sect and came pouring over here because things are unsettled? Stirring up innocent civilians while you’re at it.”

“You seem to have misunderstood. Even with this many troops away, our sect’s defenses remain secure. The civilians left of their own accord. If they were frightened because of us, then there’s nothing we can do about that... but it isn’t necessarily a bad thing, is it?”
“What?”
Jeok Cheongang narrowed his eyes. Sima Gong smiled gently, an expression at odds with his cold face.
“I have no intention of being disrespectful to you, Senior. I only meant that, amid these signs, the civilians would sense a greater danger. That, too, could be a way to save their lives.”
I had to admit one thing.
This guy can talk.
He could dress up word games and sophistry to sound convincing, then soothe the person listening with just the right manner and smile.

On top of that, he had martial arts that could rival the two Alliance Leaders of the Yangtze and the Green Forest. That was probably the biggest reason the Black Dragon Demon Gate was what it was today.
Like father, like son? They’re definitely alike in that respect. Sama Pyo was just like that when I first met him.
That was then, though.
At our first meeting, Sama Pyo had spoken and acted like a slippery eel. The longer we spent together, the more I realized he wasn’t actually much of a talker.
Was “keep your outside and inside different” something his father taught him?
I glanced between father and son—and met Sima Gong’s eyes.
“Oh, so that’s the young man. The rare genius you took in as a Disciple, Senior.”
He was speaking to Jeok Cheongang, but the interest gleaming in his eyes was directed at me.
It was already too late to pretend I hadn’t noticed his gaze and look away. I glanced at Jeok Cheongang, who was still frowning at Sima Gong. He nodded.
“I’m Jin Taekyung, of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
“I know. How could I not? There’s hardly anyone in Gansu who hasn’t heard of your fame.”
It was the same tired pleasantry people exchanged whenever they met in Murim. But he’d said it with a smile, so I had to answer in kind.
After all, the man before me was an ally—and Sama Pyo’s father.
“You’re too kind. I’ve heard a great deal about you too, Great Hero Sima.”
I clasped my hands politely. Sima Gong smiled and turned to Jeok Cheongang.
“Well, this is unexpected. I thought you’d never had a very good opinion of me, Senior.”
“Never had a good opinion of you? Me?”
“Was I mistaken?”
“Of course you were.”
Well, even Jeok Cheongang couldn’t spit in the face of a smiling man.
I gave Sima Gong a warm smile, as if to say, See?
Then Jeok Cheongang went on.
“It’s not that I have a poor opinion of you. I just don’t like you.”
“So I’ve talked behind your back a little.”
“Jin Taekyung there is lying through his teeth. ‘Heard a great deal about you,’ my ass. What kind of bullshit is—”
Whoosh. Thwack!
“Gyaaaah!”
The faint sound of something cutting through the air was followed by a sudden scream that swallowed Jeok Cheongang’s voice.
Clang! Clang! Clang!
At the same time, dazzling flashes of swordlight sprang up in every direction, and shouts rang out.
“Prepare for battle!”
“The Black Dragon Demon Gate, prepare for an enemy attack!”
“By order of the Sect Leader! Zhongnan Disciples, form the Moon-Shattering Sword Formation at once! ...What are you doing?”

The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had been ordering his Disciples to form a sword formation, but his voice trailed off in bafflement. Only then did everyone realize something was strange. Following the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s gaze, they all looked toward one person.
A homely-looking guy who’d fallen from his saddle with a thunderous scream.
No, Hyuk Mujin.
“Ugh, what the hell was that all of a—”
He groaned and staggered to his feet, then froze like a statue.
Countless eyes were fixed on him like spotlights. He blinked silently until he finally spotted me. The corners of his eyes twitched.
“Captain. That was you, wasn’t it?”
Everyone’s gaze shifted to me.
Sima Gong’s eyes in particular were fixed on me. I did my best to keep my expression calm as I opened my mouth.
“Don’t misunderstand. I don’t really know him.”
Sima Gong turned to Hyuk Mujin.
“Who are you? You don’t seem to be a Zhongnan Sect Disciple.”
“I’m Hyuk Mujin, of the Jin Family of Taiyuan,” he answered indignantly.
“So he says,” Sima Gong said.
Of all the times to be oblivious, you idiot.
I should’ve knocked him out in one shot. Since when did he get so sturdy?
Cursing myself for failing to land the Finger Qi properly, I said, “We’ve met a few times. I didn’t say I’d never met him.”
“So you do know him.”
“Hmm. I suppose I do.”
“Then what do you think caused that young man to suddenly scream and fall over?”
In the suffocating silence, I considered my options and gave the best answer I could.
“He’s always been a bit sick. He has a condition.”
Hyuk Mujin’s mouth fell open. Perhaps the pain had stimulated his salivary glands, because a translucent string of drool ran down his chin.
“See? He comes and goes a few times a day. This sort of thing happens as regularly as his three meals—”
“Wow, you’re really going to do this? You’re seriously going to do this? You want to take it all the way?”
At that critical moment, I sent a discreet Sound Transmission over Hyuk Mujin’s shoulder.
More precisely, to the quick-witted Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent behind him, whose eyes were darting in alarm.
Now!
Fortunately, Namho was nothing like Hyuk Mujin.
With speed and agility that belied his age, he stealthily dropped the strip of jerky in his hand onto the top of Hyuk Mujin’s head.
That tempting piece of jerky was enough to rouse the appetite of someone who’d gone a whole shichen without food.
“Nooo! Jerky!”
Whack!
A palm as big as a pot lid slammed down on Hyuk Mujin’s head. He collapsed, and a deathly silence followed.
It lasted until I, having barely dealt with the emergency, spoke up.
“Now, don’t mind him. Let’s all go inside.”
Why are they all looking at me like I’m a madman?

chapters.title: Chapter 1005
paragraphs: Four days.
You couldn’t exactly call that a long time.
But if you’d spent all four days riding hard, barely stopping to rest and catching snatches of sleep in the saddle, that was another matter.
Rest while you can. Who knows when we’ll have another chance?

Jin Taekyung had left them with those words, then gone off to a meeting with the leadership. The Fire Dragon Pavilion members he’d left behind had followed their Pavilion Master’s orders to the letter.
Now they’d unpacked their few belongings, bathed in warm water, and settled before a sumptuous feast that had somehow already been laid out.
Naturally, Jeok Cheongang and Sama Pyo were the exceptions.

Jeok Cheongang was the Fire King, a giant of his generation. His place at the meeting needed no explanation. And as Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, Sama Pyo belonged among the leadership too.
“Whew. I finally feel alive again.”
Ju Hwaran spoke for every member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Physical exhaustion was bad enough, but mental fatigue weighed on both body and mind far more heavily.
What could they do?
For a martial artist, crossing the line between life and death was a lifelong fate. The grief and pain brought on by war were the lot of those living through troubled times.
It had always been that way, and it would stay that way.
At least everyone in the Fire Dragon Pavilion understood their circumstances—and had accepted them.
“Our Pavilion Master was right. We have to rest as much as we can while there’s time, so we’re ready for what comes next. With that in mind, let’s eat.”
At Song Ilseom’s invitation, Hyuk Mujin looked up, his cheeks already bulging with food.
“Wha’?”
“Wha’ did you jus’ say?”
“Sounded like you said somethin’.”
Song Ilseom stared at him in silence, then answered.
“Nothing. Don’t worry about it. Go ahead and eat. The more pain you’re in, the hungrier you get.”
“Ah, okay.”
Perhaps the bump on the crown of his head was bothering him. Now that he’d paused, Hyuk Mujin took the opportunity to rub it, then buried his face in his plate again.
A moment later, he looked up and stared at Song Ilseom.
“Wait. Why’re you talkin’ down to me? I don’t like that.”
“I’ve been doing it this whole time.”
“That’s why I don’t like it. I’ve told you a bunch of times not to.”
“It’s simple. I’m older than you.”
Gulp.
Hyuk Mujin swallowed what was in his mouth and frowned.
“What a ridiculous guy. You’re only a year or two older than me.”
“Does a year or two not count as an age difference?”
“Well... I guess it does.”
“And you know perfectly well that I have more experience as a martial artist.”
“That too... I guess.”
“I’m your senior, and I’m older. So what’s the problem?”
The longer the conversation went on, the worse things got for Hyuk Mujin.
His eyes darted about as he searched for a counterargument. Then an idea came to him.
“You know how old our Captain is, right?”
“More or less.”
“He’s way younger than me.”
“So?”
“Hey, what do you mean, ‘So?’ You speak at least somewhat politely to the Captain. Why do you get to talk down to me—”
“So?”
“So. What are you going to do about it?”
There was nothing he could say to that.
As Hyuk Mujin blinked at Song Ilseom’s absurdly confident expression, anger rose from deep in his chest.
Now that he thought about it, how unfair was this?
He could put up with Jin Taekyung giving him a hard time whenever he got the chance. That much he could gladly accept as his Captain’s loyal right hand and self-proclaimed heart.

But now he was getting the same treatment from Song Ilseom—a mere wandering martial artist who’d joined them along the way. Sure, Song Ilseom was famous as hell among wanderers, and, as it turned out, he came from an impressive martial family. But still!
I mean, come on! By rank, I’m the Vice Pavilion Master of the Fire Dragon Pavilion! And the Jin Family of Taiyuan is one of the Five Great Families now!
Fire lit in Hyuk Mujin’s eyes as he glared at Song Ilseom. The roasted chicken leg he’d been holding trembled like a sword resonating with its wielder.
“Planning to throw that thing you’re holding?”
“Why? Think I can’t?”

“Of course you can’t.”
“That’s right. You know me well.”

“If you throw away food, heaven will punish you. Besides, my parents always told me to get along with the people around me.”
“What? Got something to say? Then say it quickly. I’m hungry, and I don’t want this precious food to get cold.”
Was that confidence? Cowardice?
Or both?
What is with this guy?
How could anyone be so brazen about being a coward?

“...Never mind. You had good parents.”
“They’re simple, good-hearted people. Thanks for the compliment.”
Hyuk Mujin replied as if he’d been waiting for those words, then set to work sweeping the food in front of him into his mouth with renewed vigor. Song Ilseom sighed inwardly.
Every last one of them is out of their minds.
They’d been told to rest and take it easy, but who would look at them and think they were about to go into battle?
A pack of beggars come to bankrupt an inn, maybe.
Or do they not feel fear at all?
Song Ilseom had spent years among wandering martial artists, where crazies were everywhere. But the people he’d been with for the past year or so were strange from top to bottom.
For example...
True madness.
They were on another level from any madman he’d met before.
And Hyuk Mujin, who was already plenty crazy himself, was merely average by Fire Dragon Pavilion standards.
First, there was Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King.
No words were needed. Just thinking about him made Song Ilseom’s breath catch.
Watching Jeok Cheongang up close had driven one point home once again: the law of the strong devouring the weak still ruled this world.
Otherwise, he’d have been dead several times over by now.
Why did Song Ilseom think that?
Simple.
Jeok Cheongang beat the living daylights out of anyone he didn’t like. Anyone at all. He was fair about it, at least.
Their sect, their principles, their age, their sex—it made no difference.

If they belonged to the orthodox faction, he’d cut them to the heart with a tongue sharper than a famous sword. If they were from the unorthodox faction or were dark-path figures, he’d look for an opening to throw a punch. As for fiends, he’d once said:
“I may as well tell you now: for many years, this old man’s wish has been to reform every fiend beneath heaven and make them good.”
Jin Taekyung had asked on everyone’s behalf if he’d gone senile. Jeok Cheongang had beaten his own Disciple senseless, then added, as brazen as ever:
“Of course, the only good fiend is a dead fiend.”
That was the kind of person Jeok Cheongang was.
Why else would his one and only Disciple say this about his own Master?

“I thought about it seriously, and helping the orthodox faction during the Great Faction War was the best move that old man ever made. Now he gets to be called a king and wreak havoc wherever he wants, all perfectly legally. Am I right, everyone?”
Jin Taekyung probably didn’t know.
Everyone had agreed with him, but the moment he turned away, they’d exchanged looks that all meant roughly the same thing.
Look who’s talking. How does he have the nerve to say that? Does our Captain even know what the word “conscience” means? Sorry, Young Master Jin. This is a bit much, even for you... Taishan hungry.
No one dared say it outright, but everyone knew the only person crazier than Jeok Cheongang was Jin Taekyung.
That guy’s the real lunatic, in more ways than one.
His martial arts were insane, and so was his temper.
Sometimes, for reasons known only to him, he’d act like a perfectly normal person. But when something rubbed him the wrong way, he could outdo even his Master, Jeok Cheongang.
In that sense, he’s even worse.
If Song Ilseom had to fight either Jeok Cheongang or Jin Taekyung, he’d choose the former without hesitation.
Because he thought Jeok Cheongang’s martial arts were no match for his Disciple’s anymore?
Wrong.

Even if Jeok Cheongang cursed him with every filthy word he knew until Song Ilseom feared qi deviation, even if his Flame-Extinguishing Divine Fist crushed Song Ilseom’s Eight Extraordinary Meridians, Jeok Cheongang would still be preferable.
Because he was the Fire King.
A giant known throughout the world, an old monster who had lived through ages beyond counting.
But Jin Taekyung?
...I don’t even want to think about it.
Just thinking about him made Song Ilseom’s stomach churn.
His martial prowess, now so far beyond Song Ilseom’s reach, was one thing. But his tongue, widely held to have surpassed even his Master’s, was the stuff of nightmares.
The one small comfort was that his terrifying tongue only ever seemed to show its full power against enemies.
Even aside from that, Song Ilseom was among those who got the least grief from Jin Taekyung, along with Sama Pyo and Ju Hwaran.
Even when he did something worth getting chewed out for, Jin Taekyung would just toss out a short line and turn away.
“So boring.”
Song Ilseom didn’t know exactly what the expression meant, but he could guess it wasn’t a compliment.
He said I was “so boring.” He called Sama Pyo “ten times more boring.” But he didn’t say anything to Young Lady Ju.
What else could that mean? It was obvious.
Song Ilseom had once spent a long time seriously puzzling over the exact meaning of the expression, but at some point he’d stopped caring.
Had he gotten used to it?
Maybe. Or maybe...
“Hmm.”
With that unconscious murmur, Song Ilseom surfaced from his thoughts.
Only then did he notice what was happening around him—and realize that something was terribly wrong.
“What on earth... is going on?”
It wasn’t a question directed at anyone in particular. It was closer to an exclamation of shock.
Song Ilseom froze, eyes wide. Ju Hwaran and Hyuk Mujin, both wearing serious expressions, answered in turn.
“We don’t know either. How did this happen?”
“Incredibuh! Makes no shensh!”
Ju Hwaran’s answer was full of worry. Hyuk Mujin’s was full of food.
Pth, pth!
Ordinarily, Song Ilseom would have dodged the spray of food with a quick movement. This time, he couldn’t.
Splut!
Something unpleasant touched his skin.
Hyuk Mujin froze, worried about what he’d done. But despite his fears, Song Ilseom didn’t move.
He could only stare at one person, as stunned as if he’d come face-to-face with a living dragon.
Taishan sat before a mouthwatering feast, his shoulders drooping, without moving a muscle.
“Am I seeing things?”
The disbelieving words had barely left someone’s lips when another voice answered.
“You’re seeing it right. But I’d like you to keep it down for now.”
The voice was low and subdued.
Namho, who’d sat motionless and lost in thought all this time, twitched his nose.
As if trying to catch a scent he remembered from a day not so long ago.

chapters.title: Chapter 1006
paragraphs: Rustle.
A thick animal hide unfurled across the large table. Its surface, tanned by human hands, was covered edge to edge with drawings and writing that detailed the terrain.
“As you can see, this map was made by our sect. We’ve spent many years documenting every feature of Gansu in detail, revising each change as it occurred, until it was complete.”
Sima Gong’s voice was calm, but every leader gathered around the table understood what the map meant.

A province might sound like a mere piece of the world, but even the smallest was comparable in size to a country. And it wasn’t as if they had drones or satellites. Making a map like this took enormous wealth and manpower.
The Black Dragon Demon Gate’s ability to produce one so vast and detailed showed how much control it held across Gansu. It also showed the reach of Sima Gong’s intelligence network.
“You must’ve put a lot of work into this. So what, are you trying to brag that you’ve got this whole area locked down?”
Jeok Cheongang had no use for subtlety. A faint smile appeared on Sima Gong’s lips.
“Of course not. The Kongtong Sect is one of the pillars of the Central Plains. How could we presume to claim Gansu for ourselves?”
His words were humble, but everyone knew where Sima Gong and the Black Dragon Demon Gate stood in Gansu Province.
And besides...
“This is an important meeting, but that very pillar is missing.”
It was true. The Kongtong Sect wasn’t here.
Even after I’d pointed that out, Sima Gong’s smile didn’t waver.
“No need to worry. The pillar is elsewhere, preparing to hold back the downpour that’s about to come.”
“So the Kongtong Sect has already been sent to the front lines.”
Sima Gong nodded at the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, who’d cut in.
“Just as the Sect Leader guessed. We’ve established three lines of defense stretching across Dunhuang, the Great Snow Mountain, and the Qilian Mountains in Gansu Province.”
“Three lines? Aren’t your forces spread too thin?”
The others in the room nodded at the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s concern.
If Dark Heaven’s vast army marched into Gansu, a single great battle could decide everything. But Sima Gong’s expression remained unchanged.

“They may not rival Kunlun, but the Great Snow Mountain and the Qilian Mountains are both among the ten most treacherous mountain ranges under heaven. And our enemies have that bizarre dark art they call the Moving Formation. We judged it too dangerous to concentrate all our forces in Dunhuang.”
“I agree with you, Sect Leader Sima. The question is whether you have enough forces to hold three fronts.”
Being outnumbered was our greatest obstacle.
The enemy had an army of a hundred thousand. Even if they split their forces to attack three provinces at once, that still left more than thirty thousand pouring into each one like a pack of dogs.
To face that many, we need to gather in one place. And we’ll only stand a chance if we make the most of the terrain.
That was how we’d fought in Shanxi Province not long ago. Luck and determination together had won us the day.

Anyone could see the problem, whether they knew military strategy or not. And Sima Gong was no village bumpkin. He was the Black Night King, the man who’d built the Black Dragon Demon Gate into a major power. Could he really have missed something so obvious?
No way.
He met everyone’s gaze without a trace of unease. I could sense the confidence behind his calm.
“You already have enough forces in Gansu.”
Sima Gong’s smile deepened.

“About a month ago, I put all of Gansu Murim on alert. Our sect, the Kongtong Sect, and every other martial faction in the area had already been keeping watch for some time, so we were able to gather our forces quickly.”
Which means...
“Thirty thousand. That’s how many we’ve assembled so far. We’ve mobilized everything Gansu Murim has.”
The leaders’ eyes widened. Mine did too.
Thirty thousand?
It was an enormous force. Shanxi Province had fielded only fifteen thousand to hold Eight Spring Gorge against the forces of the Great Steppe.
And Sima Gong had specified Gansu Murim. All thirty thousand were martial artists. There was no comparing that to Shanxi’s army, more than half of which had been government soldiers.

Granted, Shanxi Murim had already suffered grievous losses in the conflict with the Mount Heng Sword Sect and the Head Elder’s betrayal. Even taking that into account, thirty thousand was almost beyond imagining.
“W-where did you find that many people?”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had voiced what everyone must have been wondering. Jeok Cheongang, who’d been watching with a frown, spoke before Sima Gong could answer.
“Unorthodox factions have always had numbers, if nothing else. Isn’t that right?”
Sima Gong smiled and nodded.
“I won’t deny it.”
“Even so, thirty thousand would be nearly impossible for the Nine Sects and One Gang of the Central Plains.”
“That’s also true. Would the Great Nation have stood idly by if this many ruffians, liable to turn the swords at their waists against the state at any moment, had gathered?”

The phrase the government and Murim shall not interfere in one another’s affairs had been rendered nearly meaningless since the Son of Heaven declared Dark Heaven traitors. But the principle had arisen for a reason.
It was an unspoken rule that had arisen naturally alongside Murim itself.

A stone that stuck out was bound to get hammered down. The countless martial factions scattered across the land had long checked one another and made agreements to avoid conflict. In turn, the Great Nation tolerated them so long as they posed no threat to its foundations.
People even said that dynasties changed, but Murim remained.

Now Gansu Murim had crossed that unspoken line. They’d gathered thirty thousand martial artists in the frontier, not even the Central Plains. That was an army they couldn’t have raised even if they’d turned every martial faction in Gansu Province upside down and shaken them out.
Which means...
Only one possibility remained. The majority had no affiliation with any particular sect. They were the sort of people who followed only their own needs and interests.
“You even scraped together the dark-path figures. You must’ve been desperate.”
The dark path.
Those people had coexisted uneasily with Murim for ages. Several faces darkened at the mention of them, and the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s eyes grew especially grave.
“Sect Leader Sima. Is what Great Hero Jeok said true?”
Sima Gong answered calmly.
“Some of them are dark-path figures. Is that a problem?”
“Well...”

“I won’t pretend otherwise. I’m an unorthodox martial artist. The Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance have their roots in the dark path. Ah, and so does that son of mine over there.”
Sama Pyo, silent until now, looked shaken at being singled out by his father. But Sima Gong spoke again, drawing everyone’s attention back.
“And all the people I just mentioned have one thing in common. Do you know what it is?”
They did. Everyone in the room knew.
Yet they remained silent, their expressions heavy.
All but one.
“They fought for the Murim Alliance, and they’re fighting for it now.”
Jeok Cheongang.
Sima Gong’s reflection appeared in his reddish, fever-bright eyes, befitting the title of Fire King.
“Unorthodox, dark-path figures, or nobodies who crawled in from God knows where—I don’t give a damn. If the weapons in their hands are pointed at Dark Heaven, that’s all that matters.”
Sima Gong nodded, his face set.
“As it was in the past, so it will be this time.”
“I’m not doubting you. But dark-path figures who’ve drifted all the way out to this frontier must be a rotten lot. If something goes wrong...”
“I’ll stake my head on it.”
Jeok Cheongang stared at him in silence. Then he turned and swept his gaze around the room.
“What do you all think?”
Respected elders of Gansu Murim had come to greet us alongside Sima Gong, but Jeok Cheongang wasn’t asking them. His question was for the senior members of the Zhongnan Sect who’d traveled with us.
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord stood at their center, hesitating. His Senior Brothers, the Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword, answered one after the other.
“Someone once said it doesn’t matter whether a cat is white or black, so long as it catches mice.”

“The Sima Gong I know is a comrade-in-arms and a hero, someone who weathered the war alongside us, before he is an unorthodox martial artist. That a man like him should have to stake his life on this—isn’t that a crying shame?”
I watched the two old Daoists pour out their answers as smoothly as if they’d been waiting for their turn. Then Jeok Cheongang looked my way.
“So, are you done stuffing your face with honey?”
He meant I’d been sitting there with my mouth full, acting like I couldn’t speak. I smacked my lips and answered.
“Yeah. It was sweet.”
“You’ve held that precious honey in your mouth long enough. You must have something to say by now.”
“Is this something I get to decide?”
“Not a chance. Who do you think you are?”
I gave a short laugh and looked around.

Most of the faces were unfamiliar; I knew neither their names nor their titles. There were senior members of the Black Dragon Demon Gate and leaders of Gansu Murim, each of them heading a martial faction large or small.
Sima Gong was at their center.
“Can I ask a few questions?”
“Anything.”
“I doubt you made all these decisions alone. Am I right?”
“Of course. The Sect Leaders here agreed, as did the Kongtong Sect.”
“Then if Dark Heaven isn’t targeting Gansu...”
