sentences.text: Rustle.
A thick animal hide unfurled across the large table.
Its surface, tanned by human hands, was covered edge to edge with drawings and writing that detailed the terrain.
“As you can see, this map was made by our sect.
We’ve spent many years documenting every feature of Gansu in detail, revising each change as it occurred, until it was complete.”
Sima Gong’s voice was calm, but every leader gathered around the table understood what the map meant.
A province might sound like a mere piece of the world, but even the smallest was comparable in size to a country.
And it wasn’t as if they had drones or satellites.
Making a map like this took enormous wealth and manpower.
The Black Dragon Demon Gate’s ability to produce one so vast and detailed showed how much control it held across Gansu.
It also showed the reach of Sima Gong’s intelligence network.
“You must’ve put a lot of work into this.
So what, are you trying to brag that you’ve got this whole area locked down?”
Jeok Cheongang had no use for subtlety.
A faint smile appeared on Sima Gong’s lips.
“Of course not.
The Kongtong Sect is one of the pillars of the Central Plains.
How could we presume to claim Gansu for ourselves?”
His words were humble, but everyone knew where Sima Gong and the Black Dragon Demon Gate stood in Gansu Province.
And besides...
“This is an important meeting, but that very pillar is missing.”
It was true.
The Kongtong Sect wasn’t here.
Even after I’d pointed that out, Sima Gong’s smile didn’t waver.
“No need to worry.
The pillar is elsewhere, preparing to hold back the downpour that’s about to come.”
“So the Kongtong Sect has already been sent to the front lines.”
Sima Gong nodded at the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, who’d cut in.
“Just as the Sect Leader guessed.
We’ve established three lines of defense stretching across Dunhuang, the Great Snow Mountain, and the Qilian Mountains in Gansu Province.”
“Three lines?
Aren’t your forces spread too thin?”
The others in the room nodded at the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s concern.
If Dark Heaven’s vast army marched into Gansu, a single great battle could decide everything.
But Sima Gong’s expression remained unchanged.
“They may not rival Kunlun, but the Great Snow Mountain and the Qilian Mountains are both among the ten most treacherous mountain ranges under heaven.
And our enemies have that bizarre dark art they call the Moving Formation.
We judged it too dangerous to concentrate all our forces in Dunhuang.”
“I agree with you, Sect Leader Sima.
The question is whether you have enough forces to hold three fronts.”
Being outnumbered was our greatest obstacle.
The enemy had an army of a hundred thousand.
Even if they split their forces to attack three provinces at once, that still left more than thirty thousand pouring into each one like a pack of dogs.
To face that many, we need to gather in one place.
And we’ll only stand a chance if we make the most of the terrain.
That was how we’d fought in Shanxi Province not long ago.
Luck and determination together had won us the day.
Anyone could see the problem, whether they knew military strategy or not.
And Sima Gong was no village bumpkin.
He was the Black Night King, the man who’d built the Black Dragon Demon Gate into a major power.
Could he really have missed something so obvious?
No way.
He met everyone’s gaze without a trace of unease.
I could sense the confidence behind his calm.
“You already have enough forces in Gansu.”
Sima Gong’s smile deepened.
“About a month ago, I put all of Gansu Murim on alert.
Our sect, the Kongtong Sect, and every other martial faction in the area had already been keeping watch for some time, so we were able to gather our forces quickly.”
Which means...
“Thirty thousand.
That’s how many we’ve assembled so far.
We’ve mobilized everything Gansu Murim has.”
The leaders’ eyes widened.
Mine did too.
Thirty thousand?
It was an enormous force.
Shanxi Province had fielded only fifteen thousand to hold Eight Spring Gorge against the forces of the Great Steppe.
And Sima Gong had specified Gansu Murim.
All thirty thousand were martial artists.
There was no comparing that to Shanxi’s army, more than half of which had been government soldiers.
Granted, Shanxi Murim had already suffered grievous losses in the conflict with the Mount Heng Sword Sect and the Head Elder’s betrayal.
Even taking that into account, thirty thousand was almost beyond imagining.
“W-where did you find that many people?”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had voiced what everyone must have been wondering.
Jeok Cheongang, who’d been watching with a frown, spoke before Sima Gong could answer.
“Unorthodox factions have always had numbers, if nothing else.
Isn’t that right?”
Sima Gong smiled and nodded.
“I won’t deny it.”
“Even so, thirty thousand would be nearly impossible for the Nine Sects and One Gang of the Central Plains.”
“That’s also true.
Would the Great Nation have stood idly by if this many ruffians, liable to turn the swords at their waists against the state at any moment, had gathered?”
The phrase the government and Murim shall not interfere in one another’s affairs had been rendered nearly meaningless since the Son of Heaven declared Dark Heaven traitors.
But the principle had arisen for a reason.
It was an unspoken rule that had arisen naturally alongside Murim itself.
A stone that stuck out was bound to get hammered down.
The countless martial factions scattered across the land had long checked one another and made agreements to avoid conflict.
In turn, the Great Nation tolerated them so long as they posed no threat to its foundations.
People even said that dynasties changed, but Murim remained.
Now Gansu Murim had crossed that unspoken line.
They’d gathered thirty thousand martial artists in the frontier, not even the Central Plains.
That was an army they couldn’t have raised even if they’d turned every martial faction in Gansu Province upside down and shaken them out.
Which means...
Only one possibility remained.
The majority had no affiliation with any particular sect.
They were the sort of people who followed only their own needs and interests.
“You even scraped together the dark-path figures.
You must’ve been desperate.”
The dark path.
Those people had coexisted uneasily with Murim for ages.
Several faces darkened at the mention of them, and the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s eyes grew especially grave.
“Sect Leader Sima.
Is what Great Hero Jeok said true?”
Sima Gong answered calmly.
“Some of them are dark-path figures.
Is that a problem?”
“Well...”
“I won’t pretend otherwise.
I’m an unorthodox martial artist.
The Yangtze River Channel League and the Green Forest Alliance have their roots in the dark path.
Ah, and so does that son of mine over there.”
Sama Pyo, silent until now, looked shaken at being singled out by his father.
But Sima Gong spoke again, drawing everyone’s attention back.
“And all the people I just mentioned have one thing in common.
Do you know what it is?”
They did.
Everyone in the room knew.
Yet they remained silent, their expressions heavy.
All but one.
“They fought for the Murim Alliance, and they’re fighting for it now.”
Jeok Cheongang.
Sima Gong’s reflection appeared in his reddish, fever-bright eyes, befitting the title of Fire King.
“Unorthodox, dark-path figures, or nobodies who crawled in from God knows where—I don’t give a damn.
If the weapons in their hands are pointed at Dark Heaven, that’s all that matters.”
Sima Gong nodded, his face set.
“As it was in the past, so it will be this time.”
“I’m not doubting you.
But dark-path figures who’ve drifted all the way out to this frontier must be a rotten lot.
If something goes wrong...”
“I’ll stake my head on it.”
Jeok Cheongang stared at him in silence.
Then he turned and swept his gaze around the room.
“What do you all think?”
Respected elders of Gansu Murim had come to greet us alongside Sima Gong, but Jeok Cheongang wasn’t asking them.
His question was for the senior members of the Zhongnan Sect who’d traveled with us.
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord stood at their center, hesitating.
His Senior Brothers, the Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword, answered one after the other.
“Someone once said it doesn’t matter whether a cat is white or black, so long as it catches mice.”

He meant I’d been sitting there with my mouth full, acting like I couldn’t speak.
I smacked my lips and answered.
“Yeah.
It was sweet.”
“You’ve held that precious honey in your mouth long enough.
You must have something to say by now.”
“Is this something I get to decide?”
“Not a chance.
Who do you think you are?”
I gave a short laugh and looked around.
Most of the faces were unfamiliar; I knew neither their names nor their titles.
There were senior members of the Black Dragon Demon Gate and leaders of Gansu Murim, each of them heading a martial faction large or small.
Sima Gong was at their center.
“Can I ask a few questions?”
“Anything.”
“I doubt you made all these decisions alone.
Am I right?”
“Of course.

“Qinghai...
Qinghai.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1007
paragraphs: For anyone born and raised in Gansu Province, the pale sandstorms that swept through year-round were nothing unusual.
Their ancestors had recorded the loess-colored plateau’s existence as far back as the days when the river flowing through the region came to be called the Yellow River.

No one knew exactly when the plateau had formed or why, but it was still there. Whenever a strong wind blew in, a cloud would rise like a waterspout and sweep across the area before vanishing, scattering fine loess like stars.
That was probably why the Black Dragon Demon Gate martial artists standing watch atop the city wall felt nothing in particular as they watched a cloud of dust approach from the far north.
“Damn it. Here we go again.”
One of the martial artists frowned. The middle-aged squad leader pulled a scrap of cloth from inside his clothes with a practiced motion.
“Shut your mouth and put on your mask. Don’t stand there trying to tough it out like last time, then complain for days afterward.”
“I really couldn’t help it that time. How are you supposed to dodge it when it hits all at once? You can’t even breathe.”
“Suit yourself. If you’d rather eat a handful of sand than your next meal.”
The others were chuckling when someone watching the cloud of dust spoke up.
“Still, this one’s little. Almost cute. Looks like it’ll die down before it reaches us. The scouts way out front are going to get covered in it, though.”
“Oh, you’re right. Captain, why’d you put on your mask?”
They’d been through this often enough to know what they were looking at. This wasn’t a sandstorm towering more than ten jang high. There was no need to make a fuss over a little cloud of dust.
Without bothering to take another look, the martial artists teased the Captain for putting on his mask so early.
“Look at you, Captain. You’ve lost your touch.”
“The Blood-Death Sword will be weeping. Heh.”
“Come on, you can tell how big it is at a glance. Why the rush? I used to be a mounted bandit, and I know thirty riders galloping side by side kick up a cloud about that size. It’s nothing.”
The Captain’s already fearsome face twisted into something monstrous.
“What?”
The laughter slowly died. His subordinates remembered how notorious the Captain had once been in the area and swallowed hard.
“W-we didn’t mean it like that, Captain...”
But his next words left them staring at him in confusion.
“No, not that.”
“Pardon?”
“The last thing he said. What was it?”
Everyone turned toward the former mounted bandit. He blinked.
“Me?”
“Yes. Say that again.”
“Uh, you can tell how big it is at a glance, so why the rush—”
“Not that, you bastard! The part after it!”
“Th-that a cloud of dust that size means about thirty riders...”
“And how many scouts left half a shichen ago?”
“Exactly thirty. Was that when they got their horses earlier? I remember because they made a huge fuss, demanding better mounts since they had to patrol until sunset...”
His voice cut off.
Only then did the martial artists realize something was wrong. Their eyes darted between one another as they carried on a silent conversation.
Wait. What’s going on?
An unusually small cloud of dust. Thirty riders. And thirty scouts.
Something feels off.
Why are they back already if they’re not due until after sunset?
That feels even more off.
Maybe someone had to take a dump?
You can shit anywhere, cover it up, and call it a latrine. What kind of lunatic would abandon a mission just to come back and relieve himself?
Doesn’t everyone? I do.
You’re a real lunatic.
This feels seriously wrong.
No matter how they put their heads together, no matter what explanation they came up with, something was clearly amiss.
Gulp.
In the strange tension, just as someone swallowed dryly—
Fwoooosh! Boom!
Hundreds of jang away, red smoke shot up from the pale cloud of dust. The Captain recognized what the signal flare assigned to the scouts meant and forced his voice out.
“Suspicious person spotted...!”
That was the signal for someone acting strangely—an unfamiliar intruder.
At last realizing what was happening, the martial artists atop the wall shouted as if coughing up blood.
“This is real! It’s really happening!”
“What are you waiting for, you bastards? Move your asses!”
“L-let the Sect Leader know! Hurry!”

The wall erupted into chaos as if a powder magazine had exploded. Meanwhile, the flare that had burst brilliantly in the sky slowly drifted down over the thirty scouts racing toward them with all their might, raising a cloud of dust.
On one of the dozens of winding hills, a group stood watching with the shadows at their backs.
“Well... this is a hell of a mess.”
There were about fifty unidentified riders. At their head, a giant of a man let out a low groan. Another man beside him scratched vigorously at his shaggy hair.
“Ah, damn it. This is driving me crazy. Didn’t your little brother tell you we should approach slowly and gently?”
The giant frowned.
“I didn’t think they’d panic and run. We even brought a white flag just in case. Why are those bastards so scared?”
“Do you really need to ask? Look at your face, Big Brother. Who’s going to take a white flag as a friendly gesture from someone who looks like you?”
Agreement erupted from all around them.
“He’s right. Your face is downright terrifying. What good’s a white flag going to do?”
“They probably thought you were offering your condolences in advance to the poor bastards about to die.”
“It wouldn’t have helped if you’d gone over dressed in white instead.”
“Then they’d think you’d put on mourning clothes in advance to offer your condolences to the poor bastards about to die.”
“No need to say another word. Not even the Heavenly Demon’s granddaddy could beat Big Brother at looking vicious.”
“Damn it. This whole thing’s going to shit, and now I’m getting nervous. What if we ride over there and they shower us with arrows?”
“Can’t be helped. Big Brother, since it’s come to this, let’s just turn around and go back.”
“Second Brother, are you scared?”
“Bah! Who’s scared? I just remembered I left something important behind!”
“Looks like you brought your shriveled-up guts along... Ah, you left your balls behind.”
“Bah! Third Brother, how dare you!”
“There you go again with the bah, bah. That only sounds impressive when a Supreme Peak master says it. You can’t pull it off, Second Brother.”
“Bah! Must you see your own coffin before you learn your lesson?”
“I’m going to lose my mind if I have to keep listening to that. You’ve picked up a weird habit. So, Big Brother, what are you going to do?”
At the question from the man called Third Brother, the giant, who’d stayed silent through the rapid-fire exchange, finally spoke.
“We’re not turning back.”
His voice was as heavy as his build. He fixed his gaze on the loess-colored wall rising beyond the heat haze.
“I know what you’re all worried about... But Great Sir asked this of us himself. If you’re men who understand loyalty, follow my lead.”
The six men who called him Big Brother stared at him, their eyes trembling at his stern words.
The mutters that followed, however, weren’t the reaction he’d hoped for.
“There he goes, putting on a show again.”
“Now we’re the bad guys.”
“He’s a bear until it suits him to be a fox. Am I right, brothers?”
“Still, we should do as Big Brother says. Besides, Great Sir himself asked us. What choice do we have?”
“Please, someone gag Second Brother. Listening to him is going to give me qi deviation.”

Most of them grumbled like children whose sweets had been taken away. But they knew, as did the giant and the dozens of riders watching from behind them, that their purpose hadn’t changed just because things had turned out this way.
The strongest reason for that certainty was the person who had sent them here.
“Let’s go. The sun’ll set at this rate.”
With the late sunset beginning to spread from the west, the giant led the fifty or so riders over the hill.
Before long, they reached the wall. Hundreds of arrowheads were trained on them, with unfamiliar faces visible between them.
“Stop! Stop! Stop! Hands up! Move and we’ll shoot!”
At the shout from some young pretty boy, the giant calmly reached inside his clothes for the white flag he’d prepared.
Or rather, he tried to.
Before he could pull it out, the young man gave an order he hadn’t expected.
“Fire!”
Fwoosh, fwoosh, fwoosh, fwoosh!
Hundreds of arrows tore through the air.
Some carried more force than others, but every arrow, large or small, had been imbued with internal energy. Instead of arcing, they plunged straight down at the unexpected visitors.
Clang-clang-clang-clang!
Sparks flew in every direction.
The giant had ridden ahead alone, leaving his dozens of subordinates behind. He survived the net of arrows that covered a thirty-jang radius and bellowed.
“Are you out of your damn mind? Who starts shooting arrows without warning?”
Jeok Cheongang, standing beside me, nodded.
“He looks vicious as hell, but this old man has to agree with him. Has some inner demon taken hold of you?”
“No, I’m fine.”
“Then why?”
“I told him to put his hands up, and he didn’t listen. That bastard tried to pull a fast one.”
“You’re insane.”

“Honestly, I didn’t think they’d actually shoot. I thought they’d ignore my order. Judging by his level, though, I figured he’d survive a volley like that, so it was a warning too. Anyway, no harm done, right?”
“Infinite Life Buddha...”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord looked appalled by my clear-cut conclusion. The Black Night King, Sima Gong, burst into hearty laughter instead.
“Haha! Straight to the point. We could’ve used someone like you on our side.”
Was that a compliment or an insult?
While I considered how to respond, the giant—whose face was so vicious I could hardly believe anyone could look like that—shouted again.
“Don’t shoot! I said don’t shoot! Can’t you see what I’m holding?”
Flap.
So that was why he’d reached inside his clothes. He was waving a large piece of cloth.
It was covered in sand and loess, leaving it a thoroughly ambiguous yellowish color.
“What on earth is that supposed to mean? What does he want us to see on that dingy yellow thing?”
“Yellow cloth... Wait, could he be a Yellow Turban?”
“That’s ridiculous. What era do you think this is? How could the Yellow Turbans still be around?”
Watching everyone debate, I felt the weighty responsibility of providing another clear-cut answer.
He’s acting suspicious, he looks vicious, and the men with him look like they’ve each got at least eighteen prior convictions.
No matter how I looked at it, only one solution came to mind.
“Prepare a volley.”
“Fire!”
Fwoosh, fwoosh, fwoosh!

Before long, they reached the wall.
Hundreds of arrowheads were trained on them, with unfamiliar faces visible between them.
“Stop!
Stop!
Stop!
Hands up!
Move and we’ll shoot!”
At the shout from some young pretty boy, the giant calmly reached inside his clothes for the white flag he’d prepared.
Or rather, he tried to.
Before he could pull it out, the young man gave an order he hadn’t expected.
“Fire!”
Fwoosh, fwoosh, fwoosh, fwoosh!
Hundreds of arrows tore through the air.
Some carried more force than others, but every arrow, large or small, had been imbued with internal energy.
Instead of arcing, they plunged straight down at the unexpected visitors.
Clang-clang-clang-clang!
Sparks flew in every direction.
The giant had ridden ahead alone, leaving his dozens of subordinates behind.
He survived the net of arrows that covered a thirty-jang radius and bellowed.
“Are you out of your damn mind?
Who starts shooting arrows without warning?”
Jeok Cheongang, standing beside me, nodded.
“He looks vicious as hell, but this old man has to agree with him.
Has some inner demon taken hold of you?”
“No, I’m fine.”
“Then why?”
“I told him to put his hands up, and he didn’t listen.
That bastard tried to pull a fast one.”
“You’re insane.”
“Honestly, I didn’t think they’d actually shoot.
I thought they’d ignore my order.
Judging by his level, though, I figured he’d survive a volley like that, so it was a warning too.
Anyway, no harm done, right?”
“Infinite Life Buddha...”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord looked appalled by my clear-cut conclusion.
The Black Night King, Sima Gong, burst into hearty laughter instead.
“Haha!
Straight to the point.
We could’ve used someone like you on our side.”
Was that a compliment or an insult?
While I considered how to respond, the giant—whose face was so vicious I could hardly believe anyone could look like that—shouted again.
“Don’t shoot!
I said don’t shoot!
Can’t you see what I’m holding?”
Flap.
So that was why he’d reached inside his clothes.
He was waving a large piece of cloth.
It was covered in sand and loess, leaving it a thoroughly ambiguous yellowish color.
“What on earth is that supposed to mean?
What does he want us to see on that dingy yellow thing?”
“Yellow cloth...
Wait, could he be a Yellow Turban?”
“That’s ridiculous.
What era do you think this is?
How could the Yellow Turbans still be around?”
Watching everyone debate, I felt the weighty responsibility of providing another clear-cut answer.
He’s acting suspicious, he looks vicious, and the men with him look like they’ve each got at least eighteen prior convictions.
No matter how I looked at it, only one solution came to mind.
“Prepare a volley.”
“Fire!”
Fwoosh, fwoosh, fwoosh!

chapters.title: Chapter 1008
paragraphs: To cut to the chase, by the time the third volley of arrows ended, the leaders of Gansu Murim had decided to let the fifty-odd suspicious-looking men—including the giant—inside the gates.
Of course, it would be misleading to call it a decision made by the entire leadership. Jeok Cheongang’s presence had a great deal to do with it.
“I don’t know what hole these mangy mutts crawled out of, but let them in alive for now.”
Then he added, addressing the murmuring leaders, “What are you agonizing over? If they seem suspicious, kill them and send them back out.”
“Oh.”
“Ah.”

It was such a clear-cut answer that even Judge Bao would’ve brought his dog-headed execution blade down with a smack. The meeting that hardly deserved to be called a meeting came to an end, and the Black Night King, Sima Gong, immediately ordered his subordinates to admit the vicious-looking visitors.
Rumble, rumble.
The massive iron gates began to open, little by little.
The giant was the first to step through the gap. He swept his bulging eyes around him.
He’d damn near shit blood dodging three volleys of arrows, and now his clothes were practically rags. His half-rolled eyes darted about, searching for someone.
Someone like the young bastard who’d suddenly ordered the archers to fire.
“Looking for someone? Keep that up and you’ll get a crick in your neck. Want me to find them for you?”
I’d come down first to greet our unexpected visitors. I tossed out the question as I stepped forward, and the giant’s eyes widened.
“You, you...!”
“I saw it all from up there. Nice job blocking them. Nice job dodging, too.”
“You look like a gisaeng’s older brother, you bastard! How dare you!”
“What did you just call me?”
My expression hardened. At the unsettling pressure coming off me, the giant flinched on instinct, then forced out another strained reply.
“I said you look like a gisaeng’s older brother...!”
“Hold on. Just hold on a second.”
“What?”
Leaving the giant’s angry, baffled question hanging, I closed my eyes.
He said I look like a gisaeng’s older brother.
What a wonderful thing to hear.
For a man of the same sex, with the same chromosomes, to say that to me was the highest praise imaginable.
I savored the lingering swell of emotion, then opened my eyes.
“Thanks. Turns out you’re a good guy.”
“So, Junggeol, where are you from?”
The giant—or rather, Ma Junggeol—nearly popped his eyes out of his head.
“How did you know?!”
“Hm? Know what?”
“My, my name.”
Seeing him stumble over his words now, I answered as casually as could be.
“Didn’t I tell you? We already introduced ourselves. You’ve forgotten that fast?”
“You must still be rattled. Fair enough. You had to dodge all those arrows.”
Ma Junggeol would probably never know that, at this very moment, a translucent holographic window was floating like a ghost above his head.
System Level: 80 Name: Ma Junggeol
Level 80.
A person’s level wasn’t an absolute measure of their strength, but even so, it was awfully low for someone I’d suspect of being a Dark Heaven lackey.
Going by what I saw earlier, he’s maybe a fairly seasoned Peak master?
Still, you couldn’t let your guard down so easily.
As I slowly looked Ma Junggeol over, his expression still dazed, the leaders atop the wall finally came down the stairs, Jeok Cheongang among them.
At the same time, the fifty-odd mounted men came rushing toward us.
“Stop!”
“Let’s talk! Let’s talk!”
“We don’t want to fight!”
“Big Brother! Are you all right?”
“Enough!”
“I’m going to lose my mind. I told you to stop doing that.”
Six men, riding side by side at the very front of the group, surrounded Ma Junggeol.
What the hell are these guys?
I was sure everyone there was thinking much the same thing.
The lanky one. The dwarf. The bulbous-nosed one. The tiny-eyed one...

Every one of them had striking features that seemed to have gone their own way. You didn’t see a combination like that every day. And Ma Junggeol, standing in the middle of those six men, was the finishing touch.
Was his father Picasso?
They all had such strong impressionist faces that even the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s martial artists—who’d spent their share of time at the bottom—instinctively reached for their sword hilts.
Shing.
As the faint sounds of friction from here and there heightened the tension, a low voice reached everyone’s ears.
“I guarantee that anyone who tries something stupid from this point on will spend a very hot time with this old man.”
No one present needed to ask who’d spoken.
And, naturally, not even Tokyo Hot could hold a candle to the JCK-444 Fire Show Special. No one wanted to star in it.
Shuffle, shuffle.
The crowd parted to either side as though fleeing a fire demon.
Jeok Cheongang emerged through the gap, leading the other leaders. He glanced at Ma Junggeol, then turned to me.
“So, who is he, and where did he come from?”
“His name is Ma Junggeol. I don’t know where he came from yet.”
“Could he be a Dark Heaven lackey?”
“We’d have to beat the truth out of him to be sure. But, as you already know, he doesn’t look or seem capable of pulling anything clever...”
“You can’t judge by a feeling alone. What do you think of the possibility that they’re deliberately hiding their strength?”
Jeok Cheongang wasn’t asking because he didn’t know. He meant for everyone listening to our conversation to hear the question. Once I understood his intent, I answered without hesitation.
“No chance.”
“You must have a reason for thinking so.”
“Old—no, Master, if they were strong enough to fool you and the others here, they’d have to have undergone at least Returning to Simplicity or Bone Transformation.”
“And?”
“Look at those faces. Supreme Peak masters who’d reached that level couldn’t possibly look like that.”
The seven terrifying-looking men, Ma Junggeol included, shuddered. What could I do? It was true.
I’d suddenly found myself playing lawyer, and I felt an inexplicable sense of duty as I continued.
“Therefore, I find no grounds to charge them with ‘vicious-looking men concealing their martial arts,’ and I rest my case.”
Jeok Cheongang nodded with an expression of admiration.
“Your argument is so logical that even this old man hardly dares to dispute it.”
“Thank you.”
“But looking at those faces—whether they’re Yellow Turbans, Dark Heaven, or men who’ve held important posts in the Demonic Cult at the very least—I can’t help but find them suspicious.”
“So what are you going to do?”
“Either they confess everything right now, or I’ll beat it out of them with the Flame Divine Palm.”
His voice was directed at me, but his gaze wasn’t.
Under Jeok Cheongang’s stare, which seemed to pour streams of fire, Ma Junggeol went pale and stammered, “A-are you really the Fire King, Great Hero Jeok Cheongang...?”
Jeok Cheongang replied with a bored look.
“Of course I’m real. Did you think I was a fake?”
“If that’s true, then the gisaeng’s older brother—no, the young man—is the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon...”
It was my turn to speak.
Smiling broadly at hearing that pleasant description again, I tried to reassure the terrified Ma Junggeol.
“Keep calling me a gisaeng’s older brother. Make yourself comfortable. Come to think of it, I was rude, speaking so casually to you all this time. I’m sorry. Okay?”
“N-no, that’s all right. But it seems there’s been a misunderstanding for a while now. May I say something to clear it up?”
“Now you’re talking. You should’ve said—spoken up sooner.”
“I was trying to explain, but you jumped straight to—”
“Go on, then. Skip the preamble.”
At my gentle but forceful urging, Ma Junggeol hesitated, then straightened his shoulders and cautiously addressed the leaders, Jeok Cheongang included.
“To cut to the chase, we came from Ningxia.”
“Hold on. Ningxia? Could you be...?”
A thought crossed my mind, and I frowned. Ma Junggeol hurriedly added, “We’re not mounted bandits!”
Jeok Cheongang muttered, “So that’s why their faces looked suspicious. They’re those mounted bandits who’ve been spreading filth all over Ningxia Province.”
“I-it’s true that I belonged to a band of mounted bandits for a short time, but that’s not who we are now...”
Just then, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord cut in, eyeing Ma Junggeol and his men with narrowed eyes.
“Infinite Life Buddha. I shouldn’t say this as a man who pursues the Way, but as Senior Jeok said, those faces clearly belong to men still in the trade.”
People nodded here and there in agreement.
Then, as if to prove why looks ruled modern society, the mood slowly turned hostile. One person spoke up.
“Ma Junggeol, Ma Junggeol... Could you be that very Ma Junggeol of Baekma Bang?”
It was the Black Night King, Sima Gong.
He’d been deep in thought with his brow furrowed. At his question, Ma Junggeol and his men—whose faces had been turning more and more sallow—visibly brightened.
“Y-you know me?”

“I’ve heard of you through the grapevine. More than ten years ago, an unknown master pacified the mounted-bandit gangs in Ningxia Province. A few of their leaders changed their ways under his guidance, joined forces, and founded a horse caravan.”
“That’s right! That’s me—or rather, that’s us!”
As though he’d finally found someone he could talk to, Ma Junggeol’s color returned. His expression grew serious as he saluted everyone with clasped hands.
“I am Ma Junggeol, Chief of Baekma Bang. The Seven Masters of Baekma Bang greet the heroes of the Murim Alliance.”
A suffocating silence pressed in from all sides.

The elegant title didn’t fit their vicious faces at all. The leaders and I silently exchanged glances, while the six men, prompted belatedly by Ma Junggeol, awkwardly copied his salute and whispered among themselves.
“Uh, is this how you do the salute, hyungs?”
“You idiot. How many times have I told you to cover your left hand with your right palm?”
“What are you talking about? The youngest did it right. Fourth Hyung’s the one doing it wrong.”
“Oh, you’re right...”
“Enough! Can’t you all shut up? Do you know what kind of place this is?”
“Sheesh. A minute ago you were shouting ‘Enough! Enough!’ at the top of your lungs. Now you lower your voice because there are masters around. Being born later is my fucking crime. My crime.”
What the hell was going on with these guys?
Their voices were low, but their conversation still came through clearly. Everyone’s eyes went flat. Only Sima Gong kept his composure as he spoke.

“Yes, I’ve heard about Baekma Bang a few times. I hear you’ve fought off the nomads who invaded through the northern Great Steppe and given plenty of help to the commoners who’ve begun settling there. But...”
Sima Gong let his voice trail off. His gaze suddenly sharpened.
“What brings you here so abruptly?”
With everyone’s attention on him, Ma Junggeol straightened his bent back and answered.
“We came here to offer our help.”
“Help with what?”
“Dark Heaven. We have important information about them.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1009
paragraphs: If Ma Junggeol had given even the slightest suspicious or flimsy reason, he would’ve been thrown straight back out the gate—or stuffed into the underground prison somewhere inside the city to have a long chat with the torture specialists.
But when he lowered his voice, the reason he gave was more important than I’d expected.
“Dark Heaven. I have important information about them.”
The moment he said it, everyone among the leadership, myself included, realized our unwelcome visitors might be a lot more useful than we’d thought.
“Well, we’ve kept our distinguished guests standing outside for far too long. Why don’t you come in for a cup of tea?”
At Sima Gong’s subtle invitation, Ma Junggeol straightened his shoulders as though nothing had happened and nodded.
“Sounds good. Just so you know, of all the teas, my brothers and I favor grain tea most.”
“I heard the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang were renowned drinkers. You’re every bit as forthright as they say. Come on in, then.”
Important conversations were best held with as few people watching as possible.
A few moments later, Ma Junggeol and his six men—no, the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang—had gone from unwelcome visitors to honored guests, each with a seat in the grand meeting hall.
“Ahhh. That’s good.”
Starting with Ma Junggeol, his six sworn brothers drained a small wine jar in one go, then smacked their lips.
“Whew, that’s really something.”
“What kind of liquor is this? It just melts on your tongue.”
“Right? It’s insane.”
“...It’s liquor. Of course it does. What the hell do you mean, ‘melts’? This is why people call you an idiot.”
“Enough! Fourth, is that any way to speak to your brothers?”
“Whew, look at you raising your voice again the second you can breathe easy. Honestly, I’d like to crack this wine jar over the back of your head right now.”
Naturally, no one’s head met the wine jar.
That was thanks to one remark from Jeok Cheongang, who’d been silently watching the seven-colored mounted-bandit rangers—or rather, the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang.
“Did you come here to drink?”
“You’ve wet your throats. Now, go on and spit it out.”
Ma Junggeol flinched at the menacing aura rolling off Jeok Cheongang, then stammered out a reply.
“F-first, I assume you already know something about the situation in Ningxia.”
“I’ve heard the basics. Because of mounted bandits like you, the place nearly became a battlefield, but it’s been quiet for the past few years. Is that right?”
“We’re no longer mounted bandits, but yes. Great Hero Jeok is right.”
“Still look like a bunch of mounted bandits to this old man, but go on.”

“There’ve been a few minor disputes over the years, but it’s become a fairly livable place. Anyone who’d done something they might feel guilty about left long ago. The ones who remain have completely turned over a new leaf and live ordinary lives, like me and my brothers. Sect Leader Sima here knows this well, too.”
Everyone’s eyes turned to Sima Gong. He nodded calmly.
“It’s true. As Ningxia Province settled down, various merchant caravans began passing through, and we heard all sorts of things from them. That was when I first heard about Baekma Bang.”
With Sima Gong backing him up, Ma Junggeol quickly picked up the thread.

“I don’t know exactly what you heard, Sect Leader Sima, but Baekma Bang is by far the largest group in Ningxia Province. Recently, we’ve even been opening a new trade route to help Ningxia Province prosper.”
“Wait. This new trade route you mentioned—is it perhaps...?”
“It’s probably where you’re thinking.”
Surprise spread across Sima Gong’s face. Watching him, I had a sudden thought.
“West. You mean west.”
My sudden words sent an invisible ripple through the room.
Naturally. The west I meant wasn’t Gansu or Qinghai.
“Xinjiang...”
The word slipped through the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s lips like a groan.

The Taeeul Merciless Sword and the Roaring Fury Swordsman had been watching Ma Junggeol with obvious disapproval for a while now, as though something about him rubbed them the wrong way. They frowned and spoke up, too.
“So that’s what this is about. Xinjiang, huh. Hah.”
“I can’t listen to this anymore. How long are we supposed to sit here listening to such ridiculous nonsense?”
Much as I hated to admit it, theirs was the reasonable reaction.
What kind of place was Xinjiang?
It was even called the Land of Ruin.
A cursed land of endless deserts, teeming with Fiends who proclaimed the world belonged to the Demonic Path.
And a mere horse-caravan group—not one of the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families—was supposed to open a trade route to Xinjiang?
What a joke.
And yet I could feel my heart beginning to beat faster.
The Taeeul Merciless Sword and the Roaring Fury Swordsman had forgotten the most important thing.
This wasn’t a pitch for investment or a business presentation.
Ma Junggeol’s story wasn’t over. The real story was only just beginning.
“That’s enough preamble, isn’t it?”
Jeok Cheongang’s low question left no doubt what he meant. Ma Junggeol drew a deep breath and spoke again.

“Even after things settled down, Ningxia Province was still in bad shape. The land was barren, and the nomads from the Great Steppe along our border raided us every harvest season. We needed a new way out.”
“So you wanted to cross the desert and open a trade route?”
“That was the idea, but it was nothing more than a dream. Even an uneducated fool like me knew people like us had no business dreaming of something so far beyond our reach. But...”
Ma Junggeol’s gaze suddenly shifted toward me.
“Not long ago, an opportunity came out of nowhere. The many nomads occupying the western Great Steppe suddenly began a mass migration.”
“Jamukha.”
The name slipped from my lips before I could stop it.
Only then did I understand why Ma Junggeol was looking at me, and what he’d meant by an unexpected opportunity.
Jamukha’s massive army had controlled the western steppe. They’d taken almost all their forces and marched into Shanxi Province. The gap they left behind had given Baekma Bang its chance.
“Then were you trying to reach Xinjiang through the steppe?”
At my question, gasps came from around the room.
Of course. There was another route, one so obvious now that everyone had forgotten it.
To the people of the Central Plains, the Great Steppe had long been another forbidden land, just like Xinjiang. But it was also the fastest shortcut across the desert.
Under everyone’s gaze, Ma Junggeol nodded, his face tense.
“That’s right.”

“I picked out the men under me who were good riders, and we kept driving our horses without stopping. After riding like mad for ten whole days, we finally saw a vast yellow stretch of land in the distance. We’d reached the desert.”
Just then, his six sworn brothers, who’d been keeping an eye on everyone’s reaction behind him, nodded and chimed in.
“Man, it was a real shitshow. Honestly, I wanted to say to hell with the Chief and the whole damn venture and turn back.”
“But what could we do? We’d already come that far. We figured we might as well set foot on the sand before going home.”
“Then we traveled another ten days or so, right?”
“Don’t remind me. Even now, just thinking about that goddamn desert makes my knees buckle.”
“Enough! What a bunch of weaklings. Even through all that hardship, I trusted Big Brother and followed him.”
The diminutive middle-aged man, who looked rather old, delivered a stern rebuke. The man with the bulbous nose snorted.

“They say even if a horse’s hooves go crooked, you should keep the reins straight. So at least get your story straight. What did you do the moment those black bastards showed up on the tenth day, Second Hyung? You didn’t even look back. You got ready to run.”
“Enough...!”
The dwarf’s face turned as red as a ripe persimmon. He lunged at the bulbous-nosed man, but I was much faster.
Snatch.
His small fist landed squarely in my grasp.
I’d caught the dwarf’s punch with ridiculous ease. I fixed the bulbous-nosed man with a cold stare.
“Say that again.”
“W-what?”
“You just said those black bastards appeared on the tenth day after you entered the desert.”
He’d said it in passing, but everyone in the room had heard him clearly.
And the moment we heard it, our suspicion turned to certainty.
“It was Dark Heaven.”
Ma Junggeol spoke up in place of the bulbous-nosed man and continued.
“There were only a few dozen of them, but I’m certain. I’ll stake my life on it.”
Sima Gong spoke in a grave voice.
“What makes you so certain?”
“We followed them.”
“What?”
“For a day and a half. That was the best we could do. But I saw it with my own eyes. That night, when the moon was unusually bright, at least a thousand tents covered the sand dunes.”
“There’s only one force in the western desert that could mobilize an army that large. Dark Heaven. Isn’t that right?”
A cold silence filled the meeting hall instead of an answer.
A thousand. Not a thousand people—a thousand tents.
What’s more, Ma Junggeol’s route across the desert was clearly closer to Gansu than Qinghai.
Even by the lowest estimate, that meant thousands, perhaps tens of thousands, of enemies were targeting Gansu Province.
And that might not even be all of them.
My mind went cold. Meanwhile, my heartbeat had grown so fast it was thundering in my ears.
Of course, it was too soon to be certain. There was still a question I needed answered before making a decision.
“You’re lucky you made it back alive.”
Sima Gong’s low voice broke the silence. Under his unfathomable gaze, Ma Junggeol licked his parched lips.
“It was close. I thought my heart was going to burst.”
“You know what I mean. Are you pretending not to?”
“We followed at a distance of exactly a hundred li. The beginning was hard, but after that, their numbers kept growing, which made it much easier.”
“A mere horse caravan followed Dark Heaven without being spotted? Is that possible?”

“I’m ashamed to say it, but we’re not an ordinary horse caravan, are we? We may not wear our hair in queues, but when it comes to riding and keeping a sharp eye out, we’re no different from the nomads.”
“You could have turned back as soon as you spotted them. Why follow them for another day and a half?”
“That... well...”
Ma Junggeol hesitated, glanced at Sima Gong, then answered cautiously.
“I’d heard that if you render a service for the good of the realm, no one holds your origins against you.”
“You were thinking about a reward?”
“Yes.”
They’d managed it because there were few enough of them to avoid notice, and because their years as mounted bandits had taught them how to survive.
Their reason was clear, too.
After a moment’s thought, I turned to Jeok Cheongang and spoke.
“Now we know for sure which battlefield we need to be on.”

You’re every bit as forthright as they say.
Come on in, then.”
Important conversations were best held with as few people watching as possible.
A few moments later, Ma Junggeol and his six men—no, the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang—had gone from unwelcome visitors to honored guests, each with a seat in the grand meeting hall.

That’s good.”

“Whew, that’s really something.”
“What kind of liquor is this?
It just melts on your tongue.”
“Right?
It’s insane.”
“...It’s liquor.
Of course it does.
What the hell do you mean, ‘melts’?
This is why people call you an idiot.”
“Enough!
Fourth, is that any way to speak to your brothers?”
“Whew, look at you raising your voice again the second you can breathe easy.
Honestly, I’d like to crack this wine jar over the back of your head right now.”
Naturally, no one’s head met the wine jar.
That was thanks to one remark from Jeok Cheongang, who’d been silently watching the seven-colored mounted-bandit rangers—or rather, the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang.
“Did you come here to drink?”
“You’ve wet your throats.
Now, go on and spit it out.”
Ma Junggeol flinched at the menacing aura rolling off Jeok Cheongang, then stammered out a reply.
“F-first, I assume you already know something about the situation in Ningxia.”
“I’ve heard the basics.
Because of mounted bandits like you, the place nearly became a battlefield, but it’s been quiet for the past few years.
Is that right?”
“We’re no longer mounted bandits, but yes.
Great Hero Jeok is right.”
“Still look like a bunch of mounted bandits to this old man, but go on.”
“There’ve been a few minor disputes over the years, but it’s become a fairly livable place.
Anyone who’d done something they might feel guilty about left long ago.
The ones who remain have completely turned over a new leaf and live ordinary lives, like me and my brothers.
Sect Leader Sima here knows this well, too.”
Everyone’s eyes turned to Sima Gong.
He nodded calmly.
“It’s true.
As Ningxia Province settled down, various merchant caravans began passing through, and we heard all sorts of things from them.
That was when I first heard about Baekma Bang.”
With Sima Gong backing him up, Ma Junggeol quickly picked up the thread.
“I don’t know exactly what you heard, Sect Leader Sima, but Baekma Bang is by far the largest group in Ningxia Province.
Recently, we’ve even been opening a new trade route to help Ningxia Province prosper.”
“Wait.
This new trade route you mentioned—is it perhaps...?”
“It’s probably where you’re thinking.”
Surprise spread across Sima Gong’s face.
Watching him, I had a sudden thought.

You mean west.”
My sudden words sent an invisible ripple through the room.
Naturally.
The west I meant wasn’t Gansu or Qinghai.

The word slipped through the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s lips like a groan.

Hah.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1010
paragraphs: “So, that’s what you’ve decided?”
At Jeok Cheongang’s question, I nodded.
“Yes. I think I need to stay here after all.”
If Ma Junggeol and his men had arrived half a day later, I’d probably already be on my way to Qinghai with the Fire Dragon Pavilion members.
Gansu had enough forces as things stood.
The Kongtong Sect and the Zhongnan Sect.
Two towering powers of the Nine Sects and One Gang stood firm here, and the Black Dragon Demon Gate, led by Sima Gong, was every bit their equal.
The dark-path figures and unorthodox factions gathered under the Black Dragon Demon Gate might have been inferior in quality, but their sheer numbers made them an enormous force.
But now the situation had changed.
The massive Dark Heaven army—estimated to number at least tens of thousands—was a problem. But the biggest reason I’d decided to stay in Gansu was time.
The time it would take them to reach us.
“When exactly did you return to Ningxia?”
Ma Junggeol answered.
“Three days ago. We arrived in the middle of the night, so I suppose you could say it was two days ago.”
“Three days ago?”
Jeok Cheongang cut in abruptly, furrowing his brow. Ma Junggeol hurriedly continued.
“W-we were facing an emergency ourselves. We were so busy sending urgent messages throughout Ningxia and getting our men moving that we barely had time to think.”
He’d apparently taken Jeok Cheongang’s reaction to mean, You arrived three days ago, so why are you only coming to us now? But I knew why Jeok Cheongang had frowned.
That was right around the time.
A memory suddenly came to mind.
Several hundred people, trembling with fear, had said mounted bandits were roaming not far away.
Ningxia Province must still have seemed lawless to them. With Ma Junggeol’s urgent message causing an uproar, they’d probably mistaken the commotion for a mounted-bandit attack.
It had all happened so recently that even the Lower District Sect member from the Shaanxi branch hadn’t known the details.
So that’s what it was.
Things come around, and everything connects.
The outcome of one incident becomes the beginning of another, until eventually it all leads here.
And Ma Junggeol’s answer—that they’d arrived three days ago—gave everyone plenty to think about.
“How long did it take you to get back?”
At the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s question, Ma Junggeol counted on his fingers.
“Let’s see. It took seven days and nights just to get out of the desert, and crossing the grasslands again took a day longer than that... About a month, I’d say.”
“Wait. Didn’t you say earlier that it took twenty days just to get there? And then you spent another day and a half following Dark Heaven.”
“That’s right. But traveling a route for the first time isn’t the same as taking it on the way back. Do you think we’re mounted bandits—no, horse caravans—for nothing?”
It was hard to argue with that.

Just as the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, a Supreme Peak master, could judge an opponent’s level and the kind of martial arts they practiced from only a few forms, no one could match mounted bandits and horse caravans at finding the fastest route.
“Too much caution can be its own poison. There’s something more important here.”
Jeok Cheongang stopped the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord before he could respond and fixed his gaze on Ma Junggeol.
“If you were leading an army of tens of thousands, how long would it take you to reach here?”
“W-well...”
Ma Junggeol thought hard for a moment, then sighed.
“That’s hard to answer. But...”
“But?”
“Assuming they had enough camels, desert horses, and supplies—and every last one of them knew enough martial arts to endure a grueling forced march... Yes. Even with delays, a month at most.”
“One month. Just a month.”
“Of course, depending on the circumstances, it could be much shorter.”
Ma Junggeol glanced around as he added that last part. Sima Gong’s face stiffened.
“What circumstances do you mean?”
“Have you forgotten? We lost more time than necessary crossing the grasslands. Where we spotted them wasn’t all that far from Gansu. Even taking that enormous force into account...”
Ma Junggeol trailed off. He swallowed hard before continuing.
“A-about twenty days should be enough.”
The air in the meeting room turned cold.
No—it froze like a glacier.
His words reminded everyone of a fact they’d briefly forgotten. They stared at one another, eyes wide.
That was right.
Unlike Ma Junggeol, who’d had to hurry back the way he came, Dark Heaven had another option.
They could advance.
Instead of detouring across the grasslands, they could break through the front by sheer force.
And if they chose a direct assault, there would be precious little time left before the fighting began.
One day, or maybe two.
Of course, that was the worst-case scenario.
No one knew whether Dark Heaven’s army had stayed there for several more days after Ma Junggeol left—or whether they were still there now.
But we had to plan for the worst.
That was war.
“I think we can throw any more armchair strategizing out the window. Don’t you all agree?”
Over Jeok Cheongang’s low voice, which broke the silence, rang a clear chime that didn’t fit the situation at all.
Ding.
Rumble, rumble.
Was this what a small mountain would look like in motion?

With the Black Dragon Demon Gate, the Zhongnan Sect, and the hundreds of martial artists Sima Gong had conscripted from nearby, our force had grown to more than two thousand—close to three thousand. I looked at the endless wave of people and horses stretching out behind me, then raised my eyes to the air.
More precisely, to the translucent holographic window floating there.

System The conditions for the current Quest have been met! Head West — Complete Quest Desert Mirage successfully completed! Quest rewards have been granted! Gained a large amount of EXP and Fame! A new linked Quest has been generated upon completion of Desert Mirage. Would you like to view the new Quest?
Barely half an hour.
That was an impossibly short time for an army of nearly three thousand to finish its preparations and set out. I certainly hadn’t had a chance to check the newly generated linked Quest.
Not that I needed to check it right away. I had a rough idea what it would say.
I adjusted my grip on the reins of my galloping horse and gave the command in my head.
Open Quest window.
Ding.

System Quest Road of Blood Long ago, this land was a trade route linking one continent to another. Today, it has fallen into grave peril. The foreign merchants with their unfamiliar features are gone. So are those who crossed the desert for foreign lands with wagons piled high with silk. The rulers of the vast desert have cut off the trade route that once brought prosperity to the Central Plains. Now they want everything within the Great Wall. The old days, when silk flowed in abundance, have become a distant, dusty past. Steel without end, blood, and corpses will be the present and future of this land. May fortune be with you. Grade: Supreme Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung Mission: Annihilate enemy forces in the Gansu region — Incomplete Reward: A large amount of EXP and Fame Linked Quest based on your choice Failure: Dark Heaven wins — Lose control of the Gansu region
As expected.
It was more or less what I’d anticipated.
Actually, I knew full well that if we failed, it wouldn’t end there.
If the Gansu front collapses, the entire west will be in danger.
War was like a line of dominoes.
No matter how carefully and thoroughly you prepared from beginning to end, one mistake could bring everything you’d built crashing down in an instant.
We have to stop them before it’s too late.
At least Gansu Murim had prepared thoroughly.
Three successive defensive lines, with thirty thousand troops deployed according to each line’s importance.
Dunhuang, the foremost of those three lines, was close enough to reach within three days if we pushed ourselves to the limit.
The Silk Road.
Better known by that name to people in the modern world, this region was an endless stretch of plains and wilderness.
There was no narrow path to slow us down, no terrain so rugged we’d have to abandon our horses.
We just had to ride until the horses collapsed from exhaustion.
The problem was...
Dark Heaven could do the same.
That was why we couldn’t afford to lose even a moment.
Even with camels and desert horses, there was a limit to how fast they could travel through the desert. But once they reached land covered in soil and grass instead of sand, that would change.
Dunhuang would be the first domino to fall, and tens of thousands of enemies would soon swarm across Gansu like locusts—
“What are you staring at so intently?”
“Checking the shape of the clouds or something?”
I wasn’t exaggerating when I said I nearly jumped out of my skin.
It wasn’t the sudden voice that startled me. It was the menacing face that filled my vision the moment I turned my head.
“Ah, damn. You scared me. What’s with you all of a sudden?”
Ma Junggeol answered, sitting as comfortably as ever on his violently bouncing saddle. A former mounted bandit and current horse-caravan chief through and through.
“Nothing much. You’ve been staring into the air for a while, so I thought I’d talk to you.”
“What’s it to you where I’m looking? And I don’t think we’re close enough to be chatting.”
“Of course we’re not. You’re the one who had them rain arrows down on me. Three times, no less.”
His already vicious face twisted into a scowl. I answered flatly.
“So?”
“...You’ve got no conscience, do you? And even if I can understand the first two times, what on earth were you thinking when you ordered them to fire the third?”
“Just thought stopping at two would make me look cold.”
“That’s it. Happy?”
At my offhand answer, Ma Junggeol gaped at me as if I were insane.
“What do you mean, ‘that’s it’? Are you even human?”
“Feels like that’s a question I should be asking you.”
“...What’s that supposed to mean?”
What did it mean? He knew perfectly well.
But I was too tenderhearted to hit him with the facts about his looks.
I silently shrugged. Looking at Ma Junggeol, I had another thought.
Still, he really is nothing like he looks.

Judging by his face alone, he looked like some evil spirit who could plunge the world into ruin. But from the way he acted, and the bits of his personality that showed through now and then, he seemed surprisingly stupid.
Even now, at the strong insistence of a few leaders who still suspected Ma Junggeol and the other horse-caravan men, he was practically being held hostage. Yet he seemed utterly carefree.

Didn’t you say earlier that it took twenty days just to get there?
And then you spent another day and a half following Dark Heaven.”
“That’s right.
But traveling a route for the first time isn’t the same as taking it on the way back.
Do you think we’re mounted bandits—no, horse caravans—for nothing?”
It was hard to argue with that.

Just as the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, a Supreme Peak master, could judge an opponent’s level and the kind of martial arts they practiced from only a few forms, no one could match mounted bandits and horse caravans at finding the fastest route.
“Too much caution can be its own poison.
There’s something more important here.”
Jeok Cheongang stopped the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord before he could respond and fixed his gaze on Ma Junggeol.
“If you were leading an army of tens of thousands, how long would it take you to reach here?”
“W-well...”
Ma Junggeol thought hard for a moment, then sighed.
“That’s hard to answer.
But...”
“But?”
“Assuming they had enough camels, desert horses, and supplies—and every last one of them knew enough martial arts to endure a grueling forced march...
Yes.
Even with delays, a month at most.”
“One month.
Just a month.”
“Of course, depending on the circumstances, it could be much shorter.”
Ma Junggeol glanced around as he added that last part.
Sima Gong’s face stiffened.
“What circumstances do you mean?”
“Have you forgotten?
We lost more time than necessary crossing the grasslands.
Where we spotted them wasn’t all that far from Gansu.
Even taking that enormous force into account...”
Ma Junggeol trailed off.
He swallowed hard before continuing.
“A-about twenty days should be enough.”
The air in the meeting room turned cold.
No—it froze like a glacier.
His words reminded everyone of a fact they’d briefly forgotten.
They stared at one another, eyes wide.
That was right.
Unlike Ma Junggeol, who’d had to hurry back the way he came, Dark Heaven had another option.
They could advance.
Instead of detouring across the grasslands, they could break through the front by sheer force.
And if they chose a direct assault, there would be precious little time left before the fighting began.
One day, or maybe two.
Of course, that was the worst-case scenario.
No one knew whether Dark Heaven’s army had stayed there for several more days after Ma Junggeol left—or whether they were still there now.
But we had to plan for the worst.
That was war.
“I think we can throw any more armchair strategizing out the window.
Don’t you all agree?”
Over Jeok Cheongang’s low voice, which broke the silence, rang a clear chime that didn’t fit the situation at all.
Ding.
Rumble, rumble.
Was this what a small mountain would look like in motion?
With the Black Dragon Demon Gate, the Zhongnan Sect, and the hundreds of martial artists Sima Gong had conscripted from nearby, our force had grown to more than two thousand—close to three thousand.
I looked at the endless wave of people and horses stretching out behind me, then raised my eyes to the air.
More precisely, to the translucent holographic window floating there.
System The conditions for the current Quest have been met!
Head West — Complete Quest Desert Mirage successfully completed!
Quest rewards have been granted!
Gained a large amount of EXP and Fame!
A new linked Quest has been generated upon completion of Desert Mirage.
Would you like to view the new Quest?
Barely half an hour.
That was an impossibly short time for an army of nearly three thousand to finish its preparations and set out.
I certainly hadn’t had a chance to check the newly generated linked Quest.
Not that I needed to check it right away.
I had a rough idea what it would say.
I adjusted my grip on the reins of my galloping horse and gave the command in my head.
Open Quest window.
Ding.
System Quest Road of Blood Long ago, this land was a trade route linking one continent to another.
Today, it has fallen into grave peril.
The foreign merchants with their unfamiliar features are gone.
So are those who crossed the desert for foreign lands with wagons piled high with silk.
The rulers of the vast desert have cut off the trade route that once brought prosperity to the Central Plains.
Now they want everything within the Great Wall.
The old days, when silk flowed in abundance, have become a distant, dusty past.
Steel without end, blood, and corpses will be the present and future of this land.
May fortune be with you.

Grade: Supreme Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung Mission: Annihilate enemy forces in the Gansu region — Incomplete Reward: A large amount of EXP and Fame Linked Quest based on your choice Failure: Dark Heaven wins — Lose control of the Gansu region
As expected.
It was more or less what I’d anticipated.
Actually, I knew full well that if we failed, it wouldn’t end there.
If the Gansu front collapses, the entire west will be in danger.
War was like a line of dominoes.
No matter how carefully and thoroughly you prepared from beginning to end, one mistake could bring everything you’d built crashing down in an instant.
We have to stop them before it’s too late.
At least Gansu Murim had prepared thoroughly.
Three successive defensive lines, with thirty thousand troops deployed according to each line’s importance.
Dunhuang, the foremost of those three lines, was close enough to reach within three days if we pushed ourselves to the limit.
The Silk Road.
Better known by that name to people in the modern world, this region was an endless stretch of plains and wilderness.
There was no narrow path to slow us down, no terrain so rugged we’d have to abandon our horses.
We just had to ride until the horses collapsed from exhaustion.
The problem was...
Dark Heaven could do the same.
That was why we couldn’t afford to lose even a moment.
Even with camels and desert horses, there was a limit to how fast they could travel through the desert.
But once they reached land covered in soil and grass instead of sand, that would change.
Dunhuang would be the first domino to fall, and tens of thousands of enemies would soon swarm across Gansu like locusts—
“What are you staring at so intently?”
“Checking the shape of the clouds or something?”
I wasn’t exaggerating when I said I nearly jumped out of my skin.
It wasn’t the sudden voice that startled me.
It was the menacing face that filled my vision the moment I turned my head.
“Ah, damn.
You scared me.
What’s with you all of a sudden?”
Ma Junggeol answered, sitting as comfortably as ever on his violently bouncing saddle.
A former mounted bandit and current horse-caravan chief through and through.
“Nothing much.
You’ve been staring into the air for a while, so I thought I’d talk to you.”
“What’s it to you where I’m looking?
And I don’t think we’re close enough to be chatting.”
“Of course we’re not.
You’re the one who had them rain arrows down on me.
Three times, no less.”
His already vicious face twisted into a scowl.
I answered flatly.
“So?”
“...You’ve got no conscience, do you?
And even if I can understand the first two times, what on earth were you thinking when you ordered them to fire the third?”
“Just thought stopping at two would make me look cold.”
“That’s it.
Happy?”
At my offhand answer, Ma Junggeol gaped at me as if I were insane.
“What do you mean, ‘that’s it’?
Are you even human?”
“Feels like that’s a question I should be asking you.”
“...What’s that supposed to mean?”
What did it mean?
He knew perfectly well.
But I was too tenderhearted to hit him with the facts about his looks.
I silently shrugged.
Looking at Ma Junggeol, I had another thought.
Still, he really is nothing like he looks.
Judging by his face alone, he looked like some evil spirit who could plunge the world into ruin.
But from the way he acted, and the bits of his personality that showed through now and then, he seemed surprisingly stupid.
Even now, at the strong insistence of a few leaders who still suspected Ma Junggeol and the other horse-caravan men, he was practically being held hostage.
Yet he seemed utterly carefree.

chapters.title: Chapter 1011
paragraphs: Suspecting someone was hardly a good thing.
But in a time of war, suspicion was another word for caution.
The longer and more closely you looked, the clearer the truth became—and the closer you came to victory.
That was the main reason Ma Junggeol and the other six members of the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang had joined our party.
Or, to be precise, the Fire Dragon Pavilion I led.
Though I was the one who volunteered to take them.
They were originally supposed to be placed under Sima Gong’s watch. But when I pointed out that he already had a sizable force to command, the decision came quickly.
They would be assigned to the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Time was so short that no one raised any further objections. Still, I saw it clearly.
The moment the decision about the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang was made, Sima Gong’s eyes sank deeper than before.
Am I imagining it? Or...
I let the thought trail off and glanced at Ma Junggeol.
He’d been grumbling about how rude it was to ignore someone standing right in front of you, but at some point he’d gone quiet.
Or so it seemed.
Thud-thud-thud!
Hooves thundered beneath us. A fierce wind wrapped around my body and rushed past.
And through it all...
Wooooong.
A faint ripple reached me, almost hidden by the noise.
This is...
I knew it instinctively. It was a flow of qi only someone who had reached a profound realm could sense.
Buried beneath the pounding hooves and rushing wind, that faint ripple carried a voice I had never heard before.
Ssshhh.
I hadn’t reasoned it out. This was an instinct I’d forgotten for a moment.
Like a child just discovering he could stand on two feet, I sent my qi toward the ripple emanating from Ma Junggeol.
It touched, mingled with, and became one with the ripple.
So naturally that even Ma Junggeol, its source, didn’t notice.
The same went for the ripples his six sworn brothers were exchanging nearby.
“...long do we have to be dragged along like this?”
The faint ripple—no, the Sound Transmission—rang clearly in my ears at last.
Ding.

System Hidden achievement A Bug in My Ear achieved! You can now detect and eavesdrop on nearby Sound Transmissions! This is another ability granted to those who reach a great realm. But don’t get too excited. The Sound Transmissions you can eavesdrop on are limited by the levels of both the target and the user!
...So I can do this now.
I blinked in a daze, then focused on the Sound Transmissions reaching my ears.
Let’s hear what they’re plotting.
“Honestly, how long do we have to be dragged along like this?”
“Exactly. What are we, hostages?”
“Whew, Father. I miss you so much today.”
“Huh? Didn’t your father pass away more than twenty years ago?”
“That’s why I miss him even more.”
“Oh.”
Ma Junggeol answered his younger brothers’ grumbling Sound Transmissions sternly.
“Now, now. Why are you all complaining? We expected this from the start.”
The second brother, who fled faster than anyone in an emergency but worshipped the Chief like the heavens the rest of the time, nodded.
“Enough! The Chief is a hundred, a thousand times right, so all of you shut up. If he hadn’t foreseen this from the beginning, would he have dragged us into such a deathtrap?”
That was the second brother for you.
There was a reason people said no younger brother could outdo his older brother.
Ma Junggeol smiled with satisfaction as the little man gently put the others in their place.
“Didn’t you hear what the Chief said earlier?”
The third brother, who always had to stick his foot in, broke in. The second blinked.
“Earlier? When?”
“Right before we left. He went off by himself, supposedly to check a perfectly good saddle, and started muttering under his breath. I listened, and...”
“And?”
“No, there’s nothing to hear. It was nothing, so don’t worry about it.”
Ma Junggeol remembered what had happened half a shichen earlier and hurried to cut him off. But the third brother’s Sound Transmission was already riding the wind.
“We’re fucked. What do we do now?”
A wind colder than the bitter north wind swept through the group.
In the heavy silence, six pairs of eyes bored mercilessly into the back of Ma Junggeol’s head. His gaze darkened.
“Chief...”
“Third Brother, is that true?”
“It’s not, is it? It isn’t, right?”
“If that’s true, then seriously...”
“E-enough! There’s no way the Chief would say that.”
“What do you mean, ‘there’s no way’? I heard him with my own ears.”
At a loss for words, Ma Junggeol’s eyes darted back and forth.
How was he supposed to answer? He’d never dreamed anyone would hear the words he’d let slip—least of all the third brother.
“That, well...”
Unable to stay silent forever, he sent a hesitant reply.
His six quick-witted brothers groaned at once.
“So it’s true.”
“It really is.”
“Ah, Mother. I want to see you so badly today.”
“Sometimes it’s like that. When someone passed away long ago, you miss them all the more.”
“Are you crazy? She’s still perfectly healthy. Why are you killing her off?”
“Oh.”
“Enough...!”
“Chief, what are we actually going to do? At this rate, they’ll drag us all the way to the front and use us to catch swords, won’t they?”
Unlike the others, who had descended into confusion, the third brother was at least facing reality. Ma Junggeol gave the faintest shake of his head.
“Don’t worry. Things are going a little—just a little—worse than I expected, but they won’t use us to catch swords like you said.”
“If it’s not swords, it’ll be arrows. Thanks, Chief. You’ve ruined all our lives.”
“Now, now. I said that won’t happen!”
“What makes you so sure? Let’s be blunt. If they give us an order, we’re in no position to refuse.”
“Well...”

“Look around. There are already several Supreme Peak masters here—people you’d be lucky to see once in your life. If those monsters start prodding us in the back and giving us the look, what choice do guys like us have except to run out and fight like hell?”
The third brother’s Sound Transmission poured out with pent-up anger. His sworn brothers joined in.
“There are those Zhongnan Sect Daoist punks treating us like outright bandits, the Black Night King himself, the Fire King, and that young Disciple of his who looks half-mad.”
“Especially that Jin Taekyung right in front of the Chief. He’s not right in the head. Have you forgotten how we nearly crossed the Sanzu River before we’d even made it through the gate?”

“Damn it, is this why we quit being mounted bandits? I’ll admit our past wasn’t exactly something to brag about, but we quit before we’d even gotten to rob anyone! We spent all day, every day sharpening our swords and never even got to draw them.”

“Enough! Now that I think about it, this is downright unfair. Have we robbed anyone? Killed any innocent civilians? We’d only just made up our minds to pull off one good score when we met Great Sir and turned over a new leaf. We’re trying to live decent lives, and this is what we get?”
“Second Brother’s right. Sure, we look like this, but if we’d gone around doing only the most vicious things like everyone else, do you think Great Sir would’ve left us alone? Isn’t that right?”
Their Sound Transmissions were full of wounded indignation. Listening to them, Ma Junggeol felt a pang in his own heart.
They were right. What had they done wrong?
He couldn’t deny that they used to be mounted bandits. But he could swear to heaven that they’d never done anything deserving punishment.
If we had, at least this treatment wouldn’t feel so unfair.
Robbing civilians?
Even when they steeled themselves and rode out to attack, they couldn’t bring themselves to do it.
What could they take from people other mounted bandits had already stripped bare? Countless times, they’d given food instead to families holding newborns too hungry to cry.
And that wasn’t all.
They might have looked like fiends, but Ma Junggeol and his six sworn brothers were timid by nature.

Robbing or killing civilians had been impossible for them from the start. And even when they occasionally came across a gutsy merchant caravan traveling to Ningxia Province, they just collected a toll and let it pass.
Why?
Simple.
Because they were scared.
Who would travel through a lawless place like Ningxia Province without a proper escort?
It was only natural for an Escort Bureau or merchant caravan to bring at least several dozen armed men. In that tense standoff, Ma Junggeol just had to put on his vicious face and say:
“So, you mean to shed blood after all?”
A face to rival any fiend’s, paired with a stern voice, made an excellent way to talk things over.
Whether the other party was an Escort Bureau, a merchant caravan, or a mounted-bandit group so practiced at killing that they were nearly ready to ascend to immortality.
That was how Ma Junggeol and his six sworn brothers had survived as mounted bandits back when their martial arts were still rudimentary.
Until the man they called Great Sir appeared.
Even now, Ma Junggeol firmly believed in Great Sir, who had led them onto the right path.
“Enough, all of you!”
At his forceful Sound Transmission, the complaints streaming from behind him stopped at once.
Ma Junggeol seized the brief opening.
“There’s nothing to worry about. Set me aside—surely Great Sir anticipated a situation like this?”
“Hmm.”
“That’s true.”
“The Chief might not have, but Great Sir is different.”
“Right. We can’t trust the Chief, but we can trust Great Sir.”
“Now that you mention it, that makes sense.”
“For once, you’re saying something right.”
The answers only made him feel stranger the longer he thought about them, but Ma Junggeol continued his Sound Transmission with a vague sense of unease.
“I sent a few men back on the pretext of relaying news to Ningxia, so Great Sir will hear about this. Until then, don’t do anything rash. Understood?”
The third brother, the one with the bulbous nose, cut in.
“But that’s only if Great Sir’s in his right mind.”
“What?”
“Well, isn’t it? You know as well as anyone how he can be a little... all over the place.”
Ma Junggeol blinked a few times, then stammered out a reply.
“H-he’ll be fine. Probably.”
Even without his uncertain answer, his sworn brothers knew no one could be sure of that.
“Damn. Now that Third Brother’s said it, I’ve got a bad feeling.”
“But hasn’t Great Sir been more or less all right lately? That’s why he’s been telling us where to go from here and all that.”
“He has. But with him, you never know when he’ll snap.”
“Great Sir was strange from the first time we met him. His hair was a tangled mess, and his face was so black with grime you’d think he hadn’t washed in days. He looked like a beggar. Still does.”
“This is bad. If Great Sir’s out of it right now, sending the men to him won’t do any good, will it?”
As his sworn brothers’ worry deepened, Ma Junggeol scrunched up his already ugly face and thought hard. At last, he spoke.
“We have no choice. One of us should go in person. Maybe seeing a familiar face will help him come to his senses sooner.”
“One of us? Who?”
“Hard to say. We’ll have to decide now.”
“And once we do, how are you going to send him? That’ll be difficult right now.”
“As the Chief, I’ll take care of that, so don’t worry—wait a minute.”
Ma Junggeol abruptly stopped his Sound Transmission and frowned.
“You’ve been awfully casual with me for a while now. Did you lose half your tongue or something? Which insolent bastard is it? Huh?”
At that very moment, an actual voice he hadn’t expected reached his ears.
“Me.”
“It’s me.”
No. Impossible. Surely not.
Muttering to himself, Ma Junggeol slowly raised his head. He’d been keeping it slightly lowered to hide his moving lips.
There, facing him, was that insolent bastard, smiling menacingly.
“Uh, uhh.”
Ma Junggeol shuddered as if possessed by a ghost. Jin Taekyung smiled warmly at him.
“Looks like there’s a lot you need to tell me. Isn’t that right?”

“But that’s only if Great Sir’s in his right mind.”
“What?”
“Well, isn’t it?
You know as well as anyone how he can be a little... all over the place.”
Ma Junggeol blinked a few times, then stammered out a reply.
“H-he’ll be fine.
Probably.”
Even without his uncertain answer, his sworn brothers knew no one could be sure of that.
“Damn.
Now that Third Brother’s said it, I’ve got a bad feeling.”
“But hasn’t Great Sir been more or less all right lately?
That’s why he’s been telling us where to go from here and all that.”
“He has.
But with him, you never know when he’ll snap.”
“Great Sir was strange from the first time we met him.
His hair was a tangled mess, and his face was so black with grime you’d think he hadn’t washed in days.
He looked like a beggar.
Still does.”
“This is bad.
If Great Sir’s out of it right now, sending the men to him won’t do any good, will it?”
As his sworn brothers’ worry deepened, Ma Junggeol scrunched up his already ugly face and thought hard.
At last, he spoke.
“We have no choice.
One of us should go in person.
Maybe seeing a familiar face will help him come to his senses sooner.”
“One of us?
Who?”
“Hard to say.
We’ll have to decide now.”
“And once we do, how are you going to send him?
That’ll be difficult right now.”
“As the Chief, I’ll take care of that, so don’t worry—wait a minute.”

“You’ve been awfully casual with me for a while now.
Did you lose half your tongue or something?
Which insolent bastard is it?
Huh?”

“It’s me.”

Surely not.

“Uh, uhh.”
