chapters.title: Chapter 1012
paragraphs: Time swept by like the wind as the horses galloped without rest.
The sunset swallowed the wilderness, and the darkness that followed pressed down on the world. Then a dim dawn crept in between them.
By the time darkness fell for the second time, Ma Junggeol’s lips, which had been moving nonstop, could finally rest.
“...And that’s what happened.”
By the end of his long story, Ma Junggeol looked as though he’d aged overnight.

He’d spent more than a full day recounting everything that had happened over the past decade or so. But I suspected the audience—growing one person at a time, starting with me—had taken an even greater toll.
Especially the pressure radiating from the giant known as the Fire King.
“What do you mean, ‘that’s what happened’? Keep talking.”
At Jeok Cheongang’s low growl, Ma Junggeol, already exhausted, looked ready to cry.
“I really am finished. I’m telling you, there’s nothing else to say.”
“If I dig around and something else comes out, it’s ten hits per syllable. Still nothing?”
“What?”
It wasn’t as if he had a stash of stories hidden away. What was there to dig for?
Ma Junggeol gave me a pleading look. I shook my head and spoke up.
“Give it a rest. And why would he say anything if it’s a hundred hits per syllable? Even if he had more to tell, he’d hold out to the death.”
“Is that so? Then I’ll lower it to ten. Spill everything.”
“Ten would still kill him.”
“Fine. One hit. That’s this old man’s final offer.”
“...You might as well tell him to make his last will. At this point, it seems like you just want to kill him.”
Jeok Cheongang frowned at my quiet objection.
“You’re too soft. Sometimes you have to squeeze a man to get even one more word out of him.”
“Look at him. You couldn’t squeeze a drop of broth out of him now.”
I wasn’t exaggerating. Ma Junggeol looked as if half his soul had left his body.
Think about it.

Ten years was easy to say. But he’d had to recall, in detail and without a wink of sleep, everything that had happened over a span long enough for mountains and rivers to change. No wonder he’d turned into a half-dried squid in just over a day.
“P-please believe me. I really told you everything. I didn’t leave a thing out.”
Ma Junggeol pleaded with tears in his eyes, and his six sworn brothers opened their mouths to back him up.
Or rather, they started to.
“What Eldest Brother said is righ—”
“Shut your mouths before I beat you. Especially you.”
The short one Jeok Cheongang had singled out froze.
“M-me?”
“Yes, you. Chatter like that one more time and you’re dead. Do you have to chime in after every sentence, you little brat?”
The short one clamped his mouth shut. Watching from beside him, the bulbous-nosed one murmured with delight.
“Finally...”
Finally what?
None of these men seemed quite right in the head, but one thing was clear.
“Mujin.”

Hyuk Mujin understood what I meant and clicked his tongue. The other members reacted much the same way, apart from Sama Pyo and Taishan, who’d joined us the day before along with the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
“Tsk. Is this really okay? It doesn’t sit right with me.”
“Benefactor—no, Young Master Jin—no, Pavilion Master.”
“I think we should at least tie them up.”
“I see it differently—damn it, this miserable saddle!”
Unlike Taishan’s shoulders, which were as comfortable as a cushioned seat, Namho was perched on a saddle that bounced violently beneath him. Grimacing at the pain in his backside, he continued:
“We should follow the Pavilion Master’s orders. That’s the right call. Besides, do you think those men would dare try anything, tied up or not?”
“I suppose not.”
Hyuk Mujin nodded in agreement. Ju Hwaran and Song Ilseom then let go of the reins they’d each been holding.
Not their own reins, of course. They belonged to the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang, who had been riding close beside them, hemmed in on all sides.
“Thank you for trusting us.”
“I’m not completely trusting you yet, so there’s no need to thank me.”
That was what I told Ma Junggeol, whose eyes had filled with tears again. Privately, though, I thought otherwise.
No matter how I look at it, they’re not spies sent by Dark Heaven.
When I first overheard their Sound Transmission, the suspicions I’d set aside had come rushing back.
At first, anyway.
Now that I’d heard Ma Junggeol’s whole story, those suspicions had given way to curiosity about someone else.
The mysterious master Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers revered as Great Sir.
—What do you think?
Jeok Cheongang’s low Sound Transmission reached my ear. I knew what he was asking, so I turned my gaze toward the road ahead and answered.
—I’m not sure.
—Are you holding back? Or...
—I really don’t know. The man they call Great Sir seems less suspicious than... strange. Unbelievably strange.
That was no exaggeration.

This mysterious Supreme Peak master had appeared out of nowhere one day and wiped out a band of mounted bandits beyond even the authorities’ control. Yet Great Sir himself remained shrouded in mystery.
They said they didn’t know his name, where he came from, or anything else about him.
The Seven Masters of Baekma Bang had served him for more than ten years. Yet none of them, Ma Junggeol included, knew who he was. Whenever we pressed them, their answers were much the same.
“No, it’s all true. That’s just what he’s like!”
“We wouldn’t dare lie to you. Please believe us.”
“You heard us talking, so you already know he’s a bit—no, more than a bit—all over the place. His name and age? Don’t even ask. They change every time. Isn’t that right, Youngest?”
“My brothers are right. Chilbok, Gaettong... Was it three years ago? He thought he was a seventeen-year-old girl named Sohyang. That’s when we gave up trying to make sense of it.”

“We don’t know when he started living in Ningxia Province, either. He just suddenly appeared, subdued the whole area with his absurd divine might, then shut himself away in his residence and wouldn’t budge. He’s been like that for nearly ten years. I know it’s hard to believe, but it’s true.”
The absurd stories kept coming, like sweet potato vines that refused to end no matter how many you pulled up. Listening to them, I couldn’t help wondering:
What the hell is that guy?
Everyone had their own ambitions.
Right or wrong, everyone had some goal they’d held in their heart at least once.
But Great Sir, as they described him, fit none of the possibilities.

He hadn’t taken over Ningxia and ruled it as a mighty conqueror. Nor did he sound like a notorious fiend hiding his identity on the frontier, or a hermit master wandering where no one would find him as his life drew to a close.

If he wanted to rule as a conqueror, there’d be no reason to hole up in a cave. If he were a fiend, he’d have tried his damnedest to keep his identity hidden—or from the start, he’d have put the mounted bandits under his command.
As for a hermit master, I hardly needed to think about it.

What kind of deranged hermit would pass up a remote mountain valley with beautiful scenery and clear water to settle on a frontier where fine dust hung in the air and yellow sand blew through all year?
Even an ignoramus like me knew the famous poet Paul Valéry. If he’d lived in Ningxia Province instead of France, he would’ve written, The yellow dust is blowing. Fuck, I want to die.
And it wasn’t as if he were some senile old man, or someone so close to death that finding a mountain valley wasn’t worth the trouble.
According to the Seven Masters, Great Sir washed so rarely that grime practically ran off him. Even so, what they could make out of his face and hear in his voice suggested a man around middle age.

When Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers brought him liquor and food, he sometimes gave them a little instruction in return. And though he mostly stayed at his residence, he went out for the occasional stroll.
He said being inside all the time felt stifling. He wanted to smell other people for a change.
He must have wandered around often enough to blend into Ningxia Province without the Seven Masters making any effort to hide who he was.
Like Beggar Number One.
This is a hermit master?
Was this what it felt like to sink into a deep mire?
The more I thought about him, the more baffled and curious I became. Then Jeok Cheongang moved his lips, apparently thinking much the same thing.
—I thought I’d lived long enough to see hundreds of cartloads of madmen... but I’ve never seen anyone like this.
—Your hair’s only just started growing back.
—...Do you want to die?
—No. But I agree with you, Old Master. I can’t make sense of him.
—Could he be one of the Lord of Heaven’s minions?
—The Lord of Heaven must have people left working for him. But if you were him, would you take someone like that on?
Jeok Cheongang answered without hesitation.
—Are you mad?
—Exactly.
—Even if I took a Flame-Extinguishing Divine Fist to the head, I wouldn’t take a man like that as a subordinate. Assuming everything those vicious-looking bastards told us is true, of course.
—But you already believe them.
—That’s...
His Sound Transmission trailed off as he turned his head. The instant the Seven Masters met his gaze, they went rigid as statues. Jeok Cheongang shook his head.
—Yes, you’re right. I can tell they aren’t lying. No—they aren’t even capable of it.
That much was plain to me, and probably to everyone else.
But even if we concluded that the Seven Masters and Great Sir posed no danger to our side, the two of us couldn’t decide everything on instinct alone.
—What will you do?
Jeok Cheongang’s Sound Transmission reached me again. After a moment’s thought, I made my decision. I gradually eased up on the reins and drew level with the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang.
“W-why now? What is it this time...?”
Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers were frightened before I’d said a word.
I studied them in silence, then asked, “How long would you need?”
“What do you mean...?”
“To bring the man you call Great Sir to where we’re headed.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1013
paragraphs: “G-Great Sir?”
Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers stared at me, eyes wide. It took them a moment to recover.
“No, why Great Sir all of a sudden...?”
I answered calmly.
“It’s not all of a sudden. He’s connected to this situation to some extent. And I’m sure you know why I’m asking, so I don’t need to spell it out, do I?”
“You suspect me... no, us of being Dark Heaven’s spies?”
“Not exactly. At least, not the people here.”
“Then you suspect Great Sir?”
I shrugged. Ma Junggeol and the rest of the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang went rigid.
“That’s ridiculous!”
“Damn it, how many times do we have to tell you he isn’t?”
“As our Chief already told you, Great Sir is absolutely not that kind of person. You heard it all for yourself, didn’t you?”
Of course I had.
I’d learned only that he was a highly unusual person—the kind you rarely came across.
But this wasn’t the time to think, Huh. People like that exist, and let it go.
“Hah! I’ll stake my neck on it if I have to!”
I scratched my chin and looked at the short man who’d shouted a beat late.
“You over there. You’ll stake your own neck?”
Apparently he hadn’t expected me to take him up on it. He flinched and worked his lips.
“I-I mean, my neck might be a bit much. Maybe my wrist...”
“A man’s word is worth a thousand pieces of gold! Of course he’ll stake it! Cut off Second Brother’s head!”
“Hey, you crazy bastard!”
While the shorty flailed at the bulbous-nosed man’s sudden offer to wager on his behalf, I spoke in a low, measured voice.
“Wrist or neck, the math doesn’t work out either way.”
“What do you mean...?”
“I’m asking because I’m curious. Do you think all these people are taking a casual trip to the next town over just because they’re bored?”
The mood turned heavy in an instant. Their wavering eyes were fixed on the backs of the countless people riding far ahead.
The Black Dragon Demon Gate. The Zhongnan Sect.
Martial artists from large and small sects throughout Gansu Murim.
And finally, me and the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
That wasn’t all. In the direction those thousands of men and horses were racing lay tens of thousands of our allies, who could be in danger at any moment.
Even if all seven of them staked their lives, not just the short man, those lives couldn’t be weighed against what was at stake.
“Am I the only one here who’s heard that war isn’t a gamble?”
I’d said it almost to myself, but neither Ma Junggeol nor anyone else dared answer.
Of course they didn’t.
They knew how absurd it would be to dismiss every suspicion about a mysterious Supreme Peak master on the word of a few horse-caravan men.
The Great War that would decide the fate of the world was still underway. War was no gamble.
Besides...
There’s good reason to be suspicious. This isn’t paranoia.
I looked Ma Junggeol straight in the eye, recalling the Sound Transmissions the Seven Masters had exchanged the day before.
“I heard something interesting in your Sound Transmissions. What do you make of that?”
“Something interesting? What...?”
“I heard you say Great Sir had told you a thing or two about which way to go. Quite recently, too.”
I put particular emphasis on the last part. Ma Junggeol’s eyes, already lowered with worry, visibly wavered.
“T-that...”
“Now I’m curious. Exactly how recently was it? And what did he tell you? Don’t you think?”
I turned to Jeok Cheongang, who had been watching. He nodded.
“Hearing you say that, this old man is curious too. Why did you keep something so important to yourselves until now?”
Looking back, it was more than enough to make anyone suspicious.

How had the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang—former mounted bandits, unremarkable wanderers who had never distinguished themselves—come up with the audacious idea of crossing the desert of the Land of Ruin?
I’d only watched them up close for a short time, but I remembered every word of their Sound Transmissions. I already had a guess.
“The idea of opening a new trade route west wasn’t yours to begin with. Am I wrong?”
If I hadn’t followed Namho’s advice the day before and moved back early, quite a few people might have been startled by what I’d just said.
But for a little over thirty meters around us, there was no one else. Ma Junggeol had only one choice left.
“...There’s nothing more to hide.”
The words slipped out after a heavy silence. They were as good as an admission.
Before his sworn brothers could hurriedly shout something, I raised a hand to silence them and calmly continued my questions.
“Why did you hide it?”

“Because Great Sir wouldn’t have wanted us to tell anyone. Thanks to him, we changed our ways and have lived well ever since. We’re not beasts. How could we go around talking openly about what he’d done?”
“Tell me more.”

“This wasn’t the first time. From more than ten years ago right up until today, Great Sir has given my younger brothers and me all kinds of advice. When we first met him, we were so overwhelmed by his divine might that we asked to become his subordinates. He refused us outright and said...”
Ma Junggeol slowly looked over his sworn brothers and their complicated expressions before continuing.

“A caterpillar ought to eat pine needles. He asked whether we wouldn’t be better off gathering mounted bandits like ourselves, men who could still change their ways, and forming a group of our own. So my brothers and I took his advice.”
“Baekma Bang...”
“That’s right. That was how Baekma Bang began. Whenever we ran into trouble after that, Great Sir showed us the right way forward. The new trade route was no different.”
“Then when you said you’d been considering a western trade route for years, was that...”
Ma Junggeol understood what I was asking and hurriedly waved his hands.

“I don’t know if you’ll believe me in a situation like this, but that part is absolutely true. Great Sir simply advised us to do it. Afterward, we started searching for a new route west and realized the grasslands were our only option. Of course, we hadn’t dared attempt it all that time.”
“And that’s how you noticed the opening in the western grasslands so quickly,” Jeok Cheongang muttered.
Ma Junggeol nodded.
“Yes. Of course, we had no idea things would take such an unexpected turn. Great Sir probably didn’t either.”
Naturally.
Even if Hong Dao, the Dharma King who could read the heavenly patterns, were still alive, how could he have predicted something years in the future in such detail?
That wouldn’t be reading the heavenly patterns. That’d be prophecy. Prophecy.
And as Ma Junggeol went on, Great Sir’s advice didn’t sound particularly extraordinary.
He’d started by helping a few good-hearted mounted bandits, who had nowhere to go and had never farmed a day in their lives, put their skills to use and establish Baekma Bang.
A new trade route beyond the desert?
It was a bold idea, not one an ordinary person would come up with easily. But from what I’d heard of his martial prowess and his past, Great Sir was far from ordinary.
It was also the kind of wish the heads of the great groups bordering the desert or ambitious merchant-house leaders might have entertained at least once.
But what was this strange feeling I couldn’t explain?
What the hell?
I shook my head to clear away my stray thoughts, then parted my lips, which had been closed for a while, toward Ma Junggeol, who was swallowing nervously.
“One last question. Whose idea was it to come find us?”
“I’m ashamed to say that was Great Sir’s advice too.”
“Thought so.”
“We could have arrived half a day sooner. But this was too serious for us to decide on our own, so we went to see Great Sir as soon as we entered Ningxia.”
“Go on.”

“We told him what happened on the grasslands and in the desert. He knocked back several bowls of liquor as though he were listening to a dog bark, then said, ‘You idiots should’ve gone to Gansu ages ago. Why are you still sitting on your asses here?’”
“And after that, well, here we are. Damn it.”
Ma Junggeol fell silent, looking half resigned. For a while, the only sounds were the horses’ rough breathing and the thunder of hooves. The bulbous-nosed man glanced around and cautiously spoke up.
“Seven days and nights. I think that should be enough.”
“What the hell are you talking about?” Jeok Cheongang asked with a frown.
The man panicked and pointed at me.

“Third Brother’s right for once. Seven days and nights will be plenty.”
“Just leave it to us. We’ll bring him back, even if we have to give it everything we’ve got.”
“W-well, it’d take seven days and nights if we’re going to the Qilian Mountains. It might take longer if it’s the Great Snow Mountain or Dunhuang.”
“It’s not as if Great Sir is some vicious fiend. Rather than stay shut away in that remote backwater, he could take this chance to serve the Murim Alliance. Don’t you think?”
“Hah! ‘Not a bad idea,’ you say? He’s already done a great service by sending the seven of us to warn you about Dark Heaven. It’s bound to be an excellent choice for Great Sir too, since...”

sentences.text: “G-Great Sir?”
Ma Junggeol and his sworn brothers stared at me, eyes wide.
It took them a moment to recover.
“No, why Great Sir all of a sudden...?”
I answered calmly.
“It’s not all of a sudden.
He’s connected to this situation to some extent.
And I’m sure you know why I’m asking, so I don’t need to spell it out, do I?”
“You suspect me... no, us of being Dark Heaven’s spies?”
“Not exactly.
At least, not the people here.”
“Then you suspect Great Sir?”
I shrugged.
Ma Junggeol and the rest of the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang went rigid.
“That’s ridiculous!”
“Damn it, how many times do we have to tell you he isn’t?”
“As our Chief already told you, Great Sir is absolutely not that kind of person.
You heard it all for yourself, didn’t you?”
Of course I had.
I’d learned only that he was a highly unusual person—the kind you rarely came across.
But this wasn’t the time to think, Huh.
People like that exist, and let it go.
“Hah!
I’ll stake my neck on it if I have to!”
I scratched my chin and looked at the short man who’d shouted a beat late.
“You over there.
You’ll stake your own neck?”
Apparently he hadn’t expected me to take him up on it.
He flinched and worked his lips.
“I-I mean, my neck might be a bit much.
Maybe my wrist...”
“A man’s word is worth a thousand pieces of gold!
Of course he’ll stake it!
Cut off Second Brother’s head!”
“Hey, you crazy bastard!”
While the shorty flailed at the bulbous-nosed man’s sudden offer to wager on his behalf, I spoke in a low, measured voice.
“Wrist or neck, the math doesn’t work out either way.”
“What do you mean...?”
“I’m asking because I’m curious.
Do you think all these people are taking a casual trip to the next town over just because they’re bored?”
The mood turned heavy in an instant.
Their wavering eyes were fixed on the backs of the countless people riding far ahead.
The Black Dragon Demon Gate.
The Zhongnan Sect.
Martial artists from large and small sects throughout Gansu Murim.
And finally, me and the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
That wasn’t all.
In the direction those thousands of men and horses were racing lay tens of thousands of our allies, who could be in danger at any moment.
Even if all seven of them staked their lives, not just the short man, those lives couldn’t be weighed against what was at stake.
“Am I the only one here who’s heard that war isn’t a gamble?”
I’d said it almost to myself, but neither Ma Junggeol nor anyone else dared answer.
Of course they didn’t.
They knew how absurd it would be to dismiss every suspicion about a mysterious Supreme Peak master on the word of a few horse-caravan men.
The Great War that would decide the fate of the world was still underway.
War was no gamble.
Besides...
There’s good reason to be suspicious.
This isn’t paranoia.
I looked Ma Junggeol straight in the eye, recalling the Sound Transmissions the Seven Masters had exchanged the day before.
“I heard something interesting in your Sound Transmissions.
What do you make of that?”
“Something interesting?
What...?”
“I heard you say Great Sir had told you a thing or two about which way to go.
Quite recently, too.”
I put particular emphasis on the last part.
Ma Junggeol’s eyes, already lowered with worry, visibly wavered.
“T-that...”
“Now I’m curious.
Exactly how recently was it?
And what did he tell you?
Don’t you think?”
I turned to Jeok Cheongang, who had been watching.
He nodded.
“Hearing you say that, this old man is curious too.
Why did you keep something so important to yourselves until now?”
Looking back, it was more than enough to make anyone suspicious.

How had the Seven Masters of Baekma Bang—former mounted bandits, unremarkable wanderers who had never distinguished themselves—come up with the audacious idea of crossing the desert of the Land of Ruin?
I’d only watched them up close for a short time, but I remembered every word of their Sound Transmissions.
I already had a guess.
“The idea of opening a new trade route west wasn’t yours to begin with.
Am I wrong?”
If I hadn’t followed Namho’s advice the day before and moved back early, quite a few people might have been startled by what I’d just said.
But for a little over thirty meters around us, there was no one else.
Ma Junggeol had only one choice left.
“...There’s nothing more to hide.”
The words slipped out after a heavy silence.
They were as good as an admission.
Before his sworn brothers could hurriedly shout something, I raised a hand to silence them and calmly continued my questions.
“Why did you hide it?”
“Because Great Sir wouldn’t have wanted us to tell anyone.
Thanks to him, we changed our ways and have lived well ever since.
We’re not beasts.
How could we go around talking openly about what he’d done?”
“Tell me more.”
“This wasn’t the first time.
From more than ten years ago right up until today, Great Sir has given my younger brothers and me all kinds of advice.
When we first met him, we were so overwhelmed by his divine might that we asked to become his subordinates.
He refused us outright and said...”
Ma Junggeol slowly looked over his sworn brothers and their complicated expressions before continuing.
“A caterpillar ought to eat pine needles.
He asked whether we wouldn’t be better off gathering mounted bandits like ourselves, men who could still change their ways, and forming a group of our own.
So my brothers and I took his advice.”
“Baekma Bang...”
“That’s right.
That was how Baekma Bang began.
Whenever we ran into trouble after that, Great Sir showed us the right way forward.
The new trade route was no different.”
“Then when you said you’d been considering a western trade route for years, was that...”
Ma Junggeol understood what I was asking and hurriedly waved his hands.
“I don’t know if you’ll believe me in a situation like this, but that part is absolutely true.
Great Sir simply advised us to do it.
Afterward, we started searching for a new route west and realized the grasslands were our only option.
Of course, we hadn’t dared attempt it all that time.”

chapters.title: Chapter 1014
paragraphs: Thud-thud-thud!
Thousands of men and horses raced across the vast plain. At their head, the martial artists of the Black Dragon Demon Gate served as both vanguard and guides.
Some, though, were busier stealing curious glances at someone riding far off to the side.
“I’d only heard about him, but he’s much younger than I expected. He doesn’t look much older than me.”
“They said he was around thirty, so that makes sense. Still, you can’t mistake the family resemblance. He’s the spitting image of the Sect Leader.”
“The Black Dragon Saber... What a killer sobriquet. So, is that rumor true?”
Was he barely twenty? The young man still had the down on his cheeks, and the middle-aged man frowned at his out-of-the-blue question.
“What rumor are you talking about? You know I’m just as clueless about the inner workings as you are, so you’re not asking because you think I’d know.”
At the older man’s open displeasure, the young one hurriedly waved his hands.
“It’s nothing. I just heard our Young Sect Leader is stronger than the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes of the Central Plains.”
“Who knows? I’ve never even seen the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.”
“Right. The Ten Dragons and Phoenixes.”
“What?”
“I didn’t mean you’d necessarily met the Young Sect Leader, Uncle.”
The middle-aged man glared at the young one as he slyly looked away, then shook his head.
“I don’t know which idiot’s been running his mouth, but don’t believe it. It’s all ridiculous bullshit.”
“Bullshit?”
“Yeah.”
“That’s strange. You told me yourself last time, Uncle. When you were dead drunk.”
“So it’s true, then? Five years ago, the man who single-handedly wiped out One Saber Cuts the Cliff, the former chief of Danhyeol Bang, and twenty of his men...”
“That’s enough. Don’t say another word.”
The middle-aged man’s firm voice cut him off, but the young man couldn’t take his awestruck eyes off the person he’d been watching.
The Black Dragon Saber, Sama Pyo.
He was the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, to which they both belonged, and the heir who would one day succeed the Black Night King, Sima Gong, as leader of the unorthodox Murim.
The young man’s martial uniform was still stiff and new, a sure sign he hadn’t been with the Black Dragon Demon Gate long. He couldn’t hide his amazement.
So the whole story was true.
Everyone knew of the bloodshed at Danhyeol Bang, once one of the powers of Gansu Murim.
Its chief, One Saber Cuts the Cliff, had been one of Gansu’s ten greatest saber masters. He and his closest men had all been found brutally murdered on the same day.
And after that?
What was there to say?
A body without a head was bound to fall. Especially in Gansu, which the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s influence had made the de facto headquarters of the unorthodox Murim.
Danhyeol Bang, once three hundred members strong, had collapsed. Five years later, it had faded from people’s minds.
No. No one had bothered to remember.
Not the minor dispute between Danhyeol Bang and the Black Dragon Demon Gate shortly before the massacre.

Not that, on the day the mysterious killer came, the Captain of the Guards—who should have been protecting the pleasure house where the chief and leaders of Danhyeol Bang had gathered to drink—had left with his men.
And not how that same Captain of the Guards had become the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s Outer Hall Master less than a month later.
It had all been forgotten. It had to be.

The identity of the killer skilled enough to slay one of Gansu’s ten greatest saber masters, the background of whoever had ordered the killing, and even where all of Danhyeol Bang’s property and farmland had gone.
But the forgetting was only on the surface. The unorthodox martial artists who knew what had happened were certain.
And they were in awe.
Just like the young man who, as an unorthodox martial artist himself, now looked at Sama Pyo with admiration.
“That’s really, really incredible. Don’t you think? No wonder he became the heir over his older half-brothers—”
The young man caught his breath.
Reflected in his trembling eyes was the middle-aged man, face twisted as he gripped his sword hilt.
“You really do have a death wish, don’t you?”
His voice was so low that even the young man riding beside him would have missed it if he hadn’t been listening closely.
But the killing intent in it seemed to squeeze the raw novice’s heart.
“W-why all of a sudden...?”
“Shut your mouth if you want to live even a few more days.”
The older man cut off his stammering and quickly scanned their surroundings.

Perhaps the vast plain had spared them. There was plenty of distance between the riders, and the thunder of thousands of hooves and the fierce wind swallowed their conversation before anyone else could hear it.
“You idiot.”
“U-Uncle.”
“I won’t say it twice. Keep your mouth shut if you want to live.”
“I-I understand.”
Leaving the trembling young man behind, the middle-aged man urged his horse faster. His expression stayed cold, but inwardly he sighed.

The kid probably had no idea how careless and stupid a mistake he’d just made. If those words—practically taboo within the Black Dragon Demon Gate—had passed from mouth to ear and reached the higher-ups, they would have cost him his life.
Maybe he’ll never know.
It takes time for a person to mature. But war can arrive without warning, and enemies can steal that time before it runs its course.
The middle-aged man’s gaze grew distant as he thought of the battle to come. Then he flinched.
What was that?
An inexplicable sense of déjà vu seized him for an instant. He hurriedly looked around, but couldn’t place the feeling. At last he turned his attention back to his duty.
He never realized that two pairs of eyes had swept over him from more than thirty yards away.
“Hyah!”
Prrr, prrr.
His fine horse raced on, breathing hard. The young man finally came to his senses and hurried after him, his face deathly pale.
“W-wait for me!”
One person speaking alone was just talking. Ten voices became a shout; more than a hundred, a roar.
Yet even as three thousand men and horses raced in the same direction, father and son could hear each other clearly.
“There are a lot of faces I don’t recognize.”
“That’s how things turned out.”
“And a few who look useful, too.”
“Even in mud scraped together in a hurry, you can find a pearl or two. Though they can crack over the smallest thing.”
The son knew what his father meant by that last remark and fell silent. His father noticed.
As he always did.
“Are those people bothering you?”
At the Black Night King Sima Gong’s quiet question, Sama Pyo kept his eyes on the road ahead.
“I don’t know what you mean.”
“Seeing the sights of the Central Plains seems to have made you fond of word games.”
“There wasn’t much worth seeing. Maybe I was cursed with bad luck, but everywhere I went, I found a sea of corpses and blood. Though I’m sure you already knew that.”

“Yes, I heard the reports. But the messenger pigeons stopped returning one day. Some mishap along the way, perhaps. I had to look into matters myself, and the distance made it hard to get information in time. The Inner Hall Master had quite a time of it.”
“It couldn’t be helped. Yunnan wasn’t a good place to send messages back and forth.”
“I’m not scolding you. Your father knows what happened at the Nanman Beast Palace. But...”
Sama Pyo listened in silence, hoping his father’s next words would be the ones he wanted to hear.
They weren’t.
As always.
“Why didn’t you send a missive after that?”
“A missive...?”
“Yes. I understand you had several chances after leaving Yunnan. In the Imperial Capital, and at the Jin Family of Taiyuan. Am I wrong?”
What was he supposed to say?
His mouth felt gritty, as if he’d chewed a fistful of sand. The wind battered his body as he answered.
“You’re half right and half wrong.”
“What?”

“In the Imperial Capital, I had to hide my identity and even disguise myself to avoid being watched. The journey there wasn’t smooth, either. And once we entered the Imperial Palace, things only got worse.”
Sima Gong studied his son’s profile as though searching for the tiniest crack.
“Go on.”
“Things didn’t improve immediately after the incident at the Imperial Palace. We had to stay there a while, then head straight for Shanxi without proper rest.”
“Unlike at the Imperial Palace, you suffered no injuries of note in Shanxi, as I understand it. Am I mistaken?”
“You’re right. That’s when I was finally able to receive the missive from our sect.”
“Then you saw the order.”
“Yes. I saw it. I’m certain.”
At the answer, given without a hint of hesitation, Sima Gong’s gaze grew darker.
“The Fire King and his Disciple were to go to Qinghai, not here. Was that what the order said?”
“It was.”
“It said our sect was in danger, and that you, at least, were to return to Gansu by any means necessary. Is that right?”
“Exactly.”
“Then, lastly—do you have a proper reason or justification for seeing my seal and still not carrying out the order?”
Sama Pyo turned and looked his father straight in the eye.
“No.”
“I won’t make excuses. I won’t give you any reason. I failed to carry out the order properly, so I’ll accept whatever punishment I deserve. Please forgive me.”
Sima Gong fell silent, taken aback by his son’s response. Then a low laugh broke the brief silence between them.
“Ha. Hahaha.”
None of the men surrounding father and son like guards reacted. They were all Peak masters, Sima Gong’s loyal hands and feet, but in their lord’s presence they might as well have been blind and deaf.
Sama Pyo was different.
He watched his father calmly until the laughter stopped and a voice took its place.
“Pyo. My son.”
The voice was soft as silk. His eyes were sharp as blades.
“If you dared to lie to my face—if you did...”
His words faded unfinished, and his eyes curved into crescents.
“Only today do I realize how right I was to send you to the Central Plains.”
Pat. Pat.
Perhaps it was the wind sweeping across the plain that made his touch feel so cold. Sima Gong patted his son’s shoulder, looking pleased.
“You’ve grown. Admirably so.”
He turned his horse and rode away. Sama Pyo watched him go in silence.
“Take care of those two from a moment ago.”
With a single sentence, Sima Gong had decided the fate of two nameless martial artists for a careless remark spoken only briefly. Sama Pyo kept watching until his father disappeared from view.
Then Taishan came over—an old friend who had been as steady as the mountain he was named for since childhood—and asked in a trembling voice, “M-my lord. Are you all right?”
“Yes. I’m fine,” Sama Pyo answered calmly.
It was strange.
They were riding across an immense plain. Why, then, did his chest feel so tight?
And why did a few faces pass through his mind beneath the gray sky spread over them all?
But Sama Pyo didn’t turn his horse around.
The place he belonged now was the Black Dragon Demon Gate, not the Fire Dragon Pavilion.

The identity of the killer skilled enough to slay one of Gansu’s ten greatest saber masters, the background of whoever had ordered the killing, and even where all of Danhyeol Bang’s property and farmland had gone.
But the forgetting was only on the surface.
The unorthodox martial artists who knew what had happened were certain.
And they were in awe.
Just like the young man who, as an unorthodox martial artist himself, now looked at Sama Pyo with admiration.
“That’s really, really incredible.
Don’t you think?
No wonder he became the heir over his older half-brothers—”
The young man caught his breath.
Reflected in his trembling eyes was the middle-aged man, face twisted as he gripped his sword hilt.
“You really do have a death wish, don’t you?”
His voice was so low that even the young man riding beside him would have missed it if he hadn’t been listening closely.
But the killing intent in it seemed to squeeze the raw novice’s heart.
“W-why all of a sudden...?”
“Shut your mouth if you want to live even a few more days.”
The older man cut off his stammering and quickly scanned their surroundings.
Perhaps the vast plain had spared them.
There was plenty of distance between the riders, and the thunder of thousands of hooves and the fierce wind swallowed their conversation before anyone else could hear it.
“You idiot.”
“U-Uncle.”
“I won’t say it twice.
Keep your mouth shut if you want to live.”
“I-I understand.”
Leaving the trembling young man behind, the middle-aged man urged his horse faster.
His expression stayed cold, but inwardly he sighed.
The kid probably had no idea how careless and stupid a mistake he’d just made.
If those words—practically taboo within the Black Dragon Demon Gate—had passed from mouth to ear and reached the higher-ups, they would have cost him his life.
Maybe he’ll never know.
It takes time for a person to mature.
But war can arrive without warning, and enemies can steal that time before it runs its course.
The middle-aged man’s gaze grew distant as he thought of the battle to come.
Then he flinched.
What was that?
An inexplicable sense of déjà vu seized him for an instant.
He hurriedly looked around, but couldn’t place the feeling.
At last he turned his attention back to his duty.
He never realized that two pairs of eyes had swept over him from more than thirty yards away.
“Hyah!”
Prrr, prrr.
His fine horse raced on, breathing hard.
The young man finally came to his senses and hurried after him, his face deathly pale.
“W-wait for me!”
One person speaking alone was just talking.
Ten voices became a shout; more than a hundred, a roar.
Yet even as three thousand men and horses raced in the same direction, father and son could hear each other clearly.
“There are a lot of faces I don’t recognize.”
“That’s how things turned out.”
“And a few who look useful, too.”
“Even in mud scraped together in a hurry, you can find a pearl or two.
Though they can crack over the smallest thing.”
The son knew what his father meant by that last remark and fell silent.
His father noticed.
As he always did.
“Are those people bothering you?”
At the Black Night King Sima Gong’s quiet question, Sama Pyo kept his eyes on the road ahead.
“I don’t know what you mean.”
“Seeing the sights of the Central Plains seems to have made you fond of word games.”
“There wasn’t much worth seeing.
Maybe I was cursed with bad luck, but everywhere I went, I found a sea of corpses and blood.
Though I’m sure you already knew that.”
“Yes, I heard the reports.
But the messenger pigeons stopped returning one day.
Some mishap along the way, perhaps.
I had to look into matters myself, and the distance made it hard to get information in time.
The Inner Hall Master had quite a time of it.”
“It couldn’t be helped.
Yunnan wasn’t a good place to send messages back and forth.”
“I’m not scolding you.
Your father knows what happened at the Nanman Beast Palace.
But...”
Sama Pyo listened in silence, hoping his father’s next words would be the ones he wanted to hear.
They weren’t.
As always.
“Why didn’t you send a missive after that?”
“A missive...?”
“Yes.
I understand you had several chances after leaving Yunnan.
In the Imperial Capital, and at the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Am I wrong?”
What was he supposed to say?
His mouth felt gritty, as if he’d chewed a fistful of sand.
The wind battered his body as he answered.
“You’re half right and half wrong.”
“What?”
“In the Imperial Capital, I had to hide my identity and even disguise myself to avoid being watched.
The journey there wasn’t smooth, either.
And once we entered the Imperial Palace, things only got worse.”
Sima Gong studied his son’s profile as though searching for the tiniest crack.
“Go on.”
“Things didn’t improve immediately after the incident at the Imperial Palace.
We had to stay there a while, then head straight for Shanxi without proper rest.”
“Unlike at the Imperial Palace, you suffered no injuries of note in Shanxi, as I understand it.
Am I mistaken?”
“You’re right.
That’s when I was finally able to receive the missive from our sect.”
“Then you saw the order.”
“Yes.
I saw it.
I’m certain.”
At the answer, given without a hint of hesitation, Sima Gong’s gaze grew darker.
“The Fire King and his Disciple were to go to Qinghai, not here.
Was that what the order said?”
“It was.”
“It said our sect was in danger, and that you, at least, were to return to Gansu by any means necessary.
Is that right?”
“Exactly.”
“Then, lastly—do you have a proper reason or justification for seeing my seal and still not carrying out the order?”
Sama Pyo turned and looked his father straight in the eye.
“No.”
“I won’t make excuses.
I won’t give you any reason.
I failed to carry out the order properly, so I’ll accept whatever punishment I deserve.
Please forgive me.”
Sima Gong fell silent, taken aback by his son’s response.
Then a low laugh broke the brief silence between them.
“Ha.
Hahaha.”
None of the men surrounding father and son like guards reacted.
They were all Peak masters, Sima Gong’s loyal hands and feet, but in their lord’s presence they might as well have been blind and deaf.
Sama Pyo was different.
He watched his father calmly until the laughter stopped and a voice took its place.
“Pyo.
My son.”
The voice was soft as silk.
His eyes were sharp as blades.
“If you dared to lie to my face—if you did...”
His words faded unfinished, and his eyes curved into crescents.
“Only today do I realize how right I was to send you to the Central Plains.”
Pat.
Pat.
Perhaps it was the wind sweeping across the plain that made his touch feel so cold.
Sima Gong patted his son’s shoulder, looking pleased.
“You’ve grown.
Admirably so.”
He turned his horse and rode away.
Sama Pyo watched him go in silence.
“Take care of those two from a moment ago.”
With a single sentence, Sima Gong had decided the fate of two nameless martial artists for a careless remark spoken only briefly.
Sama Pyo kept watching until his father disappeared from view.
Then Taishan came over—an old friend who had been as steady as the mountain he was named for since childhood—and asked in a trembling voice, “M-my lord.
Are you all right?”
“Yes.
I’m fine,” Sama Pyo answered calmly.
It was strange.
They were riding across an immense plain.
Why, then, did his chest feel so tight?
And why did a few faces pass through his mind beneath the gray sky spread over them all?
But Sama Pyo didn’t turn his horse around.
The place he belonged now was the Black Dragon Demon Gate, not the Fire Dragon Pavilion.

chapters.title: Chapter 1015
paragraphs: Our force numbered a staggering three thousand, but every last one of them was a martial artist, so we moved far faster than common sense would suggest.
Only two days after leaving Tianshui, on Gansu’s eastern edge, we had already passed Lanzhou, the provincial capital, and were pressing on without slowing down.
It must have been around then that the bitterly cold plateau and vast wilderness gave way to a narrow road lined on both sides by rocky hills of every size.
This place...

Sometimes, when I left the modern world behind and roamed the Murim, I found myself stopped short by nature’s grandeur. Places untouched by human hands, holding the passage of countless ages within them.
I let go of my reins and gazed in silence at the endless view below the plateau. A soft voice reached my ear.
“This is the Hexi Corridor. It’s called that because it runs west of the Yellow River like a corridor. I don’t know who first named it, but doesn’t it suit the place?”
I agreed, but that aside, the voice was easy to recognize. It would have been even if Sama Pyo and Taishan hadn’t been away.
There was only one person around me with a voice that fresh and clear.
“You certainly know your stuff, Young Lady Ju.”
Ju Hwaran gave a shy smile.
“It’s only natural. I did lead the Escort Bureau for a while, even if it wasn’t very long. And I am the Escort King’s granddaughter, after all.”
She had a point, but she was being modest, too.

Being born into a martial family didn’t mean you had to learn martial arts. Likewise, Ju Hwaran hadn’t been obliged to take over the family business. She knew the geography of the Central Plains and so much else through her own effort.
Come to think of it, the Yongbong Escort Bureau wasn’t in a situation all that different from the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s at first.
Both families had left their former glory behind and begun to fall into ruin.
One small difference was that, unlike the Jin Family of Taiyuan, which had three sons and a whole lot of testosterone, Ju Hwaran was an only child—and had to bear that much heavier burden alone.
Though her father, the Head of the Escort Bureau, was still there, unlike mine, even if he was bedridden.
But that was all in the past.

The Head of the Yongbong Escort Bureau had recovered his vitality and returned to the front lines. And the huge sum of gold I’d beaten out of the Taeeul Merciless Sword in return had been more than enough to pull the crumbling family back onto its feet.
And the Jin Family of Taiyuan had risen into the ranks of the Five Great Families, filling the void left by the Murong Family—or rather, the Murong household.
If Dark Heaven didn’t exist, we could’ve wrapped things up here with a happy ending for everyone.
But reality wasn’t something you could ignore. You had to face it, and opportunity always came in the midst of crisis.
That was how Ju Hwaran and the Yongbong Escort Bureau, and I and the Jin Family of Taiyuan, had overcome their crises and grown stronger.
It was only the many sacrifices we’d made along the way—and the fact that more would inevitably come—that weighed heavily on my heart.
And besides...
No. Not right now. I’ll leave it there for the moment.
I pushed away the memory of Namho coming to me just yesterday, his face unusually grave. I pushed away his low voice, too, though it still seemed to linger in my ears.
Ju Hwaran was watching me with concern. I forced a smile as if nothing were wrong.
“Ah, sorry. I was just... just thinking about something.”
“It’s all right. I understand. The coming battle must be weighing on you.”
What was I supposed to say? I couldn’t tell her something I wasn’t even certain of myself.
I watched her profile as she rode beside me, then spoke almost on impulse.
“That’s part of it. But I’ve also been thinking about relationships.”
“Relationships?”
“Between people. Trust, hopes. Things like that.”
I looked toward the narrow pass between the distant rocky hills, where thousands of our allies were pouring through like a flood.
“Nothing’s easy, I suppose, but I find this especially hard. The connections and feelings between people.”
“How they feel...”
Ju Hwaran murmured the words to herself, then added quietly, “I think I understand.”
“I thought you might, Young Lady Ju.”
She’d been through it herself. How could she not?
I still remembered it clearly: during the conflict with the Zhongnan Sect, Ju Hwaran had personally cut down Chief Escort Heo Jun, who had betrayed her from the shadows.
She once followed him like a real uncle. The wound from that must still be with her.
That was why relationships were so difficult.
You could readily give someone something, but no one knew whether they’d give as much in return, more—or nothing at all.
That’s why I’m hesitating so much, too.
Then Ju Hwaran blurted out something that swept the doubts creeping back into my mind clean away.
“It’s Wolhwa, isn’t it?”
“Y-yes?”
I’d almost agreed without thinking. I blinked at her.
What? Had I heard her wrong?
“Um, sorry, what did you just say?”
Without turning her head, Ju Hwaran answered, “The woman named Wolhwa. The Lower District Sect’s Branch Leader in Shaanxi. Isn’t she?”
“Yes. That’s right.”
“Exactly.”
“No, I meant that she’s the Branch Leader in Shaanxi.”
“Oh, really?”
“Yes.”
“And?”
“Pardon?”
“Never mind.”
What on earth was this conversation?
I stared at her, speechless. Then a violent fit of coughing cut through the pounding hooves.
“Cough! Cough! Couuugh!”
What was that idiot doing now?

I turned to say something to Hyuk Mujin, who was practically convulsing in his saddle, and saw him desperately shaking his head. Namho and Song Ilseom rode on either side of him, looking at me with pity.
A suspicion struck me.
Hmm.
Hmmm.
Was this... what I thought it was?
This isn’t exactly the best time for something like this.
Still, I had to clear up a needless misunderstanding.
Feeling a little strange, I spoke.
“Um, Young Lady Ju?”
“Yes. Go ahead.”
She kept her eyes fixed straight ahead, as if she’d spotted her family’s sworn enemy up the road. Her ears, meanwhile, had perked up.
I scratched my chin, though it didn’t itch.
“Well, this isn’t something you’re particularly curious about, but I thought I’d mention it.”
“That’s right. I’m not particularly curious, but I’ll hear you out.”
“I’m not very close with Wolhwa.”

“We did have some dealings, sure. Just a year or two ago, she was the Branch Leader in Shanxi, not Shaanxi. The Lower District Sect and I had various mutual dealings, so we got to know each other a little.”
After a brief silence, Ju Hwaran spoke.
“You talk about her awfully casually for someone you’re not close to. You even call her by her name.”
“You’ve got the wrong idea. I only call her that because she isn’t here. Face-to-face, I’d address her properly every time.”
“I see. So you sometimes exchange heartfelt missives like this one, too?”
“Missives?”
I blinked. Only then did I begin to understand why she’d brought up Wolhwa.
The missive the Lower District Sect member who’d guided us to Gansu had given me. The one sent in Wolhwa’s name.
“Was that why?”
“Why what?”
“That’s, well...”
How was I supposed to put this? Was it even a good idea to say what I was thinking?
While I hesitated, Ju Hwaran finally turned and looked me straight in the eye.
“Can I ask what was written in that missive?”
Strange.
Our saddles jolted with every pounding hoof, and the wind whipped past us. Yet her voice reached me more clearly than anything else, though it was barely half as loud as usual.
Maybe that was why I stared at her for a moment, then answered before I knew it.
“No.”
“Ah.”
Her expression dimmed slightly, and she fell silent. I went on.
“I can’t tell you what’s in it. I haven’t read it yet.”
“With everything going on, I’d forgotten about it. Want to read it together now?”
I didn’t need an answer. Her beaming smile was enough.
Inventory open. Summon.
As I slipped my hand inside my robe and spoke the command, I felt something solid between my fingers.
I pulled out the bamboo tube the Lower District Sect member had given me a few days earlier, removed the rolled-up missive, and unfolded it in front of Ju Hwaran.
Hesitation? The slightest worry?
Not a trace. Not even a pinch.
Why would I have anything like that? Wolhwa only teases me with wordplay when we meet in person. When it comes to business, she’s meticulous.
I had reason to be certain. This wasn’t the first time she’d sent me news.

Perhaps because of the agreement with the Jin Family of Taiyuan, I’d received a couple of missives while I was away. They’d contained useful information: the locations of Lower District Sect branches, how to make contact in an emergency, and the latest news from Shanxi or Shaanxi.
Information. Nothing more.
It was the Lower District Sect’s Shaanxi Branch Leader looking after a valued client, not Wolhwa writing to me personally.
So I unfolded the missive without a moment’s hesitation—and immediately realized something was wrong.
Young Master Jin, have you been well? Maybe it’s because we haven’t seen each other in so long, but I miss you terribly. I missed you so much that you appeared in my dream last night!
Rustle.
I let go on instinct, and the paper rolled back up.
Ju Hwaran had brought her horse close to mine to read along. She spoke in a voice so gentle it felt out of place.
“Could you open it again?”
“I was reading it.”
“...Um, Young Lady Ju?”
“Yes. Go ahead. I’m listening.”
I hurriedly opened my mouth, feeling like I had to say something. But her soft reply—and the steady gaze she fixed on me—sent a chill down my spine.
It was as if my body had forgotten I’d gained the power of Unaffected by Cold and Heat long ago.
How am I supposed to explain this?
I felt as though I’d stepped into a deep swamp with no way out. While I struggled to find the words, Ju Hwaran gave a faint smile.
“Never mind. It’s fine. You don’t have to say anything.”
“Y-yes?”
“Don’t mind me. Go ahead and finish reading. It sounds like a very deep and important conversation. Well, I’ll leave you to it.”
“Wait, Young Lady Ju—!”
Thud-thud-thud!
Before I could finish shouting, she urged her horse forward and sped ahead.
I stared after her, then silently unfolded the missive again.
Unlike usual, it was full of trivial personal chatter. And at the very end, it had one line that put the finishing touch on the whole thing.
Hoping for the day the Yellow River runs clear and we can meet again, Wolhwa
She really was trying to get me killed.
I stared at the words. Anyone who read them would think we were on very intimate terms.
Hyuk Mujin approached cautiously.
“Um, Captain.”
“What.”
“I can see the Qilian Mountains.”
“Get lost.”
“Yes, sir.”
God, I want to die.

chapters.title: Chapter 1016
paragraphs: I’d had a vague sense of it since we first met, but Wolhwa was impossible to figure out.
What on earth possessed her to send me a missive like this out of nowhere?
A Meeting When the Yellow River Runs Clear.
I didn’t know much about classical idioms, but even a rough, literal translation left plenty of room for misunderstanding.
A meeting like the river running clear.
Wasn’t that the sort of thing you’d say only to someone you were at least flirting with?
This is going to give the gossip mill a real boost.
Of course, I wasn’t delusional enough to get the wrong idea over a single missive.
I’d known for a long time that Wolhwa’s interest in me was limited to her being a member of the Lower District Sect. It had absolutely nothing to do with romantic feelings.
But...
The problem is that Young Lady Ju might misunderstand—not me.
I muttered to myself and put the crumpled missive back in my Inventory.
It bothered me a little, but there was nothing I could do about it for now. Time would sort it out eventually, and far more important problems stood in my way.
And at this very moment—
Whoosh.
A cold wind swept across the plateau, and a vast mountain range finally came into view. It was a sign that we’d taken another step toward those problems.
That’s...
My eyes widened before I knew it.
Vast. Dazzling.
That was my first impression of the Qilian Mountains.
“I’d only heard about them. But seeing them for real... wow.”
Hyuk Mujin murmured, sounding dazed.
But he wasn’t the only one. Everyone was staring in wonder, myself included.
Sheer cliffs lined a mountain range that stretched on without end like the body of a dragon. Between them, peaks pierced the clouds, rising so high they seemed to hold up the sky.
And that wasn’t all.
Perpetual snow painted the mountains white in places, lending them an air of mystery, as though we’d stepped into another world.
Yet the narrow gorges between the cliffs were long and constricted, like entrances to hell. The mountains were a natural fortress.
This is even more than I’d heard.
The Eight Spring Gorge, which had changed Shanxi’s fortunes time and time again, felt like a hill behind the village compared to the Qilian Mountains before us.
But the drawback was just as obvious.
“It’s too vast.”
At Song Ilseom’s brief remark, I nodded quietly.
He was right. The Qilian Mountains weren’t merely large. They were immense.

The range stretched for thousands of li, beginning in southwestern Gansu and reaching all the way to Qinghai. Spread a hastily assembled net across all that ground, and it would be torn apart in an instant.
Especially if the big fish we were trying to catch was Dark Heaven.
So, as soon as we entered the Qilian Mountains—which were already surrounded by the Gansu martial artists’ tight defenses—the leaders gathered in one place to discuss this problem first.
Or, more precisely, Jeok Cheongang and I did.
“There are too many troops stationed in the rear for what they’re meant to do. So, what I’m saying is—”
“Pull them out. All of them.”

Jeok Cheongang cut in before I could finish. He picked at his ear, then added, “I had a bad feeling when I heard about it, but seeing the place confirms it. Even if we threw every last man at the Great Snow Mountain and Dunhuang into this, we couldn’t seal it off completely. We’d be better off gathering them all and throwing them onto another front.”
Jeok Cheongang swept his gaze over the gathering like a landlord telling a troublesome tenant to clear out. Then his eyes came to rest on one man.
“I thought you, at least, would know that much. Was I mistaken?”
The Black Night King, Sima Gong, answered with a gentle smile.
“Thank you for thinking so highly of me. But I, and the Sect Leaders and Family Heads gathered here, know the Gansu region better than anyone. The Qilian Mountains included, of course.”
“Know it better than anyone...”
Jeok Cheongang repeated Sima Gong’s words softly, as if turning them over, then spoke in an even voice.
“That sounds like you’re telling me to shut up if I don’t know enough.”
“How could we dare show such disrespect to you, Senior Jeok, of all people? Please take back your words.”
“Please calm yourself, Great Hero Jeok.”
“We reached this decision only after thorough discussion.”
After Sima Gong’s smooth apology, the Sect Leaders and Family Heads of Gansu Murim, who’d been watching for a cue, clasped their hands in salute one after another.
Like lackeys following their boss.
And that was when, as I silently watched the scene before me, I noticed the only one among them holding his back straight.
Sama Pyo.
Our eyes met for a moment. He wore that same unreadable expression of his. Then Sama Pyo quietly lowered his head too, following his father’s lead.
Swish.
Perhaps it was the sudden silence that made the brush of clothing sound so loud.
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord spoke.

“It is difficult for this poor Daoist to judge. Everyone here is a leader of Gansu Murim, and I would like to believe you have made the right decision. But... I also think Great Hero Jeok’s concern is entirely possible.”
“More than possible. I’d say there’s a nine-in-ten chance he’s right.”
Everyone turned to look at me. I went on without the slightest embarrassment.

“Even with thirty thousand allied troops and several thousand more, splitting them up to maintain three fronts means we won’t be worth a damn anywhere. There’s a reason people say you live if you stick together and die if you scatter.”
“Thank you for reminding us all of the most basic principle, which everyone here had somehow forgotten.”
The Roaring Fury Swordsman let out a short, derisive laugh. I shrugged at him.
“You don’t have to thank me that much. People forget things now and then when they get old. Though this one’s pretty basic.”
“Oh, sorry. Was that too cheeky?”
I hadn’t said it to get under his skin. I meant it.
Seeing the Roaring Fury Swordsman’s face turn red, I realized I might’ve gone too far—but what could I do when the words came out on their own?
Well, we were all in the same boat now. He’d understand.
Or not.
“You—no, you...”

Maybe the cheek of a young punk talking back had made his blood boil. The Roaring Fury Swordsman glanced at Jeok Cheongang, and seemed to be starting to hyperventilate. Someone else stepped in for him.
“Stick together and live, scatter and die. True enough. But not in a situation like this.”
I guess that was what fellow disciples were for.
I looked straight at the Taeeul Merciless Sword, who’d stepped in at just the right moment.
“What do you mean by ‘a situation like this’?”
“Are you asking because you don’t know, or are you pretending not to?”
The Taeeul Merciless Sword frowned.
“You seem to have forgotten what monstrous dark arts they wield.”
Nobody here failed to understand what the Taeeul Merciless Sword meant. I certainly hadn’t.
“The Moving Formation. Right. They have that.”
I nodded, then spoke again, as calmly as if nothing were wrong.
“So?”
“What!”
“What did you say?”
The questions came from all sides at once.
But I’d expected that reaction. Otherwise, I wouldn’t have brought it up.
“On the way here, I thought of something I wanted to ask...”
I let the words trail off and slowly looked around the gathering.
“If you’re so wary of the Moving Formation, why did you station an army of over thirty thousand in the front in the first place?”
Silence pressed down on us.
It didn’t lift until someone, who’d been watching the situation with calm eyes, suddenly spoke.
“For the greater good.”
The Black Night King, Sima Gong. Him again.
Speaking on everyone’s behalf, Sima Gong continued in a low, steady voice.

“What you said earlier was right. If we spread ourselves out carelessly, we’ll accomplish nothing. So we put our heads together and considered it carefully, and this is the conclusion we reached: divide our forces among three fronts, so they can return to the rear at any time.”
At first glance, it sounded reasonable.
It was the same argument they’d made when the leaders first gathered.
But...
That was only true, as I’d just said, at first glance.
“It seems like a long way to go back. If Dark Heaven appears in the rear through the Moving Formation, how are we supposed to catch up with them?”
If tens of thousands of locusts descended on a field, it wouldn’t take even half a day for everything to disappear.
Dark Heaven was that swarm of locusts.
And their fangs and wings were too savage and fast for us to make up a delay of several days and catch them.
By the time our allies arrived, Gansu would already be laid waste, and Dark Heaven would be heading for the Central Plains.
Did these men really not know that? They’d been fixtures in Gansu for decades, some for more than a century.
Of course they knew.
They had to.
Sima Gong’s next words turned my suspicion into certainty.
“That’s right. Without a doubt.”

At that brief reply, Jeok Cheongang and I understood what he meant, and our gazes grew intent. But not everyone understood. The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord, for one, was looking at Sima Gong with a puzzled expression.
“Sect Leader Sima. What exactly do you mean by...?”
His words trailed off.
But the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord led the great Zhongnan Sect. Before Sima Gong’s reply had faded, a thought occurred to him, and his face stiffened.
“Surely you don’t mean to stand by and let it happen? Even if they use the Moving Formation to bypass our lines and ravage the rear?”
Sima Gong answered evenly.
“Stand by and let it happen? Nothing of the sort. We’ve simply chosen the option with the best chance of victory.”
“Wait. Then what happens to the rear? To the common people and martial artists still there?”
“I told you. It’s for the greater good.”
“Sect Leader Sima!”
Crash!
The chair shattered in an instant.
But even as the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord shouted and sprang to his feet, Sima Gong’s voice didn’t waver in the slightest.

“If Dark Heaven crosses the desert and attacks us head-on, we’ll immediately concentrate every force there. They might use the Moving Formation to take the rear instead... but that would be the worst move they could make.”
A fish that tore through a net from the outside could come and go as it pleased. But if it passed through the net as if by teleportation, it would find itself trapped inside.
A two-front war.
That was Sima Gong’s plan.
Effective, but it would demand enormous sacrifice.
A truly unorthodox scheme.
But...
Was that all there was to it?
“Whether we defend this place or burn it to the ground is our choice. Neither the Zhongnan Sect nor the Jin Family of Taiyuan owns it.”
Sima Gong’s icy gaze silenced the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord. I watched him, my own gaze sinking deep.

chapters.title: Chapter 1017
paragraphs: Sima Gong and the leaders of Gansu Murim had made their position perfectly clear:
- Don’t go demanding this and that in someone else’s territory.
Honestly, there wasn’t much room to argue with that.

Every one of them was an old fixture who’d ruled Gansu Murim for decades at the very least, and some for more than a century. Besides, ever since the Great Faction War, interfering too much in another sect’s affairs had been taboo.
And then there was the Black Dragon Demon Gate, standing at the center of it all. What kind of place was it?
Despite its relatively short history of only a few decades, it wielded tremendous influence throughout Gansu. It was, without question, a pillar of the unorthodox faction.
At least in Gansu, it stood shoulder to shoulder with the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang. In fact, it might have built an even stronger power base by now—a true regional overlord.
With Sima Gong, the beginning and end of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, speaking so bluntly, even the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had no choice but to back down after briefly letting his anger show.
But someone else had watched it all without so much as twitching an eyebrow.
“Why are you growling? You sound like a yellow dog whose food bowl’s been taken away.”
There was only one person here who could compare the Black Night King himself to a yellow dog.
The Fire King, Jeok Cheongang.
At last, the giant who’d left his mark on the distant history of Murim parted his lips. The icy gleam in Sima Gong’s eyes settled.
“I suppose I should growl. I’ll do it as much as I must to protect my food bowl.”
“And it never crossed your mind that someone else’s life might depend on that food bowl?”
“It’s for the greater good.”
“You mean your own good. The good of the select few who follow you and the Black Dragon Demon Gate.”
Jeok Cheongang slowly looked around the room.
There were around twenty people here, not counting those from the Zhongnan Sect and the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
As he looked from one leader of Gansu Murim to the next, an unmistakable sneer curled his lips.

“Come to think of it, isn’t it strange? As I understand it, Gansu has at least fifty sects and martial families, yet not even half of them are here. Ah... were the others already sent to different fronts?”
“They’re already carrying out other assignments,” Sima Gong answered dryly.
“So they were left behind. To delay Dark Heaven for even half a day if it uses the Moving Formation to appear in the rear.”
“Everyone agreed to it.”
“And before you got that agreement, did you lay out all the facts? Or did you put a sword to their throats first?”
“With all due respect, there’s something I’d like to say while we’re at it.”
“‘With all due respect’ already puts me in a shitty mood, but I suppose that’s what you’ve got a mouth for. Go on, then. Spit it out.”
Sima Gong let out a short breath at Jeok Cheongang’s continuing barbs. Then, with a calm expression, he spoke.
“We of Gansu Murim will not accept interference from outsiders in this decision, in any form. Even if it comes from the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families. Or...”
Sima Gong’s gaze swept past the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord and me, then stopped on Jeok Cheongang.
“Even if it comes from you, Senior.”
The air around us lurched.
Stiffened hands and feet came standard. The slight bobbing of people’s throats was an added bonus.
Even if it was Sima Gong, who was he speaking to?
Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King himself.
A terrifying old monster said to rank among the top five in the Central Plains when it came to martial arts—and first when it came to a foul temper.
He’d answered Jeok Cheongang in a downright challenging tone. No wonder everyone reacted as if they’d been burned.
Everyone except me.
That’s far enough for today.
I’d been watching events unfold the whole time, and I made up my mind.
Then, at a moment nobody expected, I clapped my hands together hard.
Clap!
The sharp sound broke the silence, short and yet seemingly endless. Everyone turned toward me, startled as if they’d just woken from a dream. I blinked at them with perfect composure.
“Oh, sorry. A damn mosquito was buzzing around.”
Of course, I was lying.
With snow that never melted lying all around us, what mosquito?
But the point was that my sudden clap had instantly broken the tension, which had been spiraling toward disaster.
And the two men at the center of it understood why I’d clapped at once.
“You’ve grown up some. Come a long way.”
At last, Jeok Cheongang spoke in a low voice. Sima Gong, as if nothing had happened, respectfully clasped his hands in salute.
“I still have a long way to go. I hope you’ll look kindly on this inadequate junior.”
Jeok Cheongang looked at me and put on a frown, as though something displeased him.
“You certainly do have a long way to go. Just thinking about what lies ahead, it’s one obstacle after another. Isn’t it?”
“With you here alongside us, Senior, what need have we of an army?”
Sima Gong put particular emphasis on alongside us, then lifted his head and looked at me.
“You truly have a perceptive Disciple.”
“I don’t know about perceptive. He’s good at reading a room.”

“Remarkable martial prowess, and a mind that sees several moves ahead. He’s a blessing to all Murim. My son ought to have spent more time watching and learning from you while he had the chance... What do you think of him?”
At Sima Gong’s sudden question, I answered without hesitation.
“He’s useful.”
“What?”
“Now that I’ve spent some time with him, he’s a pretty decent kid. A little gloomy, though.”
By Murim’s reckoning, Sama Pyo was much older than me.
But even though I’d just thrown the whole idea of respecting my elders to the dogs, Sima Gong only smiled in a way I couldn’t quite read.
“Thank you for saying so. It makes all the effort I put into raising him worthwhile.”

Over his shoulder, I saw Sama Pyo standing there without a trace of expression. It struck me that Sima Gong sounded less like a father talking about raising his son than a craftsman talking about a piece he’d made.
But the thought vanished as quickly as it had come, and I spoke again.
“So, you don’t plan to change your decision?”
“Decision. A choice made by firmly settling on a course of action or attitude.”
“So that’s a no. Then can I assume the Kongtong Sect’s position is the same?”
“The Kongtong Sect opposed it, but that changes nothing. All of Gansu Murim reached this decision after extensive discussion.”
Maybe. But was this really what Gansu Murim wanted?
Or...
Was it only what the Black Dragon Demon Gate wanted?
I swallowed the words hovering on the tip of my tongue and thought for a moment.
Inventory.
I mentally felt for an item stowed somewhere in that bottomless, pitch-black subspace.
But then I shook my head.
No matter how I looked at it, the timing wasn’t right yet.
Not now, at least.
“Then let’s do that.”
“What?”
The startled question came from neither Jeok Cheongang, who was frowning, nor Sima Gong.
It was the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord. He stared at me with wide eyes.
“You’re willing to accept this as it stands? Are you serious?”
Right then, before I could answer, two other voices cut the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord off.
“Everywhere you go, people have their own rules. Our Zhongnan is no different.”
“Eldest Senior Brother is right. Junior Brother, remember how you ought to conduct yourself as our sect’s Sect Leader.”
The Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword.
Those were the two who had spoken.
After hearing his Senior Brothers speak in turn, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord muttered as though groaning.
“Senior Brothers. But how can we let this happen?”
“We understand how you feel, Sect Leader. But further discord could jeopardize what we’re trying to accomplish.”
Sima Gong calmly but firmly cut off the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord before he could continue. Then he surveyed the room and went on.
“I hope everyone will remember this. We are allies united beneath the Murim Alliance’s banner, and we must not create discord over a decision that has already been made. Much less...”
Sima Gong’s deeply lowered gaze suddenly came to rest on me.
“Acting alone without seeking everyone’s agreement is even less acceptable. Wouldn’t you say?”
I already knew what Sima Gong meant, so I nodded.
“I’ll keep that in mind.”
“I hope sending those horse caravans away wasn’t a grievous mistake for our allies.”
“There won’t be any problem. At least, if my expectations are right.”
“His name was Ma Junggeol, wasn’t it? If you’d let that man go as well... we would’ve been disappointed in you. Very disappointed.”
