sentences.text: Sima Gong and the leaders of Gansu Murim had made their position perfectly clear:
- Don’t go demanding this and that in someone else’s territory.
Honestly, there wasn’t much room to argue with that.
Every one of them was an old fixture who’d ruled Gansu Murim for decades at the very least, and some for more than a century.
Besides, ever since the Great Faction War, interfering too much in another sect’s affairs had been taboo.
And then there was the Black Dragon Demon Gate, standing at the center of it all.
What kind of place was it?
Despite its relatively short history of only a few decades, it wielded tremendous influence throughout Gansu.
It was, without question, a pillar of the unorthodox faction.
At least in Gansu, it stood shoulder to shoulder with the Kongtong Sect, one of the Nine Sects and One Gang.
In fact, it might have built an even stronger power base by now—a true regional overlord.
With Sima Gong, the beginning and end of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, speaking so bluntly, even the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had no choice but to back down after briefly letting his anger show.
But someone else had watched it all without so much as twitching an eyebrow.
“Why are you growling?
You sound like a yellow dog whose food bowl’s been taken away.”
There was only one person here who could compare the Black Night King himself to a yellow dog.
The Fire King, Jeok Cheongang.
At last, the giant who’d left his mark on the distant history of Murim parted his lips.
The icy gleam in Sima Gong’s eyes settled.
“I suppose I should growl.
I’ll do it as much as I must to protect my food bowl.”
“And it never crossed your mind that someone else’s life might depend on that food bowl?”
“It’s for the greater good.”
“You mean your own good.
The good of the select few who follow you and the Black Dragon Demon Gate.”
Jeok Cheongang slowly looked around the room.
There were around twenty people here, not counting those from the Zhongnan Sect and the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
As he looked from one leader of Gansu Murim to the next, an unmistakable sneer curled his lips.
“Come to think of it, isn’t it strange?
As I understand it, Gansu has at least fifty sects and martial families, yet not even half of them are here.
Ah... were the others already sent to different fronts?”
“They’re already carrying out other assignments,” Sima Gong answered dryly.
“So they were left behind.
To delay Dark Heaven for even half a day if it uses the Moving Formation to appear in the rear.”
“Everyone agreed to it.”
“And before you got that agreement, did you lay out all the facts?
Or did you put a sword to their throats first?”
“With all due respect, there’s something I’d like to say while we’re at it.”
“‘With all due respect’ already puts me in a shitty mood, but I suppose that’s what you’ve got a mouth for.
Go on, then.
Spit it out.”
Sima Gong let out a short breath at Jeok Cheongang’s continuing barbs.
Then, with a calm expression, he spoke.
“We of Gansu Murim will not accept interference from outsiders in this decision, in any form.
Even if it comes from the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families.
Sima Gong’s gaze swept past the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord and me, then stopped on Jeok Cheongang.
“Even if it comes from you, Senior.”
The air around us lurched.
Stiffened hands and feet came standard.
The slight bobbing of people’s throats was an added bonus.
Even if it was Sima Gong, who was he speaking to?
Jeok Cheongang, the Fire King himself.
A terrifying old monster said to rank among the top five in the Central Plains when it came to martial arts—and first when it came to a foul temper.
He’d answered Jeok Cheongang in a downright challenging tone.
No wonder everyone reacted as if they’d been burned.
Everyone except me.
That’s far enough for today.
I’d been watching events unfold the whole time, and I made up my mind.
Then, at a moment nobody expected, I clapped my hands together hard.
Clap!
The sharp sound broke the silence, short and yet seemingly endless.
Everyone turned toward me, startled as if they’d just woken from a dream.
I blinked at them with perfect composure.
“Oh, sorry.
A damn mosquito was buzzing around.”
Of course, I was lying.
With snow that never melted lying all around us, what mosquito?
But the point was that my sudden clap had instantly broken the tension, which had been spiraling toward disaster.
And the two men at the center of it understood why I’d clapped at once.
“You’ve grown up some.
Come a long way.”
At last, Jeok Cheongang spoke in a low voice.
Sima Gong, as if nothing had happened, respectfully clasped his hands in salute.
“I still have a long way to go.
I hope you’ll look kindly on this inadequate junior.”
Jeok Cheongang looked at me and put on a frown, as though something displeased him.
“You certainly do have a long way to go.
Just thinking about what lies ahead, it’s one obstacle after another.
Isn’t it?”
“With you here alongside us, Senior, what need have we of an army?”
Sima Gong put particular emphasis on alongside us, then lifted his head and looked at me.
“You truly have a perceptive Disciple.”
“I don’t know about perceptive.
He’s good at reading a room.”
“Remarkable martial prowess, and a mind that sees several moves ahead.
He’s a blessing to all Murim.
My son ought to have spent more time watching and learning from you while he had the chance...
What do you think of him?”
At Sima Gong’s sudden question, I answered without hesitation.
“He’s useful.”
“What?”
“Now that I’ve spent some time with him, he’s a pretty decent kid.
A little gloomy, though.”
By Murim’s reckoning, Sama Pyo was much older than me.
But even though I’d just thrown the whole idea of respecting my elders to the dogs, Sima Gong only smiled in a way I couldn’t quite read.
“Thank you for saying so.
It makes all the effort I put into raising him worthwhile.”
Over his shoulder, I saw Sama Pyo standing there without a trace of expression.
It struck me that Sima Gong sounded less like a father talking about raising his son than a craftsman talking about a piece he’d made.
But the thought vanished as quickly as it had come, and I spoke again.
“So, you don’t plan to change your decision?”
“Decision.
A choice made by firmly settling on a course of action or attitude.”
“So that’s a no.
Then can I assume the Kongtong Sect’s position is the same?”
“The Kongtong Sect opposed it, but that changes nothing.
All of Gansu Murim reached this decision after extensive discussion.”
Maybe.
But was this really what Gansu Murim wanted?
Or...
Was it only what the Black Dragon Demon Gate wanted?
I swallowed the words hovering on the tip of my tongue and thought for a moment.
Inventory.
I mentally felt for an item stowed somewhere in that bottomless, pitch-black subspace.
But then I shook my head.
No matter how I looked at it, the timing wasn’t right yet.
Not now, at least.
“Then let’s do that.”
“What?”
The startled question came from neither Jeok Cheongang, who was frowning, nor Sima Gong.
It was the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord.
He stared at me with wide eyes.
“You’re willing to accept this as it stands?
Are you serious?”

“Everywhere you go, people have their own rules.
Our Zhongnan is no different.”
“Eldest Senior Brother is right.
Junior Brother, remember how you ought to conduct yourself as our sect’s Sect Leader.”
The Roaring Fury Swordsman and the Taeeul Merciless Sword.
Those were the two who had spoken.
After hearing his Senior Brothers speak in turn, the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord muttered as though groaning.
“Senior Brothers.
But how can we let this happen?”
“We understand how you feel, Sect Leader.
But further discord could jeopardize what we’re trying to accomplish.”
Sima Gong calmly but firmly cut off the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord before he could continue.
Then he surveyed the room and went on.
“I hope everyone will remember this.

Much less...”
Sima Gong’s deeply lowered gaze suddenly came to rest on me.

Wouldn’t you say?”
I already knew what Sima Gong meant, so I nodded.

chapters.title: Chapter 1018
paragraphs: “He was burning a secret letter alone, without anyone knowing.”
The words slipped from my lips in a low murmur.
Jeok Cheongang’s gaze, fixed on me, had grown dark and still.
“Could Namho have been mistaken?”
“That...”
I fell silent instead of finishing the sentence. Jeok Cheongang let out a quiet sigh.
“Damn it. So it’s true.”
At first, I’d thought the whole thing was a simple misunderstanding. A minor incident we could clear up by calling Sama Pyo over and talking to him directly.
But...
“Elder Nam was certain by the time he told me.”
“I thought so. If he’s only just brought it up, he must have spent all this time thinking it through.”
“Yes. At first, even he wasn’t sure. He didn’t have any solid evidence to back it up, either.”
Growing old meant your senses grew dull. Namho had said he’d gone over it again and again.

Was the smell that had lingered in Sama Pyo’s room the same kind he’d encountered so many times as an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion? Or were his dulled senses leading him to suspect them for no reason?
And after more than seven days and nights of worry, this old Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent had reached only one conclusion.
“It was definitely the smell of oiled paper burning. I’m certain now.”
Oiled paper—paper treated with oil.
It was customary to oil the paper used for missives so it wouldn’t get wet or tear easily. Naturally, it smelled different when burned than dry paper did.
“Another reason to oil paper is that it burns easily. The less you want a letter discovered, the faster you need to destroy the evidence.”

Namho had spent a lifetime as an intelligence agent. Though he’d found no trace of anything beyond the faint smell of something burning in the room, from that moment on he never let go of his suspicions about Sama Pyo and Taishan.

“I watched them from the day we left Shanxi Province. But until just a few days ago, I still couldn’t be sure whether it really was oiled paper I’d smelled—or, if it was, who had sent it and from where.”
There was one reason above all that Namho had hesitated to trust his judgment.
“He said the smell was unusual.”
“The smell? You mean the burning paper?”
“Yes. He said it was quite different from any of the burning smells he knew.”
“Burning paper smells like burning paper. What does that—”
“I’ve heard every region has its own customs and food. Even the animals they get their oil from are different.”
At that, Jeok Cheongang suddenly furrowed his brow.
“Wait. Could it be?”
“Elder Nam said there’s an animal found only in Gansu and Qinghai. Is that right?”
“Camels...!”
Jeok Cheongang gave a muffled gasp and nodded.
“So that was the source of the unusual smell.”
“Elder Nam’s spent his whole life in the Central Plains and Nanman. It wouldn’t have been easy for him to recognize it.”
“Right. Those odd-looking beasts are hard to come across. They live only in Qinghai and western Gansu.”
Besides, in Murim these days, people usually made animal oil from cows, horses, sheep, and pigs.
But on the day we first entered Gansu Province, Namho had been taking a break with the other Fire Dragon Pavilion members when he stumbled upon an unexpected clue.

“An incredible coincidence, really. I had no appetite, so I was sitting alone, lost in thought, when I caught a whiff of a smell I’d encountered before. I asked what it was. Camel meat, they told me.”
That clue had finally given Namho the certainty he needed. He told me Sama Pyo had received a secret letter, and that it must have come from Gansu or Qinghai.
As for who had sent it, everyone who knew about the letter had a vague idea already.
Qinghai was only a possibility Namho had raised alongside Gansu. There was just one person who would have sent a secret letter all the way to Shanxi Province, thousands of li away.
“The Black Night King, Sima Gong...”
At my murmur, which sounded almost like I was talking to myself, Jeok Cheongang spat roughly.
“You’ve gotten bold. You really have.”
“What do you think the letter said?”
“Do you have a guess?”
“I do.”
“Then tell me.”
“At the very least, I’m pretty sure it wasn’t ‘Is my son eating well?’”
A vein bulged at Jeok Cheongang’s temple.
“You call that an answer? Even that Taishan—or Gangsan, whatever his name is—could tell you that.”
“Taishan might not.”
“...Honestly, I can’t argue with you on that one. Speaking of that oversized fool, how was he on the way here?”
“Elder Nam said he was acting strange. The closer we got to Gansu, the more he picked at his food, and he moped around all day.”
Of course, “picked at his food” was a slight—no, a considerable—stretch. He was still stuffing his face five times a day. How was that picking at his food? He was eating until he was full.
But considering how much Taishan usually ate, five meals a day was practically intermittent fasting.
And the closer we got to Gansu, the more miserable he looked. There was no shortage of things that seemed strange.
Knowing Sama Pyo, he might’ve kept it from Taishan, too.
Whatever the case, only one thing mattered right now.
While they were still in Shanxi Province, a secret letter had passed between father and son. It contained something they wanted hidden, and whatever it was, it couldn’t be good news for us.
I didn’t want to think about it, but if the worst really did happen...
“Hmm.”
I shook my head, trying to force the thought away. Jeok Cheongang had been watching me. Now he spoke without warning.
“Worried?”
“About what?”
“That you might have to cut down Sama Pyo and Taishan with your own hands.”
Step.
I stopped without realizing it.
I’d been walking almost mechanically, but now I stood stock-still, staring silently at Jeok Cheongang.
“You look like you have a lot to say.”
“Since you’ve gone quiet, let this old man tell you an interesting story.”
I didn’t answer, and Jeok Cheongang didn’t wait for one.
“During the Great Faction War, when the world was going up in flames, I met a man called the Junzi Saber.”
We started walking again. My voice came out troubled.
“That’s quite a title.”

“Like hell it is. At first, I didn’t care for it much. The title was so embarrassingly grand it made my fingers curl up—and nearly break. But after spending some time with him, cutting down Demonic Cult bastards, I found he was a pretty useful fellow.”
“Useful how?”
“As a person and as a martial artist.”
“That’s quite a compliment, coming from you, Old Master.”

“Others thought even more highly of him. He came from a distinguished martial family, though it had fallen on hard times. He was an exceptional fighter with a strong sense of justice. No matter how dangerous things got, he led the way and never backed down.”
He’d been the very model of a chivalrous hero. First to charge, last to retreat, willing to give his life for others.
But I already had a feeling how this story, which had come out of nowhere, would end.
“Why are you talking about him entirely in the past tense? You sound like you regret what happened.”
A bitter smile crossed Jeok Cheongang’s lips.
“You’re a sharp one.”
“Was he a traitor?”
“Yes. He was a Demonic Cult lackey. But he hadn’t been one from the beginning.”
“You mean...”
“Do you remember what I told you about the Junzi Saber’s origins?”
“Yes. He was from a distinguished martial family in Qinghai.”

“In truth, the family had been destroyed in a war with another sect. ‘Torn apart’ would be more accurate than ‘fallen on hard times.’ The only family he knew was an old retainer who’d raised him from infancy by begging women to nurse him.”
The only family he knew.
Suddenly, I thought I understood why a chivalrous hero whose name and face I’d never known had gone over to the Demonic Cult.
“There was a surviving relative.”

“His eldest brother, apparently. He’d been the Lesser Family Head, yet somehow survived the destruction of their family. An extraordinary stroke of luck. With that luck, and an even greater thirst for revenge, he crossed the desert and sought refuge with the Demonic Cult... You’re sharp enough to guess what happened next.”
Why did I feel as though I could see the Korean flag waving before my eyes?
A classic movie I’d seen long ago came to mind, but only for a moment. I’d cried my eyes out watching that movie. This story would have a different ending.
And the meaning of that ending must be why Jeok Cheongang had dredged up such an unpleasant memory.
“The Junzi Saber died, didn’t he?”
Jeok Cheongang answered quietly.
“Yes. I killed him myself.”
“Do you regret it?”
“Regret it? What do you think you’d do in my place?”
“If Sama Pyo and Taishan are plotting something on Sima Gong’s secret orders—and those orders have something to do with Dark Heaven... what would you do?”
I fell silent.
Only a year. It wasn’t long enough to form a deep bond. We’d lived in different circumstances, and we had different personalities.
So why couldn’t I answer?
My lips stayed pressed together, though this was a question I should have answered without hesitation.
What would you do?
Jeok Cheongang’s question echoed in my ears, colliding again and again without end.
Around the time the three thousand troops, after several days of nonstop marching, reached the Qilian Mountains and were taking a brief but sweet rest—
Elsewhere, in a pitch-black secret chamber where not a ray of light entered, three people faced one another.
“Things have gone wrong. Very wrong.”
“The Fire King—that damned old monster—what’s he doing here?”
The two voices came at the man in the seat of honor the moment he sat down. He answered them.
“What’s done is done. The situation has changed, so I asked you both here to work out a new plan.”
“Things have gone badly from the start, yet you’re brimming with confidence without offering a single excuse.”
“This time, Sect Leader Sima, you’ll have to convince us.”
“...Convince you.”
The eyes of the man in the seat of honor—the Black Night King, Sima Gong—suddenly gleamed.
He stared into the darkness at the two old Daoists facing him.

I didn’t want to think about it, but if the worst really did happen...
“Hmm.”
I shook my head, trying to force the thought away.
Jeok Cheongang had been watching me.
Now he spoke without warning.
“Worried?”
“About what?”
“That you might have to cut down Sama Pyo and Taishan with your own hands.”
Step.
I stopped without realizing it.
I’d been walking almost mechanically, but now I stood stock-still, staring silently at Jeok Cheongang.
“You look like you have a lot to say.”
“Since you’ve gone quiet, let this old man tell you an interesting story.”
I didn’t answer, and Jeok Cheongang didn’t wait for one.
“During the Great Faction War, when the world was going up in flames, I met a man called the Junzi Saber.”
We started walking again.
My voice came out troubled.
“That’s quite a title.”
“Like hell it is.
At first, I didn’t care for it much.
The title was so embarrassingly grand it made my fingers curl up—and nearly break.
But after spending some time with him, cutting down Demonic Cult bastards, I found he was a pretty useful fellow.”
“Useful how?”
“As a person and as a martial artist.”
“That’s quite a compliment, coming from you, Old Master.”
“Others thought even more highly of him.
He came from a distinguished martial family, though it had fallen on hard times.
He was an exceptional fighter with a strong sense of justice.
No matter how dangerous things got, he led the way and never backed down.”
He’d been the very model of a chivalrous hero.
First to charge, last to retreat, willing to give his life for others.
But I already had a feeling how this story, which had come out of nowhere, would end.
“Why are you talking about him entirely in the past tense?
You sound like you regret what happened.”
A bitter smile crossed Jeok Cheongang’s lips.
“You’re a sharp one.”
“Was he a traitor?”
“Yes.
He was a Demonic Cult lackey.
But he hadn’t been one from the beginning.”
“You mean...”
“Do you remember what I told you about the Junzi Saber’s origins?”
“Yes.
He was from a distinguished martial family in Qinghai.”
“In truth, the family had been destroyed in a war with another sect.
‘Torn apart’ would be more accurate than ‘fallen on hard times.’ The only family he knew was an old retainer who’d raised him from infancy by begging women to nurse him.”
The only family he knew.
Suddenly, I thought I understood why a chivalrous hero whose name and face I’d never known had gone over to the Demonic Cult.
“There was a surviving relative.”
“His eldest brother, apparently.
He’d been the Lesser Family Head, yet somehow survived the destruction of their family.
An extraordinary stroke of luck.
With that luck, and an even greater thirst for revenge, he crossed the desert and sought refuge with the Demonic Cult...
You’re sharp enough to guess what happened next.”
Why did I feel as though I could see the Korean flag waving before my eyes?
A classic movie I’d seen long ago came to mind, but only for a moment.
I’d cried my eyes out watching that movie.
This story would have a different ending.
And the meaning of that ending must be why Jeok Cheongang had dredged up such an unpleasant memory.
“The Junzi Saber died, didn’t he?”
Jeok Cheongang answered quietly.
“Yes.
I killed him myself.”
“Do you regret it?”
“Regret it?
What do you think you’d do in my place?”
“If Sama Pyo and Taishan are plotting something on Sima Gong’s secret orders—and those orders have something to do with Dark Heaven... what would you do?”
I fell silent.
Only a year.
It wasn’t long enough to form a deep bond.
We’d lived in different circumstances, and we had different personalities.
So why couldn’t I answer?
My lips stayed pressed together, though this was a question I should have answered without hesitation.
What would you do?
Jeok Cheongang’s question echoed in my ears, colliding again and again without end.
Around the time the three thousand troops, after several days of nonstop marching, reached the Qilian Mountains and were taking a brief but sweet rest—
Elsewhere, in a pitch-black secret chamber where not a ray of light entered, three people faced one another.
“Things have gone wrong.
Very wrong.”
“The Fire King—that damned old monster—what’s he doing here?”
The two voices came at the man in the seat of honor the moment he sat down.
He answered them.
“What’s done is done.
The situation has changed, so I asked you both here to work out a new plan.”
“Things have gone badly from the start, yet you’re brimming with confidence without offering a single excuse.”
“This time, Sect Leader Sima, you’ll have to convince us.”
“...Convince you.”
The eyes of the man in the seat of honor—the Black Night King, Sima Gong—suddenly gleamed.
He stared into the darkness at the two old Daoists facing him.

chapters.title: Chapter 1019
paragraphs: Boom, boom, boom.
Rough drumbeats echoed across the rugged ridges of the Qilian Mountains. Their brief, welcome rest was over, and people began getting to their feet and assembling.
Jeok Cheongang, the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, and I were no exception. We just had a little more time to spare because there were fewer of us.
“Whew. Even a quick nap makes a difference, doesn’t it?”
Hyuk Mujin had just woken up and was stretching as he spoke.
“Sure does,” I said.
“Huh? You say that, but you look awfully gloomy.”
“You’re imagining it.”
“Doesn’t seem like it. You look like you haven’t slept at all.”
“No. I’m just not fully awake yet.”
“Ah, you should’ve slept, even for a bit. Sleep’s the best medicine at a time like this.”
“...Are you not hearing me?”
Did this bastard have himself on mute or something?
At my incredulous stare, Hyuk Mujin shrugged.
“Oh, come on, Captain. I could tell something was wrong the moment I saw your face. You’ve got something on your mind, don’t you?”
Sharp instincts.
But no matter how he asked, my current position meant I couldn’t just come out and tell him the truth.
Think about it. How would the Fire Dragon Pavilion members react if they learned the truth about Sama Pyo right now?
The more people who know, the harder it is to keep a secret.
Hyuk Mujin had noticed something the moment he saw my face. Someone keeping an eye on us might notice too.
Worry had a way of showing, whether you meant it to or not.
So there was only one answer I could give him.
“When anything could happen at any moment, who wouldn’t be worried? Huh?”
“Well, that’s true. It’s just... you seem a little different from usual, Captain.”
Unable to fault my reasoning, Hyuk Mujin scratched the back of his head. Then he spoke again, more tentatively.
“But, Captain.”
“What? Something important?”
“No, not really. I just wanted to tell you I’m not worried about anything.”
“What?”
“You said it just now, didn’t you? If you have nothing to worry about in a situation like this, are you even human?”
“And?”
“I don’t know what you’ll think of this, but ever since I started following you, I haven’t really felt worried. Maybe everything we’ve been through has made me too gutsy for my own good, but...”
He kept sneaking glances at me as he spoke. Then he turned toward a distant mountain and murmured as if to himself.
“You’re always there, Captain. I know you’ll fight alongside me, every time. So no matter how dangerous things get, I’m not afraid.”
“Of course, don’t let that put any extra pressure on you. What I’m trying to say is... Well, it’s...”
Maybe things had gotten too awkward. Maybe his thoughts were tangled. Either way, he couldn’t seem to finish.
I watched him for a moment, then supplied the words in my usual, deliberately curt voice.
“Don’t get caught up in pointless worries. I’ve always trusted you. That’s basically what you’re trying to say, right?”
“That’s... right.”
“Then why are you stumbling over it? You’re old enough to say what you mean.”
Hyuk Mujin looked indignant at the sudden jab about his age.
“Then start treating me like I’m older than you before you say that. Have you got no shame?”
“Mujin.”
“What?”
“Go get in formation before I pluck every last hair from down below. Can’t you hear the drums?”
“...Honestly. The way you talk, anyone listening would think I did all the talking. You got plenty of words in yourself.”
“What was that?”
“I’m going! I’m going!”
He ran off with his lips stuck out. I couldn’t help letting out a quiet laugh.
“‘I’m going’ is a casual way to say it, you punk.”
But my mutter reached no one. The words scattered into the air, and my pale breath briefly obscured something falling from above.
Tap.
A moment later, I felt its cold touch.
I looked up. Countless snowflakes were drifting down between clouds of every size.
Boom, boom, boom.
The drums sounded again, right on cue. I started walking, repeating Hyuk Mujin’s words to myself.
He trusted me, no matter what happened.
At the same time, I thought of the two people who weren’t here.
Had I failed to earn your trust because I hadn’t shown you enough? Or...
Had I been the only fool who thought we’d become dependable comrades and friends?
Crunch.
I planted my foot firmly on the ground, already turning white beneath the snow.
By the time the unceasing drumbeats stopped, the number of people and horses heading west over the Qilian Mountains had grown enough for anyone to notice.
Grind. Grrind.
The mountain ridges groaned beneath a force numbering in the thousands.
Sama Pyo was counting the flags visible between the bare branches. Just after they crossed yet another hill and entered the wilderness again, he spoke.
“That’s unexpected.”
He offered no preamble, but neither he nor the person beside him thought anything of it. Father and son were used to this.
“What is?”
His father answered without turning his head. Sama Pyo studied his profile.
“That you agreed to their demands.”
“Their demands?”
“At the meeting, you even argued with them to get your way. Yet in the end, you reinforced our troops with part of the force stationed in the Qilian Mountains. Three thousand of them, no less.”
Sama Pyo was right.
When the drums announcing the end of the brief rest stopped, nearly half the Black Dragon Demon Gate’s martial artists stationed in the Qilian Mountains had already assembled ahead of them.
“Is that a problem?”
“I’m only surprised. It isn’t like you.”
“Isn’t like me?”
Only then did his father turn to look him in the eye. Sama Pyo lowered his head slightly.
“It was only a small question that occurred to me.”
“Then tell me what you’re thinking.”
“I thought you would never reverse a decision once you’d made it. Especially for outsiders.”
“Why?”
“Because that’s what I’ve always seen you do.”
“Raise your head.”
Sama Pyo obediently did as his father’s dry voice commanded. His father’s eyes, black as obsidian, were already gleaming at him.
“Have you forgotten what I taught you already? Never be certain about any situation—or any person.”
“Circumstances can change suddenly. To survive and grow stronger in this harsh world, you must keep questioning what you know and adjust your calculations to every change. This time is no different.”
A few years ago—no, even one year ago—Sama Pyo would have listened in silence.
So why did his father’s voice seem as distant as an echo today, though Sima Gong was right beside him?
Question everything. Keep calculating... You haven’t changed at all.
Sama Pyo was reminded, painfully, of what kind of man his father was and the life he’d led.

Because Sima Gong had doubted and guarded against everything, the Black Dragon Demon Gate had survived even the Great Faction War. Because his calculations had been precise to the last detail, it had prospered beyond measure.
But anyone who knew the martial world knew one more thing: blood relatives were not exempt from the suspicion and calculation that had made Sima Gong who he was.
Seven older brothers. Nine older sisters.
Sama Pyo thought of where they had all ended up—children of the same father, born to different mothers.
That’s right. Those calculations are how I became the Young Sect Leader, too.
That was the Black Night King, Sima Gong.

He would stop at nothing to survive and rule. He would put even his own children on the scales, weigh their worth, and cast the others aside without hesitation to appoint his most capable child—his seventeenth—as Young Sect Leader.
In that sense, he was a man of the unorthodox factions through and through. And the blood Sama Pyo had inherited from him ran beneath his skin.
It was like a shackle he couldn’t put so much as a scratch on, no matter how he struggled. Beneath the crushing weight of the iron ball chained to it, Sama Pyo’s body and mind bent.
“I’ll take those words to heart as though they were worth gold and jade.”
It wasn’t a mere empty platitude or a ruse. The words came from deep within his heart, and his father sensed his son’s feelings just as clearly.
Pyo, it seems that boy is finally coming to his senses.
Sima Gong murmured inwardly and felt his spirits lift.
After all, who was Sama Pyo? The heir he’d finally had in his old age, the son who would someday inherit everything.

His innate martial talent was at least the equal of the Ten Dragons and Phoenixes, the finest young prodigies in the Central Plains. It might even surpass theirs. He had a shrewd mind as well. He was a born leader.
But something started to change in him after he joined the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
His first act of defiance.
Without an order or even permission from Sima Gong, the Sect Leader, his son had joined the Fire Dragon Pavilion on his own. By the time Sima Gong learned of it, the deed was done.
The Fire Dragon Pavilion and the Azure Dragon Pavilion were newly established strike forces under the Alliance Leader’s direct command. Countless eyes were watching the actions of the two pavilions.
And in the Fire Dragon Pavilion his son had joined, there was him.
Jin Taekyung.
The Hidden Dragon of Shanxi, who had risen to become the Divine Dragon of the world. A young giant of Murim.
Every step he took left a deep, enormous mark. His path was strewn with the corpses and blood of countless enemies, while praise and cheers followed him from people throughout the land.
Sima Gong could only watch, hoping that his son’s sudden defiance might give the Black Dragon Demon Gate another chance to soar.
But the secret correspondence he should have received never came, and Sama Pyo’s attitude, when they met for the first time in a year, had seemed somehow different.
At least, until just now.
I’ll still have to keep watching him... But for now, I can breathe a little easier.
And it was just as Sima Gong let out a quiet laugh to himself at the sight of his son gradually returning to his old self that it happened.
Shhhwick—BOOM!
Several hundred jang away, a red flame shot up above a barren hill and exploded, bathing his eyes in its brilliant light.
No—everyone’s.

chapters.title: Chapter 1020
paragraphs: It happened in an instant no one could have predicted.
Whoosh—BOOM!
Even from several hundred jang away, everyone—including me—could see the burst of red light blazing across the distant sky and hear the explosion that followed.
A signal flare!
No doubt about it. The scouts who’d gone ahead of the main force had fired it. And it was red—the signal for extreme danger.
Clang! Clang! Clang!
Everyone froze for a moment. Then, as the danger sank in, weapons came free of their sheaths.
“Prepare for battle!”
“Disciples of the Martial Might Sword Sect, prepare for an enemy ambush!”
“Zhongnan Sect Disciples, form the Moon-Shattering Sword Formation!”
The sudden shift in their aura seemed to make the air tremble.

All around me flashed a mountain of sabers and a forest of swords. As our allies moved in unison to the shouted orders, I kicked off from the saddle, leaving a quick word for Hyuk Mujin, who was closest to me.
“Hold your position until I get back.”
“W-wait a—!”
Whoosh!
A fierce gust swallowed Hyuk Mujin’s voice, and the distance of a dozen jang disappeared in an instant.
Buoyancy swept through my body. I stepped lightly on empty air, on the wind, soaring upward even as I raced forward.
“Th-there!”
“Archers! What are you waiting for? The enemy’s here! Fire!”
“You idiots, lower your bows! He’s one of ours!”
My movements were so free that a few people below, still caught up in the confusion, mistook me for an enemy.
Someone was following close behind me.
“You don’t give an old man a moment’s peace. What in the world is going on?”
The familiar voice came with the effortless footfalls of Stepping on Empty Air, as though Jeok Cheongang were running along the ground.
I answered without turning around. “Something must have happened to the scouts who went ahead.”
“Something happened? You don’t mean what this old man thinks you mean?”
“We don’t know yet. But one thing’s certain...”
I fixed my gaze on the dust cloud rising over the distant, winding sand dunes.
“Whatever’s happening, it can’t be good news.”
A quarter of an hour later, I realized once again that bad premonitions, as always, never missed.
“Cough. D-Dunhuang. Dunhuang has...!”

The unfamiliar man’s lips were parched, his face pale, and his clothes little more than rags. The scouts were covered in dust but otherwise looked unharmed. He looked as though hardship and desperation had clung to every part of him.
His voice trembled as he finished.
“It’s fallen... to them.”
Not one of us had any doubt who he meant by “them.”
Dark Heaven.
The Fiends beyond the vast desert had finally crossed the river of sand and set foot in human territory.
The stranger was a messenger sent from the Great Snow Mountain. The news he brought stunned the entire leadership.
“S-say that again. What, what did you just say?”

The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord was the Sect Leader of the prestigious Zhongnan Sect, a man who should have remained steady in any situation. Yet he stammered, and no one showed so much as a trace of amusement.
No—they couldn’t have. Everyone there felt just as he did. What had come from the messenger’s lips was almost impossible to believe.
But when he repeated his account, it didn’t change.
“I-I regret to report...”
“Start from the beginning. Explain it slowly—come on!”
The messenger squeezed his eyes shut, unable to continue. Then he bit down on his lip and, under the barrage of sharp commands, managed to speak.
“It began when Jade Gate Pass was breached.”
As far as I knew, Jade Gate Pass had long ago been a major gateway on the Silk Road connecting the Central Plains with the Western Regions.
It stood in a wide-open stretch of desert. A small earthen fortress had been built there, making it an ideal place to watch the surrounding area.
In other words, a strategic point perfectly suited to monitoring the border with a small force.
Small, of course, only compared with the total force Gansu’s Murim had mobilized. At the recent leadership meeting, we’d heard that at least a hundred scouts were stationed at Jade Gate Pass.
No—at least a hundred scouts had been stationed there.
By now, they were probably all dead.
“Are you saying they all died? Every single one?”
“We had no way to confirm it, but that is likely. The enemy apparently went undetected until it was within three hundred li of Dunhuang.”
“Then when exactly did Dunhuang fall into enemy hands?”
“About three days ago, I was told.”
“Three days ago...!”
Low groans rose from the leadership. I spoke up.
“Wait. I heard you came from the Great Snow Mountain, not Dunhuang. Who told you this?”
“I never learned his Daoist name, but he was a Kongtong Sect Daoist who had been defending Dunhuang.”
“You don’t know his Daoist name?”
“N-no.”
I frowned.

The Kongtong Sect was a Daoist sect, and to its members, a Daoist name was as good as their own. Just as the monks of Shaolin Temple had abandoned their worldly names and introduced themselves by their Dharma names, Daoist names were basic introductions among martial artists.
That he hadn’t even done that suggested two possibilities.
First, the messenger standing before us had brought false information.
Or...
He died in such a desperate situation that he didn’t even have time to give his Daoist name.
The messenger’s next words supported my second guess.
“I was too flustered to mention it earlier, but the Daoist was already seriously injured when I first saw him. He died moments after reaching the Great Snow Mountain.”
“Good heavens.”
Someone let out a groan.
The mood grew heavier, and not only because the unknown Daoist had died.

A messenger in Murim had to be fast enough to break through an enemy encirclement, with the martial skill to back it up. If the man Kongtong had sent died moments after arriving, what state had the forces at Dunhuang been in?
Of course, everyone there—including me—already knew what had happened to them. We’d only been trying to deny the shocking news we’d heard.
“So it was true. All of it.”
The messenger answered Jeok Cheongang’s cold mutter.
“It’s a terrible report, hard to believe, but that’s what I was told.”
It hadn’t exactly been a pleasant dream. Still, it was time to wake up and face the cruel reality.
The others remained silent, looking as though they still couldn’t believe it. A chill ran down my spine as I forced the words out.
“At least two thousand dead, and three thousand seriously injured or missing. Is that right?”
The messenger didn’t answer. He only lowered his head in exhaustion. Seeing him, everyone was finally forced to accept the reality they’d put off for as long as they could.
“H-how can this make any sense...?”
“What can we do? It’s already happened.”
“Ten thousand. A full ten thousand! How could a force that large be defeated so easily?”
Yes. Ten thousand. A full ten thousand.
Yet the force defending Dunhuang under the Kongtong Sect had lost half its numbers—even though they’d fought a defensive battle.
In just half a day.
And that wasn’t the only bad news.

“About thirty percent of the Kongtong Sect’s strength was lost. During the desperate retreat, two Perfected Ones serving as Kongtong Elders and all one hundred members of the Demon-Subduing Squad died at Dunhuang.”
Gasps sounded all around us.
This was the Kongtong Sect. One of the Nine Sects and One Gang. One of the fifteen great pillars supporting the martial world.

And Kongtong had been broken. Its forces had retreated, leaving behind two Elders said to have reached Supreme Peak more than a decade ago and the Demon-Subduing Squad, whose fame had spread even to the Central Plains.
“Then... the Sect Leader? What happened to the Sect Leader?”
At the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord’s urgent question, everyone held their breath and waited for the messenger’s answer.
By modern standards, thirty percent casualties would be catastrophic enough to call a force annihilated. Murim judged things differently.
What mattered was whether its masters survived. No matter how devastating the losses, if the head of the force was still alive, there was hope.
The Kongtong Sect Leader was Gansu’s strongest martial artist, said to be half a step ahead of even the Black Night King, Sima Gong. If he’d survived, they could still counterattack.

“Thank goodness. Heaven was watching over him.”
Sighs of relief escaped all around them. At that moment, someone suddenly spoke.
“And?”
“Pardon?”
“I asked what happened next.”
Most of the leadership had risen and fallen with every word of the report. This voice remained calm.
Sima Gong stared at the messenger with a deeply sunken gaze and spoke again.
“If the Sect Leader withdrew with the surviving troops, he must have headed for the Great Snow Mountain. Yet from what you’ve said, there’s been no word of him since. Why is that?”

A few members of the leadership nodded hopefully. But I wasn’t so sure.
If the messenger, who must have escaped the battlefield ahead of everyone else, was injured that badly...

Dark Heaven’s great army would already be sweeping the area around Dunhuang like a net as it advanced toward the Great Snow Mountain—hunting down the survivors and moving to break the second defensive line in its path.
They’re moving absurdly fast. Faster than I ever imagined.
At that moment, I realized we had no choice left.
“We’re not too late yet. Send a messenger at once and mobilize every force in the Qilian Mountains.”
“What?”
Sima Gong frowned at my abrupt words.
“What did you just say?”
“I said to mobilize every force stationed in the Qilian Mountains. If the Great Snow Mountain falls, it’s over.”
“We’ve already discussed that and reached a conclusion.”
I shrugged at his dark gaze.
“Then change the conclusion.”
“Ah, just so there’s no misunderstanding.”
The next moment, I pulled something from inside my clothes and added in a low voice,
“This isn’t a suggestion. It’s an order.”
Marquis of Shangshan, Jin Taekyung.
Sima Gong’s eyes widened as he stared at the identity tablet, its characters engraved in elegant script.

Whoosh—BOOM!
Even from several hundred jang away, everyone—including me—could see the burst of red light blazing across the distant sky and hear the explosion that followed.
A signal flare!
No doubt about it.
The scouts who’d gone ahead of the main force had fired it.
And it was red—the signal for extreme danger.
Clang!
Clang!
Clang!
Everyone froze for a moment.
Then, as the danger sank in, weapons came free of their sheaths.
“Prepare for battle!”
“Disciples of the Martial Might Sword Sect, prepare for an enemy ambush!”
“Zhongnan Sect Disciples, form the Moon-Shattering Sword Formation!”
The sudden shift in their aura seemed to make the air tremble.
All around me flashed a mountain of sabers and a forest of swords.
As our allies moved in unison to the shouted orders, I kicked off from the saddle, leaving a quick word for Hyuk Mujin, who was closest to me.
“Hold your position until I get back.”
“W-wait a—!”
Whoosh!
A fierce gust swallowed Hyuk Mujin’s voice, and the distance of a dozen jang disappeared in an instant.
Buoyancy swept through my body.
I stepped lightly on empty air, on the wind, soaring upward even as I raced forward.

Fire!”

The news he brought stunned the entire leadership.

The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord was the Sect Leader of the prestigious Zhongnan Sect, a man who should have remained steady in any situation.

No—they couldn’t have.
Everyone there felt just as he did.
What had come from the messenger’s lips was almost impossible to believe.

chapters.title: Chapter 1021
paragraphs: The truth was, until a little while ago, I hadn’t planned to go this far.

The rule that officials and martial artists didn’t interfere with each other hadn’t come from nowhere. In a world where the two sides barely spared each other a glance, flaunting either side’s authority would only breed resentment.
But authority could be remarkably effective when used at the right moment.
Like now.
“Marquis of Shangshan...”
A low groan slipped from someone’s lips, breaking the brief silence.
In the heavy, sunken atmosphere, Sima Gong stared wide-eyed at the identity tablet in my hand. It was then that he spoke.
“So it isn’t a request. It’s an order.”
His voice was dry as sand. His gaze, gone cold, shifted to my face.
“How interesting. Truly interesting.”
The corners of his mouth were stiff despite his words. I scratched the back of my head.
“I’m glad you find it interesting, but I’d rather hear your answer than your opinion. As you know, every fifteen minutes feels like three autumns right now.”
“Am I to understand that you meant every word you said a moment ago?”
“Oh? You still didn’t understand? Strange. I thought I’d made myself clear.”

“Well, if you insist, I’ll say it again. Scrape together every last soldier you’ve got holed up in the Qilian Mountains and bring them to the Great Snow Mountain. Right now. That’s an order from the Marquis of Shangshan.”
Stifled gasps rose among the leaders.
Who was Sima Gong, the Black Night King?
He shared control of Gansu with the Kongtong Sect—or rather, he now held a far stronger position than they did.
It was still speculation, but if this crisis passed and peace returned, the badly battered Kongtong Sect wouldn’t be able to stand against the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
But...
So what?
I calmly surveyed Sima Gong and the other leaders, one by one.
At that moment, they didn’t look like heads of factions bearing the weight of immense responsibility and tens of thousands of lives. They looked like gambling addicts.
Fools fiddling with the tiles in their hands while tens of thousands of lives were wagered on the table.
This was when you used authority.
Even if it brought fierce opposition and discord.
Right then, one of the leaders spoke.
“From what I’ve heard, your words and conduct have been getting more and more out of line.”
I looked over. His face was fairly familiar.

He was the Sect Leader of a mid-sized sect with around two hundred disciples, a man with some influence in Gansu. He’d always stood near Sima Gong whenever the leaders gathered, so I recognized him more readily than the others.
A close associate, you might say.
“I’ll say this much: I agree with Sect Leader Seok.”
“Young Hero Jin—no, Great Hero Jin—we respect the sense of justice you’ve shown us, but surely there are bounds you ought to observe.”

“Although the Great Nation’s imperial court is now standing with us against the great enemy Dark Heaven, that doesn’t mean you should invoke your title as a marquis to strong-arm us like this over Murim’s affairs.”

Birds of a feather flock together; crabs side with crabs. Maybe it was the support of the neighbors, each adding their own word while watching the room. Or maybe it was because Jeok Cheongang stood there with his arms crossed, quietly watching without saying a thing.
Whatever the reason, Sect Leader Seok sounded bolder when he spoke again. Like a loyal dog checking his master’s mood, he stole a glance at the silent Sima Gong.
“You see? Everyone feels the same way. And Sect Leader Sima here gave the matter careful thought before—”
I was almost curious what nonsense he’d come out with next. But patience had never been my strong suit.
“So?”
I cut him off, then added quietly, “Is there a problem?”
The Sect Leader stared at me in silence, as though he’d been struck dumb. Then, his face stiff, he replied,
“And if there is?”
“Put up with it.”
“What... did you just say?”

“Put up with it, even if it feels dirty and unfair. What are you going to do about it, even if it pisses you off? Does a marquis appointed by the Son of Heaven—no, by His August Majesty the Emperor himself—look like jack shit to you?”
“T-that’s not what I meant!”
His face went red as he shouted. I couldn’t help laughing.

“Or we can set our titles aside and fight it out. I won’t tell His Majesty. We’ve only just joined hands with the Murim Alliance, and it’d be bad for both sides if something happened now. Right? Don’t you think?”
My words were directed at the Sect Leader in front of me. My gaze wasn’t.
Sima Gong met my eyes, and he wasn’t stupid enough to miss the point.
“Those are memorable words.”
The moment he spoke, the room fell deathly silent.
At last, Sima Gong spoke, looking at me with an expression I couldn’t read.
“You’re right. I, too, am a subject of the Great Nation. I should obey an order from a marquis appointed by His Majesty.”
Eyes shifted uneasily around the room. They probably hadn’t expected Sima Gong to concede so readily.
I’d more or less expected it.
“May I take that to mean you’ll do as I ask?”
“You may. This time, I’ll yield.”
“So there won’t be a second time.”
“What can I do? I have my pride, which I must uphold even if it kills me, and my own judgment. I trust you and the Senior over there will understand that much.”
Sima Gong was even wearing a faint smile now. My gaze darkened.
What the hell is this guy?
He was definitely hiding something, but I couldn’t tell what it was. No—he wasn’t giving me the slightest opening to catch a glimpse.
I came on strong on purpose, and he barely reacted.
I hadn’t invoked the authority of a marquis and tried to force him into line simply because the situation was urgent.
Even a boulder weighing ten thousand geun would shake when struck. I’d hoped his reaction would tell me what he was thinking—and how many of the leaders here were with him.
I’d learned a little about the latter. With Sima Gong, I’d failed spectacularly.
And until I knew what he was hiding, Sima Gong and I were allies under the same banner.
“As you said, every fifteen minutes feels like three autumns right now. Is there anything else you need to say?”
I was silent for a moment. His gaze met mine across the space between us, but I could read nothing in it.
“No.”
“Good. Then I’ll send someone at once to bring in every force in the Qilian Mountains. Does Zhongnan agree?”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had been looking back and forth between us in confusion. He spoke at last.
“If the Great Snow Mountain falls, Gansu will be hanging by a thread. I see no reason to disagree.”

“Then it’s settled. Family Heads, Sect Leaders—inform your martial artists and see that they’re fully prepared. We must reach the Great Snow Mountain ahead of the enemy, within half a day at the latest.”
The leaders of Gansu’s Murim exchanged wary glances, then performed the clasped-fist salute. Sima Gong was hurrying back to his saddle when he suddenly stopped.
As though he’d forgotten something, he let out a quiet “Ah” and turned toward me.
“Could I ask one favor?”
“What favor?”
“I’d like to entrust my son to you again. The one I borrowed for a while. What do you say?”
My eyes widened. Sima Gong gave a hearty laugh and continued.

“I was glad to see a blood relative I hadn’t seen in a long time, so I kept him by my side for a few days. But in wartime, we must strictly separate public duty from private affairs. He’s a member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion before he’s the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate. Isn’t that right?”
Sama Pyo hesitated, then answered flatly.
“...That’s right.”
What was Sima Gong up to?
Truthfully, I already had a good idea of Sima Gong’s intentions. But I couldn’t let that show—not in a situation like this.
I nodded, keeping my expression and tone as calm as I could.
“Of course. I’ve been waiting for him to come back.”
“Glad to hear it. I’ll take that as a yes and send him to the rear shortly. With no telling what might happen next, a father and son ought to have a chance to say goodbye.”
At Sima Gong’s faint smile, I found myself newly certain of the suspicion I didn’t want to believe.
Before he was a member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion, Sama Pyo was Sima Gong’s son and the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
From now on, he’d be with us not as a comrade, but as a spy.
Damn it.
I gave a deep clasped-fist salute and turned away to hide the look on my face.
Thud, thud, thud, thud!
The five thousand men and horses surged forward at full speed the moment they set out.
The ground shook as though an earthquake had struck. A cloud of dust rose amid the thunder of hooves, thick enough to hide them from any prying eyes.
“Do you know why I want you to stay by Jin Taekyung’s side?”
Sima Gong studied his son’s face as he asked. Sama Pyo’s voice didn’t waver.
“What do you want me to do?”
“What you suspect. Watch their every move.”
“A difficult task.”
“Why do you say that?”
“Because I mustn’t draw needless suspicion.”
Sama Pyo had already accepted the order. Sima Gong smiled inwardly, satisfied.
No questions. No doubts.
That was exactly the way he wanted his son to be—and the way he’d wanted him to be again.
“Aren’t you curious why I’m giving you this order?”
“I’ll simply obey. It must be for the good of our sect.”
At his son’s unhesitating answer, a faint smile touched Sima Gong’s lips.

“Yes. It’s all for the resurgence of our family and the Black Dragon Demon Gate. Before long, it will all be yours. You’ll be the undisputed ruler of Gansu then, and you may even expand into the Central Plains.”
“You mean...”
His son let the words trail off. Sima Gong gave a small nod.
“There can’t be two tigers on one mountain.”
“Things didn’t go as we first expected, but that changes nothing. Whatever stands in our way, we’ll get what we want.”
As always.
The words he added quietly were swallowed by the wind. His son watched his father’s eyes gleam with ambition, then turned his horse with a respectful clasped-fist salute.
There was no tender father-son farewell of the kind Sima Gong had spoken of to Jin Taekyung.
As always.

“Although the Great Nation’s imperial court is now standing with us against the great enemy Dark Heaven, that doesn’t mean you should invoke your title as a marquis to strong-arm us like this over Murim’s affairs.”
Birds of a feather flock together; crabs side with crabs.
Maybe it was the support of the neighbors, each adding their own word while watching the room.
Or maybe it was because Jeok Cheongang stood there with his arms crossed, quietly watching without saying a thing.
Whatever the reason, Sect Leader Seok sounded bolder when he spoke again.
Like a loyal dog checking his master’s mood, he stole a glance at the silent Sima Gong.
“You see?
Everyone feels the same way.
And Sect Leader Sima here gave the matter careful thought before—”
I was almost curious what nonsense he’d come out with next.
But patience had never been my strong suit.
“So?”
I cut him off, then added quietly, “Is there a problem?”
The Sect Leader stared at me in silence, as though he’d been struck dumb.
Then, his face stiff, he replied,
“And if there is?”
“Put up with it.”
“What... did you just say?”
“Put up with it, even if it feels dirty and unfair.
What are you going to do about it, even if it pisses you off?
Does a marquis appointed by the Son of Heaven—no, by His August Majesty the Emperor himself—look like jack shit to you?”
“T-that’s not what I meant!”
His face went red as he shouted.
I couldn’t help laughing.
“Or we can set our titles aside and fight it out.
I won’t tell His Majesty.
We’ve only just joined hands with the Murim Alliance, and it’d be bad for both sides if something happened now.
Right?
Don’t you think?”
My words were directed at the Sect Leader in front of me.
My gaze wasn’t.
Sima Gong met my eyes, and he wasn’t stupid enough to miss the point.
“Those are memorable words.”
The moment he spoke, the room fell deathly silent.
At last, Sima Gong spoke, looking at me with an expression I couldn’t read.
“You’re right.
I, too, am a subject of the Great Nation.
I should obey an order from a marquis appointed by His Majesty.”
Eyes shifted uneasily around the room.
They probably hadn’t expected Sima Gong to concede so readily.
I’d more or less expected it.
“May I take that to mean you’ll do as I ask?”
“You may.
This time, I’ll yield.”
“So there won’t be a second time.”
“What can I do?
I have my pride, which I must uphold even if it kills me, and my own judgment.
I trust you and the Senior over there will understand that much.”
Sima Gong was even wearing a faint smile now.
My gaze darkened.
What the hell is this guy?
He was definitely hiding something, but I couldn’t tell what it was.
No—he wasn’t giving me the slightest opening to catch a glimpse.
I came on strong on purpose, and he barely reacted.
I hadn’t invoked the authority of a marquis and tried to force him into line simply because the situation was urgent.
Even a boulder weighing ten thousand geun would shake when struck.
I’d hoped his reaction would tell me what he was thinking—and how many of the leaders here were with him.
I’d learned a little about the latter.
With Sima Gong, I’d failed spectacularly.
And until I knew what he was hiding, Sima Gong and I were allies under the same banner.
“As you said, every fifteen minutes feels like three autumns right now.
Is there anything else you need to say?”
I was silent for a moment.
His gaze met mine across the space between us, but I could read nothing in it.
“No.”
“Good.
Then I’ll send someone at once to bring in every force in the Qilian Mountains.
Does Zhongnan agree?”
The Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord had been looking back and forth between us in confusion.
He spoke at last.
“If the Great Snow Mountain falls, Gansu will be hanging by a thread.
I see no reason to disagree.”
“Then it’s settled.
Family Heads, Sect Leaders—inform your martial artists and see that they’re fully prepared.
We must reach the Great Snow Mountain ahead of the enemy, within half a day at the latest.”
The leaders of Gansu’s Murim exchanged wary glances, then performed the clasped-fist salute.
Sima Gong was hurrying back to his saddle when he suddenly stopped.
As though he’d forgotten something, he let out a quiet “Ah” and turned toward me.
“Could I ask one favor?”
“What favor?”
“I’d like to entrust my son to you again.
The one I borrowed for a while.
What do you say?”
My eyes widened.
Sima Gong gave a hearty laugh and continued.
“I was glad to see a blood relative I hadn’t seen in a long time, so I kept him by my side for a few days.
But in wartime, we must strictly separate public duty from private affairs.
He’s a member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion before he’s the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
Isn’t that right?”
Sama Pyo hesitated, then answered flatly.
“...That’s right.”
What was Sima Gong up to?
Truthfully, I already had a good idea of Sima Gong’s intentions.
But I couldn’t let that show—not in a situation like this.
I nodded, keeping my expression and tone as calm as I could.
“Of course.
I’ve been waiting for him to come back.”
“Glad to hear it.
I’ll take that as a yes and send him to the rear shortly.
With no telling what might happen next, a father and son ought to have a chance to say goodbye.”
At Sima Gong’s faint smile, I found myself newly certain of the suspicion I didn’t want to believe.
Before he was a member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion, Sama Pyo was Sima Gong’s son and the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
From now on, he’d be with us not as a comrade, but as a spy.
Damn it.
I gave a deep clasped-fist salute and turned away to hide the look on my face.
Thud, thud, thud, thud!
The five thousand men and horses surged forward at full speed the moment they set out.
The ground shook as though an earthquake had struck.
A cloud of dust rose amid the thunder of hooves, thick enough to hide them from any prying eyes.
“Do you know why I want you to stay by Jin Taekyung’s side?”
Sima Gong studied his son’s face as he asked.
Sama Pyo’s voice didn’t waver.
“What do you want me to do?”
“What you suspect.
Watch their every move.”
“A difficult task.”
“Why do you say that?”
“Because I mustn’t draw needless suspicion.”
Sama Pyo had already accepted the order.
Sima Gong smiled inwardly, satisfied.
No questions.
No doubts.
That was exactly the way he wanted his son to be—and the way he’d wanted him to be again.
“Aren’t you curious why I’m giving you this order?”
“I’ll simply obey.
It must be for the good of our sect.”
At his son’s unhesitating answer, a faint smile touched Sima Gong’s lips.
“Yes.
It’s all for the resurgence of our family and the Black Dragon Demon Gate.
Before long, it will all be yours.
You’ll be the undisputed ruler of Gansu then, and you may even expand into the Central Plains.”
“You mean...”
His son let the words trail off.
Sima Gong gave a small nod.
“There can’t be two tigers on one mountain.”
“Things didn’t go as we first expected, but that changes nothing.
Whatever stands in our way, we’ll get what we want.”
As always.
The words he added quietly were swallowed by the wind.
His son watched his father’s eyes gleam with ambition, then turned his horse with a respectful clasped-fist salute.
There was no tender father-son farewell of the kind Sima Gong had spoken of to Jin Taekyung.
As always.

chapters.title: Chapter 1022
paragraphs: The five thousand men and horses raced forward as though their lives depended on it.
To lighten their loads by even a single geun, they threw away the food and supplies they’d brought in the barest quantities. They whipped their horses on without a thought for pacing them.
If a horse foamed at the mouth and collapsed, its rider ran on foot, pouring every last bit of internal energy into a movement technique.
It was a forced march that would exhaust even a well-trained martial artist.
Unlike the martial artists of Gansu, the Zhongnan Sect and Fire Dragon Pavilion members had managed only a couple of brief rests. To them, the final half day must have felt like ten years.
But because we’d pushed everyone to their limits, we caught sight of the snow-white mountain range as the first light of dawn reached us from behind.
The Great Snow Mountain.
True to its name, the snow-covered range shone in the dawn light, dazzlingly white and strangely out of place.
No—perhaps the strangest thing was the fickle weather.
Just two hours ago, there was nothing but desert around us.
I glanced up at the sky, now dumping great flakes of snow as if the desert had never been there, then looked back at the Great Snow Mountain.
Dozens of high peaks touched the clouds, with the range winding between them.
The immense natural barrier lay quiet, still partly shrouded in darkness. Among the five thousand men and horses slowing as they drew closer, wariness and unease hung in the air.
It was only natural.
By now, everyone had heard the news that the front line at Dunhuang, built around the Kongtong Sect, had been utterly crushed half a day ago.
Of course, given the distance and the time, it’s unlikely the Great Snow Mountain has already fallen to Dark Heaven...
War was a monster too unpredictable to reduce to probabilities.
Especially when the enemy wielded strange powers that the words dark arts could hardly begin to describe.
Still, I never thought the Kongtong Sect would fall this easily.
To be fair, the Kongtong Sect wasn’t among the strongest of the Nine Sects and One Gang.
Even so, it had three Supreme Peak masters, including its Sect Leader. By all accounts, its disciples from the main temple—the core of its strength—were accomplished martial artists too.
Yet they hadn’t held out for days. They hadn’t even lasted half a day. Even I, after clashing with Dark Heaven several times, had trouble gauging the enemy’s strength.
The Kongtong Sect must have had enough time to prepare, and enough strength to defend itself.
Three Supreme Peak masters at the heart of the Kongtong Sect. A thousand disciples. And a force of no fewer than ten thousand rallied around them.
Thanks to Ma Junggeol’s information, we knew Dark Heaven’s army numbered at least thirty thousand. But there was an enormous difference between defending a fortress and attacking one.
Hearing that Dark Heaven had overcome that difference and crushed our forces so one-sidedly brought one possibility to mind.
They have at least three Supreme Peak masters. If not... then they have one extraordinary master. Someone powerful enough to dominate the battlefield through sheer martial might.
The first possibility would be a relief. The second would make for a hard fight.
Just as not every martial artist was alike, neither were the people called superhuman.
From the foot of a mountain, you couldn’t tell how many trees grew on its vast slopes or how many steep gorges cut through it.
Dozens of peaks might look much the same from afar, but up close, their heights were anything but equal.
A difference like that between superhumans must have been why our force of ten thousand, including the Kongtong Sect, had suffered near-annihilation and been forced to retreat.
Our force is formidable too. Did Dark Heaven really send tens of thousands of troops into Gansu without knowing that?
Jeok Cheongang, me, the three old Daoists of the Zhongnan Sect, and Sima Gong, the Black Night King.
There were six Supreme Peak masters right here. And thousands of men and horses crossing Gansu were bound to be noticed.
In the end, I reached one conclusion.
They advanced into Gansu because they believed they could win.
Then what made them so confident despite losing four Demon Lords and a Demon Empress?
The Blood Lord, who had vanished after the Shaolin Bloodshed?
Some other force Dark Heaven had yet to reveal?
Or...
The Lord of Heaven?
Just as those two words slipped from my lips without my realizing it, a chill ran down my spine by instinct.
Whoosh!
A sharp whistle suddenly cut through the air. I turned toward it and saw flames rising one after another from deep in the Great Snow Mountain.
Boom. Boom. Boom!
Once, twice. Then three times at the end.
Fireworks burst across the sky in quick succession, and a red line appeared along the snow-blanketed mountainside.
That’s...
A signal.
The forces who had taken the Great Snow Mountain were signaling with fireworks and torches.
Sighs of relief passed through the people who’d been on edge.

Hyuk Mujin and Song Ilseom, their hands resting on their sword hilts as if ready to draw at any moment, were no exception. Neither were Ju Hwaran and Namho, who had been watching ahead with tense faces.
There was one exception: Sama Pyo, who had rejoined the Fire Dragon Pavilion half a day earlier.
...That guy.
I wanted to ask him right then and there.
Why hadn’t he said a word all this time?
How could he stay so composed, as if he’d known what to expect, while everyone else had been tense and wary?
But I didn’t ask. I couldn’t.
I watched Sama Pyo riding alongside the still-dejected Taishan, my gaze tangled with conflicting thoughts, then quietly turned away.
If Sama Pyo and Taishan are up to something on Sima Gong’s secret orders, and those orders are connected to Dark Heaven... what would you do?
Hell if I know. What should I do?
With that question still unanswered in my heart, I silently tightened my grip on the reins.
Unlike the reality before me, the dawn spreading from the east was bathing the Great Snow Mountain in light.
“Guh... ack.”
The man’s lips trembled as he vomited a mouthful of dark red blood.
His Daoist robe, once as white as snow, had long since been stained with blood and dust. His unfocused eyes could barely make out what was in front of him.
Yet he didn’t let go of the sword in his hand. He couldn’t.
Not yet. It isn’t over.
His ever-reliable Senior Brother, his tiger-like Senior Martial Uncle, and the young Junior Sister he’d thought of as a niece were no longer by his side.
They were dead. Every last one of them.
Some had been beheaded. Some had been pierced through the heart. Others had been torn apart so completely that not a trace remained.
That was why he had to get up. He had to take revenge.
Crunch.
Blood welled between his teeth as he clenched them with all his strength.
His senses had gone numb. He couldn’t even smell the blood.
He swallowed his own blood as though it were the water of life.
Forcing his unsteady legs beneath him, he swung the beloved sword his Master and his sect had bestowed upon him at the enemy before him.
With more desperation than ever. With the last scrap of strength he had left.
“Ugh. Aaargh!”
He brought the sword down with a shout so fierce that the veins stood out in his neck. At that moment, a strange sensation seized him.
Shhh.
It was as if time had stopped.
The air against his skin, the wind blowing from somewhere, even the sword blade descending at the motion of his hand—
Everything slowed. Everything grew clear.
This is...
The man shuddered.
In all his thirty-some years of life, he had felt this sensation only once before.
On the day he’d finally reached the Peak realm after grueling training, just before enlightenment came to him.
No-self.
The moment of insight every martial artist longed for: a brief instant in which they forgot even their own existence and advanced toward a higher realm.
Ah. Aah.
His eyes trembled.
His focus returned. In his now-clear vision, he saw a middle-aged man trapped in the slowed flow of time.
No—a monster who had slaughtered more than a hundred members of his sect single-handedly.
But not anymore.
Only moments ago, the monster had moved too fast for his eyes to follow. Now it stood frozen, unable to move, while his sword descended toward the crown of its head.
Die.
The man was certain.
This enlightenment had made his martial might advance by leaps and bounds.
He had broken through the wall that had held him back for so long. His Demon-Subduing Sword had finally reached eight-tenths mastery, and it would cut the monster down.
Then, in the next instant—
Whoosh! Clack.
The monster shot out a hand like a streak of light and seized the blade.
Only then did the man understand.
It had all been a delusion.
Time hadn’t slowed. Only he had.
Crack!
His beloved sword shattered, and the sorrowful dream broke with it. The monster’s smile filled his vacant gaze.
“That was quite a sight, watching you flail around by yourself. What do you say? Shall I give you one more chance, just in case?”
The man stared blankly at the enemy before him.
Up close, the monster looked like an utterly ordinary middle-aged man—apart from the blood covering him from head to toe.
Maybe that was why, even after feeling the truth of what he was down to his bones, even knowing that he was beyond reason, the man forced his voice out.
“Why... why are you doing this?”
“What?”
The monster—no, the middle-aged man—furrowed his brow.
“Why am I doing this? What a pathetic question. You might as well ask a fisherman why he catches fish.”
“And this is all your own fault. I told you I’d spare you for now if you surrendered quietly, but you had to... Honestly, those damned Daoist bastards don’t listen until they see blood.”
The middle-aged man sighed deeply and gave him a pitying look.
“From the looks of it, I won’t get the answer I want from you either.”
Already on the threshold of his final rally, the man answered faintly.
“Heaven... Heaven will punish you.”
“What? Heaven’s punishment? Did you just say Heaven’s punishment?”
The middle-aged man’s eyes widened. Then he began to chuckle. In an instant, his hand blurred and pierced the man’s chest.
Crack!
His back arched as bone and flesh were crushed. Through his darkening vision, he saw a few wisps of cloud drifting across the sky as if nothing had happened.
Then a voice pierced his ears for the last time.
“Can you see it? The new Heaven.”
Crunch. Thud!
The hand pulled free, and his body crumpled.
The middle-aged man stepped on the corpse of the Kongtong Sword Dragon, the Kongtong Sect’s foremost young prodigy, then turned toward the vast mountain range in the distance.
The Great Snow Mountain.
Soon it would be stained red with countless streams of blood. For now, it shone dazzlingly in the rising sunlight.
“Now, let’s have some fun.”
The middle-aged man smiled. Behind him, a tremendous rumble began to shake the earth.
